title: Study questions: moving molecules across membranes
text: Study questions in the style of the written exam. Write your answer first (a few sentences, or a labelled sketch where it helps), then compare with the model answer. Each question is tagged with its learning outcome (ELO). Questions tagged [VG] are of the kind used for the higher grade: predict, compare, explain an unexpected result or design an experiment.

title: Study questions: moving molecules across membranes
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Which kinds of molecules cross a pure lipid bilayer, and which do not? Explain the rule with the structure of the bilayer, and give one example of each kind. [ELO 2]






Model answer





The middle of the bilayer is a hydrophobic layer of fatty acid tails. A molecule crosses only if it can leave water and dissolve in this layer. Small hydrophobic molecules cross fast (O₂, CO₂, steroid hormones). Small uncharged polar molecules cross more slowly (water, urea). Larger polar molecules cross very slowly (glucose). Ions practically do not cross (Na⁺, K⁺), because their charge and their shell of water make it very costly to enter the oily core; a pure bilayer is about 10⁹ times more permeable to water than to Na⁺ or K⁺. Large and charged molecules (ATP, proteins) do not cross. Everything that does not cross fast enough needs a transport protein.




2. Give the typical concentrations of Na⁺, K⁺ and Ca²⁺ inside and outside a mammalian cell. Explain why these differences are called a steady state and not an equilibrium. [ELO 2]






Model answer





Na⁺: about 12 mM inside, 145 mM outside. K⁺: about 140 mM inside, 5 mM outside. Ca²⁺: about 100 nM (0.0001 mM) free in the cytosol, about 2 mM outside. At equilibrium there would be no net movement and no energy needed. Here ions leak down their gradients all the time, and pumps (Na⁺/K⁺ pump, Ca²⁺ pumps) spend ATP all the time to move them back. The concentrations stay constant only because leak and pumping balance: a steady state. If ATP runs out, the gradients disappear.




3. Compare a channel and a transporter. Give at least four differences. [ELO 2]






Model answer














Channel
Transporter




How it works
water-filled pore, open to both sides at once when open
binds the solute; alternating access, open to one side at a time


Speed
up to about 10⁸ ions/s
about 10²–10⁴ molecules/s


Direction
only down the (electro)chemical gradient
passive, or active when coupled to ATP or another gradient


Kinetics
rate rises with the gradient, practically no saturation
saturates (Vmax, Km) like an enzyme


Control
gated (opens and closes)
regulated, e.g. by number of transporters in the membrane



Examples: K⁺ channel; GLUT1, SGLT1, Na⁺/K⁺ pump.




4. Describe the alternating-access mechanism of a uniporter such as GLUT1. Why can GLUT1 not move glucose against its gradient? [ELO 2]






Model answer





The transporter has a glucose-binding site in the middle of the membrane. (1) It is open to the outside; glucose binds. (2) The outer gate closes, so glucose is trapped (occluded). (3) The protein opens to the inside and glucose is released. (4) The empty transporter returns to the outward-open shape. The binding site is never open to both sides at once. Each step is reversible and no energy is put in, so the cycle runs equally well in both directions. The net flow is therefore from the side with more glucose to the side with less: always downhill.




5. Explain the difference between primary and secondary active transport. Use the Na⁺/K⁺ pump and SGLT1 as examples. [ELO 2]






Model answer





In primary active transport the transport protein uses energy directly, usually by hydrolysing ATP. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump hydrolyses one ATP per cycle to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, against both gradients. In secondary active transport the protein uses the energy stored in another ion gradient, which a primary pump made. SGLT1 lets 2 Na⁺ flow into the cell, down their electrochemical gradient, and couples this to moving 1 glucose into the cell, even against the glucose gradient. SGLT1 uses no ATP itself, but if the Na⁺/K⁺ pump stops, the Na⁺ gradient runs down and SGLT1 stops too.




6. Describe the reaction cycle of the Na⁺/K⁺ pump in four steps. Why is it called electrogenic? [ELO 2]






Model answer






Open to the cytosol, high affinity for Na⁺: 3 Na⁺ bind. (2) ATP phosphorylates an aspartate in the pump; the pump switches to the outward-open shape with low Na⁺ affinity and releases 3 Na⁺ outside. (3) 2 K⁺ bind from the outside; this triggers removal of the phosphate. (4) The pump returns to the inward-open shape and releases 2 K⁺ into the cytosol. Each cycle moves 3 positive charges out and 2 in, so one net positive charge leaves the cell: the pump produces a small electric current and is electrogenic.





7. Name three families of ATP-driven pumps and give one example and one function for each. Which related machine runs “backwards”, and what does it make? [ELO 2] [ELO 5]






Model answer





P-type pumps (phosphorylate themselves): the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, which keeps Na⁺ low and K⁺ high in the cell; the Ca²⁺ pumps (in the plasma membrane and SERCA in the ER), which keep cytosolic Ca²⁺ at about 100 nM. V-type pumps: the H⁺ pump that acidifies lysosomes (pH 4.5–5) and endosomes. ABC transporters: P-glycoprotein, which exports drugs and other hydrophobic molecules from cells. The F-type ATP synthase in the inner mitochondrial membrane is built like a V-type pump but runs in reverse: H⁺ flowing down its gradient into the matrix drives the synthesis of ATP.




8. Draw a gut epithelial cell and show how glucose is moved from the gut lumen to the blood. Label the apical and basolateral membranes, the transporters, the direction of each flow, and the tight junctions. [ELO 2]






Model answer





Your sketch should show: apical membrane (with microvilli) facing the lumen, carrying SGLT1: 2 Na⁺ + 1 glucose into the cell. Basolateral membrane facing the blood, carrying GLUT2: glucose out of the cell, down its gradient; and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, using ATP. Tight junctions near the apical end between neighbouring cells, sealing the gap so glucose cannot leak back, and keeping apical and basolateral proteins in their own membrane. Glucose concentration in the cell is high enough to drive it out through GLUT2.




9. What are aquaporins, and how do cells move water if no pump for water exists? [ELO 2]






Model answer





Aquaporins are water channels: four subunits, each with a narrow pore through which water passes in single file, up to about 10⁹ molecules per second. The pore excludes ions, including H⁺, so gradients are not lost. Water always moves passively by osmosis, towards the side with the higher concentration of dissolved particles. Cells therefore move water by moving solutes first (for example Na⁺ with pumps and transporters); water follows through aquaporins. In the kidney collecting duct, vasopressin causes AQP2 to be inserted into the membrane, so more water is taken back.

title: Study questions: moving molecules across membranes
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
10. [VG] Researchers treat isolated intestinal epithelium with ouabain on the blood side. Predict what happens over the next hour to (a) Na⁺ inside the cells, (b) glucose uptake from the lumen, and (c) glucose transport into the blood. Explain each step. What result would you expect if ouabain were added only on the lumen side? [ELO 2]






Model answer





Ouabain blocks the Na⁺/K⁺ pump from the extracellular side; in epithelial cells the pump is in the basolateral membrane, so ouabain on the blood side reaches it. (a) Na⁺ leaks in (including through SGLT1) but is no longer pumped out: Na⁺ inside rises and K⁺ falls; the membrane potential also becomes less negative. (b) SGLT1 depends on the inward Na⁺ gradient (and the negative inside). As the gradient runs down, glucose uptake from the lumen falls, and SGLT1 can no longer concentrate glucose. (c) Less glucose reaches the cell, so less glucose crosses to the blood through GLUT2, even though GLUT2 itself is not blocked. On the lumen side only, ouabain would have little or no effect at first, because there are no pumps in the apical membrane and tight junctions stop the drug from reaching the basolateral side. This experiment shows both the coupling of secondary to primary active transport and the polarity of the epithelium.




11. [VG] A new protein, X, is suspected to be a transporter for the amino acid leucine. Design experiments to show (a) that leucine uptake depends on X, (b) that X itself is enough to transport leucine, and (c) whether X is a uniporter or a Na⁺-coupled symporter. [ELO 2] [ELO 1]






Model answer






Measure the initial rate of uptake of radiolabelled (or fluorescent) leucine at many concentrations in cells with X and in cells where X is knocked out (CRISPR) or knocked down, and in cells that overexpress X. If X is the transporter, uptake saturates (Vmax, Km), is lower without X and higher with more X, and is competed by unlabelled leucine but not by an unrelated molecule. (b) Purify X and reconstitute it in liposomes. Leucine should enter liposomes that contain X, but not empty liposomes; since nothing else is present, X is sufficient. (c) Repeat uptake with Na⁺ replaced by another cation (e.g. choline⁺ or K⁺) outside. A Na⁺-coupled symporter stops working (or slows strongly) without external Na⁺, and it can accumulate leucine above the outside concentration; in liposomes, uptake should depend on an imposed Na⁺ gradient. A uniporter works without Na⁺ and only brings the inside up to the outside concentration. Controls: same cell number, short time points (initial rates), cold or no-transporter background.





12. [VG] Explain how (a) digoxin makes the heart beat more strongly, and (b) P-glycoprotein can make a tumour resistant to several unrelated anticancer drugs at the same time. In each case, name the transport protein and say what it normally does. [ELO 2] [ELO 9]






Model answer






Digoxin partly blocks the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (normally: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP) in heart muscle cells. Na⁺ inside rises a little, so the Na⁺ gradient is smaller. The Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger, which normally uses Na⁺ flowing in to push Ca²⁺ out, therefore removes less Ca²⁺. More Ca²⁺ stays in the cell and is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so more Ca²⁺ is released at each beat and contraction is stronger. Because the pump is in every cell, too much digoxin is toxic, and the safe dose range is narrow. (b) P-glycoprotein (ABCB1) is an ABC transporter that uses ATP to export hydrophobic molecules from cells; it normally protects tissues such as the gut, liver and the blood–brain barrier from toxins. Its binding cavity is large and accepts many different hydrophobic molecules. A cancer cell that makes a lot of P-glycoprotein pumps out several unrelated chemotherapy drugs, so their concentration inside the cell stays too low to kill it: multidrug resistance.

title: Quiz: membrane structure
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture Membrane structure. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. A student says: “Phospholipids form a bilayer because their tails attract each other strongly.” What is the main driving force instead? [ELO 2]






Hint





Think about \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\). Whose entropy changes when tails come together?









Answer





The hydrophobic effect. A hydrocarbon tail in water forces the water molecules around it into an ordered cage (low entropy). When tails come together, most of this water is released, so the entropy of the water rises. The large positive \(\Delta S\) makes \(\Delta G\) negative, so assembly is spontaneous. Attractions between tails (van der Waals contacts) help, but they are not the main force.




Q2. Rank these membranes from least to most fluid at 25 °C: (a) tails of 18 carbons, all saturated; (b) tails of 18 carbons, each with one cis double bond; (c) tails of 14 carbons, all saturated. [ELO 2]






Hint





What reduces the contact between neighbouring tails?









Answer





(a) < (c) < (b) is the expected order. Long, straight, saturated tails (a) pack most tightly. Shorter tails (c) have less contact, so they are more fluid. A cis double bond (b) puts a kink in every tail, which disturbs packing strongly, so (b) is the most fluid. (For pure lipids: 18:0 PC melts at about 55 °C, 14:0 PC at about 24 °C, 18:1 PC far below 0 °C.)




Q3. Cholesterol is often called a “fluidity buffer”. What does it do at 37 °C, and what does it do in the cold? [ELO 2]






Hint





Its rigid ring plate sits next to the first part of the tails.









Answer





At 37 °C the rigid rings stiffen the tails near the head groups, so the membrane becomes less fluid and less leaky to small water-soluble molecules. In the cold, cholesterol gets between the tails and stops them from packing into a gel, so the membrane stays fluid instead of freezing. It moves fluidity towards the middle in both cases.




Q4. Why is phosphatidylserine (PS) found almost only in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane, and what does it mean when PS appears on the outside? [ELO 2]






Hint





Two kinds of enzyme: one uses ATP, one does not.









Answer





Spontaneous flip-flop is very slow, and flippases (P-type ATPases) use ATP to move any PS that reaches the outer leaflet back inside. When a scramblase is switched on (and, in apoptosis, the flippase is switched off by caspases), lipids mix and PS appears on the outside. On a dying cell it is an “eat me” signal for phagocytes. On activated platelets it forms a surface on which clotting factors assemble.




Q5. A protein comes off a membrane when you wash it with 1 M NaCl. Is it an integral or a peripheral protein? What would you need to release an integral protein? [ELO 2]






Hint





High salt breaks ionic interactions. What holds an integral protein in the bilayer?









Answer





It is a peripheral protein: it was held by ionic and other non-covalent contacts with head groups or other proteins, and high salt (or high pH) breaks them while the bilayer stays intact. An integral protein has hydrophobic segments inside the bilayer, so you need a detergent to dissolve the bilayer and coat those segments.




Q6. A hydropathy plot of a new protein of 420 amino acids shows one broad peak above the threshold near the N-terminus (residues 8–27) and none elsewhere. What is your best prediction, and what is the main alternative? [ELO 2]






Hint





What else is a stretch of hydrophobic residues at the very start of a protein? (You will meet it in the protein-sorting lectures.)









Answer





About 20 hydrophobic residues fit one transmembrane α-helix, so the best prediction is a single-pass membrane protein anchored near its N-terminus. The main alternative is that the hydrophobic stretch is an ER signal sequence, which is cut off after the protein enters the ER, giving a soluble secreted protein. A hydropathy plot is a prediction; check it, for example by testing whether the mature protein needs detergent to be released from membranes.




Q7. In a FRAP experiment on a GFP-tagged membrane protein, the fluorescence in the bleached spot comes back to only 50 % of the starting level. What does this tell you? [ELO 1] [ELO 2]






Hint





Where do the molecules that refill the spot come from?









Answer





Recovery happens when unbleached molecules diffuse into the spot. Here about half of the protein is mobile and half is immobile on the time scale of the experiment: those molecules stay where they are, for example because they are bound to the cortical cytoskeleton, to other proteins or to a neighbouring cell. The speed of recovery (t½) of the mobile half gives its diffusion coefficient.




Q8. The ionisable lipid in a lipid nanoparticle has a pKa of about 6.5. Explain why this pKa suits both the time in blood and the time in the endosome. [ELO 2]






Hint





Compare pH 7.4 (blood) and pH 5–6 (late endosome) with the pKa.









Answer





At pH 7.4, above the pKa, most of the amine is uncharged, so the particle surface is close to neutral: fewer interactions with blood proteins and cell membranes, and less toxicity. In the endosome the pH falls to 5–6, below the pKa, so the lipid becomes positively charged. It then pairs with negatively charged lipids of the endosome membrane, disturbs that membrane, and lets some RNA escape into the cytosol. (During manufacture at pH 4 the positive charge is what binds the negative RNA.)

title: Membrane structure
section: About this lecture

title: Membrane structure
section: The question: a barrier that flows
text:
The question: a barrier that flows







Human blood, scanning EM: red blood cells (discs), white blood cells (rough surface), platelets (small).


A red blood cell is about 8 µm wide. Many capillaries are only about 3–5 µm wide. The cell folds to squeeze through, again and again during its 120-day life.
Its plasma membrane is only about 5 nm thick: two layers of lipid molecules.
Yet it never tears open, and it keeps ions and haemoglobin inside.

How can a film two molecules thick be both a tight barrier and a liquid that flows?


Look at these red blood cells in a scanning electron microscope. They are flat discs, about eight micrometres across, with a dip in the middle. The rough round cells are white blood cells, and the small fragments are platelets. A red blood cell has no nucleus and no internal membranes; it is little more than a bag of haemoglobin wrapped in a plasma membrane. That membrane is only about five nanometres thick, one thousandth of a micrometre times five, yet it holds. Every time the cell passes through a narrow capillary it bends and folds, and then springs back. If the membrane were a solid sheet, like a plastic film, it would crack. If it were simply oil, it would break up. Today we will see how a membrane can be both: a liquid in its own plane, and a tight barrier across it. Red blood cells are also where much of membrane biology started, because they are easy to get and have only one membrane. We will meet them again three times today: in the recap, in freeze-fracture images and in blood groups.

title: Membrane structure
section: Recap, and one step further: why lipids self-assemble
text:
Recap, and one step further: why lipids self-assemble


Recap: membrane lipids are amphipathic: a polar head and two hydrophobic tails. In water they form a bilayer, tails inside.
Why? A tail alone forces water molecules into an ordered cage. Tails that come together free that water: the entropy of water rises, so ΔG < 0. This is the hydrophobic effect.
A bilayer edge would expose tails to water, so a bilayer closes on itself into a sealed compartment, and a small tear reseals.


This is the one recap slide. You know from biochemistry that membrane lipids are amphipathic, and that they form a bilayer in water. Now use your chemistry to ask why. You might think that the tails attract each other strongly. They do a little, but that is not the main force. When a hydrocarbon tail sits in water, the water molecules next to it cannot form hydrogen bonds with it, so they line up in an ordered cage around it. Ordered water means low entropy. When many tails come together, most of those water molecules are released into the bulk liquid, and their entropy rises. In ΔG equals ΔH minus T times ΔS, the large positive ΔS makes ΔG negative, so assembly is spontaneous. We call this the hydrophobic effect. It explains three things we need. Bilayers form without any enzyme. They have no free edges, because an edge would expose tails to water, so they close into sealed compartments. And a small hole closes again by itself. Historical note: in 1925 Gorter and Grendel extracted the lipids from red blood cells and found they covered twice the cell’s surface: the first hint of a bilayer.

title: Membrane structure
section: Three classes of membrane lipid
text:
Three classes of membrane lipid


Glycerophospholipids (PC, PE, PS, PI): glycerol backbone, two fatty-acid tails. Most membrane lipid.
Sphingolipids: sphingosine backbone. Sphingomyelin; glycolipids carry sugars and face the outside.
Cholesterol: a rigid ring plate with a small OH head. In the plasma membrane, about one for every phospholipid.


A real membrane contains hundreds of different lipid species, but three classes cover most of them. The glycerophospholipids are built on glycerol, which carries two fatty-acid tails and a phosphate. The group on the phosphate gives the name: choline gives phosphatidylcholine, PC, the most common one; serine gives phosphatidylserine, PS, which has a net negative charge; ethanolamine gives PE, and inositol gives PI, which the cell uses for signalling, as you will see in the signalling lectures. The sphingolipids are built on sphingosine, an amino alcohol that already carries one long tail; a second fatty acid is attached. Their tails are usually long and saturated, so they pack tightly. Sphingomyelin has the same choline-phosphate head as PC. If the head is a chain of sugars instead, the lipid is a glycolipid; these are always on the outside of the cell. The third class is the sterols, which in animal cells means cholesterol. It is small and rigid, with a tiny polar OH head. The plasma membrane has a lot of it, almost one cholesterol molecule per phospholipid, while the ER has very little. So each organelle membrane has its own lipid mixture.

title: Membrane structure
section: A bilayer is a two-dimensional liquid
text:
A bilayer is a two-dimensional liquid







Molecular dynamics simulation of a PC bilayer. Red and white: water; cyan: lipid tails.


About 5 nm thick; the hydrophobic core is about 3 nm.
The tails are disordered and move all the time.
A lipid swaps places with its neighbour about 10⁷ times per second, so it moves about 2 µm in 1 s within its own leaflet (lateral diffusion).
It also spins about its long axis and flexes its tails.
But moving to the other leaflet (flip-flop) is very rare: about once a month for a phospholipid. The polar head would have to cross the oily core.
So: liquid in the plane, a barrier across it.



This image is not a micrograph. It is one frame from a computer simulation, called molecular dynamics, in which the forces between every atom are calculated and the molecules are allowed to move. The red and white balls at top and bottom are water. The cyan lines are the lipid tails, and the head groups sit at the two water surfaces. Notice how disordered the tails are: they are not straight sticks like in textbook cartoons, but bend and wriggle all the time. Experiments agree with simulations: a lipid changes place with its neighbour about ten million times per second, and it can travel about two micrometres, the length of a bacterium, in one second. It also spins about its long axis and its tails flex. What it almost never does is move to the other leaflet. For that, the charged head group would have to pass through three nanometres of hydrocarbon, which costs a lot of energy. A phospholipid flips on its own less than about once a month. This answers part of our question: in the plane the membrane is a liquid that can flow and bend, but across it, it is a strong barrier.

title: Membrane structure
section: What sets membrane fluidity?
text:
What sets membrane fluidity?


Shorter tails and cis double bonds (kinks) mean less contact between tails: more fluid.
Cholesterol stiffens the tails near the heads (less fluid, less leaky at 37 °C), but stops them freezing in the cold: a fluidity buffer.
Cells adjust their lipids to keep fluidity right: bacteria and fish grown in the cold make more unsaturated tails.


Fluidity is not fixed; it depends on how well the tails pack. Long straight tails touch along their whole length, so van der Waals contacts hold them together and the membrane is stiffer. Short tails touch less. A cis double bond puts a permanent kink in a tail, about thirty degrees, so kinked tails cannot pack tightly and the membrane is more fluid. That is the same reason olive oil is liquid and butter is solid at room temperature. Temperature works in the same direction as for any liquid: cool a pure lipid bilayer and at a certain temperature it freezes into an ordered gel. Cholesterol has two effects. At body temperature its rigid rings sit next to the first part of the tails and stiffen them, so the membrane becomes less fluid and less leaky to small water-soluble molecules. In the cold, it gets between tails and stops them from crystallising, so the membrane does not freeze. Living cells keep their fluidity in a working range. Bacteria grown in the cold make more unsaturated fatty acids, and fish in cold water do the same. Membrane proteins, such as transporters, need this fluidity to work.

title: Membrane structure
section: Two leaflets, two compositions: lipid asymmetry
text:
Two leaflets, two compositions: lipid asymmetry


Outer leaflet: mostly PC, sphingomyelin, glycolipids. Inner leaflet: PS, PE, PI.
Flippases use ATP to keep PS inside. Scramblases mix the leaflets without ATP.
Exposed PS means “eat me” (dying cells, more in the cell-death lectures) and “clot here” (activated platelets).


The two leaflets of the plasma membrane have different lipids. The outer leaflet is rich in PC, sphingomyelin and glycolipids; the inner leaflet holds almost all the PS and most of the PE and PI. Because flip-flop is so slow, this difference is stable, but the cell also maintains it actively. Flippases are P-type ATPases: they use ATP to pick up PS and PE from the outer leaflet and move them to the inner one. Scramblases do not use energy; when they are switched on they let lipids move both ways, so the asymmetry is lost. Why should you care? First, the negative PS on the inner face attracts positively charged regions of proteins, so it helps signalling proteins find the membrane. Second, PS on the outside is a signal. When a cell dies by apoptosis, enzymes called caspases switch the flippase off and a scramblase on, so PS appears on the surface, and phagocytes recognise it as “eat me”. You will see this again in the cell-death lectures. In activated platelets, calcium switches on a scramblase; the exposed PS forms a surface on which clotting factors assemble. Patients who lack this scramblase have a bleeding disorder.

title: Membrane structure
section: Bending a membrane
text:
Bending a membrane


A flat bilayer is the easy shape. Vesicles, tubules and the folds of the ER and mitochondria need curvature.
Cells bend membranes with cone-shaped lipids, curved proteins and wedges; for vesicles, also with protein coats (see the vesicle traffic lectures).


Cells are full of curved membranes: small vesicles about fifty nanometres across, tubules of the ER, the folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane. A bilayer prefers to be flat, so curvature costs energy, and the cell pays it in three main ways. First, lipid shape. PC is roughly a cylinder: its head is as wide as its tails, so it packs flat. PE has a small head and is cone-shaped; a lysolipid, with one tail removed, is an inverted cone. If one leaflet collects cone-shaped lipids, it curves. Second, proteins with a curved shape. BAR-domain proteins are banana-shaped dimers with positive charges on their curved face; they bind negatively charged lipids and hold the membrane in their shape. Third, wedges: some proteins push an amphipathic helix, which has one oily face, in among the head groups of one leaflet only. That leaflet gets wider than the other, and the membrane bends. In the vesicle traffic lectures you will see protein coats, such as clathrin, which combine these tricks to pull a vesicle out of a membrane. This is one slide of a big field; the point is that shape is made, not given.

title: Membrane structure
section: How proteins sit in a membrane
text:
How proteins sit in a membrane


Integral: cross the bilayer once (single-pass) or many times (multi-pass), as α-helices or a β-barrel.
Lipid-anchored: a covalently attached fatty acid or prenyl group (cytosol side) or a GPI anchor (outside).
Peripheral: bound to other proteins or to head groups; washed off with salt or a change in pH.


About a third of human genes encode membrane proteins, and more than half of all drug targets are membrane proteins, so this slide matters. There are three ways to be attached. Integral proteins cross the bilayer. A single-pass protein, such as many receptors, crosses once with one alpha-helix; a multi-pass protein crosses many times, like the seven-helix receptors you will meet in signalling. In the outer membranes of bacteria, mitochondria and chloroplasts, proteins cross instead as a beta-barrel. To remove an integral protein you must dissolve the bilayer with detergent. Lipid-anchored proteins do not cross the membrane at all: a lipid chain, attached covalently to the protein, dips into one leaflet. On the cytosolic side the anchor is a fatty acid such as myristate or palmitate, or a prenyl group; Ras, a protein you will meet in signalling and cancer, is held this way. On the outside the anchor is GPI, a glycolipid made in the ER. Peripheral proteins bind by non-covalent contacts to other proteins or to head groups, so a high-salt or high-pH wash removes them while the membrane stays intact.

title: Membrane structure
section: Crossing the bilayer: α-helix or β-barrel
text:
Crossing the bilayer: α-helix or β-barrel



Aquaporin-1 (PDB 1J4N): bundles of α-helices. Two chains in blue and red.


Sucrose porin from Salmonella (PDB 1A0S): an 18-strand β-barrel.


Inside the bilayer there is no water to bond with the peptide backbone (its C=O and N–H groups).
An α-helix bonds its backbone to itself. About 20 hydrophobic amino acids span the 3 nm core.
A β-barrel closes a sheet into a tube, so every strand has neighbours to bond with. Hydrophobic side chains face the lipids; the inside can be a water-filled pore.



Why do membrane proteins only use two shapes to cross the bilayer? The protein backbone has polar groups: every peptide bond has a C equals O and an N–H. In water these make hydrogen bonds with water molecules. In the hydrocarbon core of the bilayer there is no water, so an unpaired backbone group would cost a lot of energy. An alpha-helix solves this by bonding each peptide group to the one four residues further along. The side chains point outwards, and if they are hydrophobic, such as leucine, isoleucine, valine and phenylalanine, the helix sits happily among the lipid tails. Each residue adds 0.15 nanometres, so about twenty residues span the three-nanometre core. On the left is aquaporin, the water channel of red blood cells and kidney: each chain is a bundle of six such helices. A beta-strand cannot satisfy its own backbone, but a beta-sheet rolled up into a closed barrel can: every strand bonds to its two neighbours. Side chains alternate, so every other one faces the lipids and the others face the inside, which is often a water-filled pore, as in this porin. You will see much more of these structures in the transport and ion channel lectures.

title: Membrane structure
section: Predicting transmembrane helices: hydropathy plots
text:
Predicting transmembrane helices: hydropathy plots


Give each amino acid a hydropathy score (e.g. Ile +4.5, Leu +3.8, Arg −4.5). Slide a window of about 19 residues along the sequence and plot the average.
A peak of about 20 residues above the threshold predicts one transmembrane α-helix.
Prediction, not proof: β-barrels and short or partly polar helices are missed. Test with structures and topology experiments.


From the last slide follows a simple rule: a stretch of about twenty hydrophobic amino acids is probably a transmembrane helix. A hydropathy plot finds such stretches from the sequence alone. Each amino acid gets a score for how much it prefers oil over water; in the common Kyte–Doolittle scale isoleucine scores plus 4.5, leucine plus 3.8, and arginine minus 4.5. A computer takes a window of about nineteen residues, averages their scores, plots the value at the window centre, moves one residue on, and repeats. Short hydrophobic patches average out, but a stretch of twenty hydrophobic residues gives a broad peak. With this window, peaks above about 1.6 usually mean a transmembrane helix. On the left, a protein with one peak is single-pass, like glycophorin of the red blood cell. On the right, seven peaks suggest seven transmembrane helices, the pattern of bacteriorhodopsin and of the G-protein-coupled receptors. The curves here are illustrative. Be critical: the method misses beta-barrels, whose strands are short and alternate polar and nonpolar, and it can be fooled by helices that line a water-filled pore. Modern tools, and AlphaFold, do better, but the idea is the same.

title: Membrane structure
section: Getting membrane proteins out: detergents
text:
Getting membrane proteins out: detergents


A detergent has one tail and a large head: it forms small micelles, not bilayers.
It replaces the lipids around the protein’s hydrophobic belt, so the protein becomes soluble in water.
Choose the detergent for the job: SDS to unfold and separate by size; mild detergents to purify a working protein (for activity, structure, drugs).


You cannot purify a membrane protein in plain buffer: its hydrophobic belt would make it clump and precipitate. Detergents solve this. A detergent is a small amphipathic molecule with a single tail and a relatively big head, so it is cone-shaped and packs into small spherical micelles rather than bilayers. Above a certain concentration, called the critical micelle concentration, detergent molecules enter the bilayer, break it up into mixed micelles of lipid and detergent, and coat the hydrophobic surface of each membrane protein. The protein is now a soluble protein–detergent complex. Detergents differ. SDS, which you know from SDS-PAGE, is charged and strong: it binds all along the polypeptide and unfolds it, which is what you want to separate proteins by size, but the protein no longer works. Mild, uncharged detergents such as Triton X-100 or dodecyl maltoside, DDM, coat the hydrophobic belt but leave the folded structure alone. That is how membrane proteins are purified for activity tests and for cryo-EM structures, including structures of drug targets such as receptors and channels. The same mild detergents are used to permeabilise cells for immunofluorescence.

title: Membrane structure
section: How do we know? Membrane proteins move
text:
How do we know? Membrane proteins move


Cell fusion (1970): after fusion, mouse and human surface proteins mixed in about 40 min at 37 °C, but not in the cold. Proteins diffuse in the membrane.
FRAP: bleach the fluorescent molecules in a spot with a laser and watch others diffuse back in. The speed gives the diffusion coefficient; the part that never recovers is immobile (held by the cytoskeleton or other proteins).


Two experiments convinced people that membrane proteins move. In 1970 Larry Frye and Michael Edidin fused a mouse cell with a human cell, using a virus that makes membranes fuse. They labelled mouse surface proteins with a green antibody and human proteins with a red one. Right after fusion, each colour stayed on its own half of the hybrid cell. Forty minutes later at 37 degrees, the colours were completely mixed. In the cold the mixing did not happen, and drugs that block protein synthesis or ATP production did not stop it, so this was diffusion, not new proteins. The modern method is FRAP, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching. You label a protein or lipid, for example as a GFP fusion, then use a strong laser to bleach a small spot. The fluorescence in the spot comes back as unbleached molecules diffuse in from around. How fast it recovers gives the diffusion coefficient. Typical membrane proteins diffuse ten to a hundred times more slowly than lipids. Often the recovery stops below the starting level: that fraction of the protein is immobile, tied to the cytoskeleton or to other cells.

title: Membrane structure
section: How do we know? Freeze-fracture EM shows proteins inside the bilayer
text:
How do we know? Freeze-fracture EM shows proteins inside the bilayer









Freeze-fracture replica of the plasma membrane of baker’s yeast. Each small bump is a particle, mostly integral proteins; the long grooves are folds of the membrane. Scale bar (top) 0.1 µm.


How do we know that proteins sit inside the bilayer and do not just coat its surface? The answer came from freeze-fracture electron microscopy in the 1960s and 70s. A cell is frozen very quickly and then cracked with a cold knife. The crack follows the path of least resistance, and in a frozen membrane that is the plane between the two leaflets, where only weak contacts between tail ends hold them together. So the bilayer splits into two halves, and you look at the inside face of each half. Platinum is evaporated from an angle, which shadows the bumps, and the cell material is dissolved away; the thin metal copy, the replica, is viewed in the transmission electron microscope. Pure lipid bilayers give smooth faces. Real membranes are covered in particles about eight to ten nanometres across, and the number of particles goes up and down with the amount of protein in the membrane. These particles are integral membrane proteins. Most stay with the cytosolic half, the P face, leaving pits in the E face. The image shows the yeast plasma membrane, crowded with particles. This was direct evidence for the fluid mosaic model of Singer and Nicolson, 1972.

title: Membrane structure
section: Not a uniform sea: membrane domains
text:
Not a uniform sea: membrane domains


Lipid rafts: sphingolipid- and cholesterol-rich nano-domains may gather some proteins for signalling. Honest caveat: they are too small and short-lived to see directly in living cells, and early evidence (detergent-resistant membranes) was weak.
Fences: in epithelia, the tight junction keeps apical and basolateral membranes apart. The cortical cytoskeleton under the membrane also slows diffusion.


The fluid mosaic model is right, but the membrane is not a perfectly mixed sea. Two kinds of domain are worth knowing. The first is the lipid raft. In artificial membranes, sphingomyelin and cholesterol separate from unsaturated PC into a thicker, more ordered phase. Rafts are thought to be the cell’s version: small patches that gather GPI-anchored proteins and some signalling proteins. Be careful. Early evidence came from the fact that some membrane fractions do not dissolve in cold Triton X-100, but the detergent itself can create such domains. In living cells, rafts, if they exist, are smaller than about two hundred nanometres and last less than a second, so they are hard to see directly. The second kind of domain is clear and important. In an epithelium, the tight junction seals neighbouring cells together near the top, and it also acts as a fence: proteins and outer-leaflet lipids cannot diffuse past it. So the apical membrane, facing the gut lumen for example, keeps different transporters from the basolateral membrane. The transport lecture uses this to explain how glucose crosses the gut wall.

title: Membrane structure
section: The sugar coat: glycocalyx and blood groups
text:
The sugar coat: glycocalyx and blood groups

Sugars on glycoproteins, glycolipids and proteoglycans form the glycocalyx, always on the outside (they are added in the ER and Golgi lumen). It protects the cell, holds water and is used in cell recognition.
ABO blood groups are the tips of sugar chains on red blood cells. One gene, three alleles: the enzyme adds GalNAc (A), galactose (B) or nothing (O).


The plasma has antibodies against the sugars you lack: the wrong transfusion makes the antibodies attack the donor’s red blood cells.

The outside of every cell is covered in carbohydrate: sugar chains on proteins and lipids, and large proteoglycans. Together they form the glycocalyx, the sugar coat. Remember topology from the cell tour: sugars are added in the lumen of the ER and Golgi, and the lumen side becomes the outside, so the sugars always face outwards. The coat protects the membrane, binds water, makes cells slippery, and carries information. White blood cells and blood vessel walls, for example, recognise each other’s sugars, through sugar-binding proteins called selectins, when white cells leave the blood to fight an infection. Blood groups are the classic example. Red blood cells carry a core chain ending in galactose with a fucose: the H antigen. One gene encodes a glycosyltransferase in the Golgi. The A version adds N-acetylgalactosamine, the B version adds galactose, and the O version is broken and adds nothing. An AB person has both enzymes. Because we meet similar sugars on gut bacteria, we make antibodies against the sugars we do not have. A type A person has anti-B antibodies, so blood from a type B donor would be attacked and the red cells destroyed.

title: Membrane structure
section: Why it matters: lipid nanoparticles deliver RNA
text:
Why it matters: lipid nanoparticles deliver RNA


RNA is large and negative: it cannot cross a bilayer, and enzymes in blood destroy it. An LNP packs it in lipid.
Patisiran (2018), the first siRNA drug: silences transthyretin mRNA in the liver (hereditary amyloidosis). The mRNA COVID-19 vaccines use the same four-lipid design.
Only a few per cent of the RNA escapes the endosome: how LNPs get in and out is in the endocytosis lecture.


Here the rules of today become medicine. RNA drugs face two problems: RNA is quickly destroyed by enzymes in blood, and a big, negatively charged molecule cannot cross the hydrophobic core of a membrane. A lipid nanoparticle solves both by hiding the RNA inside lipids. It has four components, and you can now explain each one. The ionisable lipid has an amine head whose charge depends on pH. At pH 4, when the particle is made, it is positive and binds the negative RNA. In blood at pH 7.4 it is almost neutral, which makes it less toxic. After the particle is taken up by endocytosis, the endosome becomes acidic, the lipid becomes positive again, pairs with negative lipids of the endosome membrane, and disturbs it, so some RNA escapes into the cytosol. The helper phospholipid, DSPC, and cholesterol give structure. The PEG-lipid controls particle size and stops particles sticking together. Patisiran, approved in 2018, carries a small interfering RNA that destroys transthyretin mRNA in liver cells; misfolded transthyretin causes a hereditary amyloidosis. The COVID-19 vaccines use the same design with mRNA. You meet vaccines again in Immunologi, and drug development in Kliniska prövningar och läkemedelsutveckling.

title: Membrane structure
section: Why it matters: liposomal doxorubicin (Doxil)
text:
Why it matters: liposomal doxorubicin (Doxil)


Doxorubicin blocks topoisomerase II and kills dividing cells, but damages the heart (dose-limiting).
In a rigid, PEG-coated liposome (approved 1995), it circulates for days. Tumour vessels are leaky (EPR effect), heart capillaries are tight: less heart damage, new side effect in the skin (hand–foot syndrome).
Caveat: EPR is strong in mouse tumours but varies a lot between human tumours; survival is similar to free drug.


Doxorubicin is an old and effective cancer drug. It inserts between DNA bases and traps topoisomerase II on cut DNA, which kills dividing cells. Its big problem is the heart: above a lifetime dose it damages heart muscle, even years later. Liposomal doxorubicin packs the drug into a liposome of about ninety nanometres, a small bilayer vesicle. The lipids are saturated phospholipid plus cholesterol, so the bilayer is stiff and the drug does not leak out. Inside, the drug is loaded with a gradient and forms a crystal. The outside carries a PEG coat that hides the particle from phagocytes, so it circulates for days instead of being cleared in minutes. Most normal capillaries, including those of the heart, have a tight wall, so the particle stays in the blood. Many tumour vessels have gaps of hundreds of nanometres and poor lymph drainage, so particles leak in and stay: the enhanced permeability and retention, or EPR, effect. In patients, Doxil causes much less heart damage. But be honest: EPR was found in fast-growing mouse tumours, it varies widely in human tumours, and in trials survival was similar to free doxorubicin. The gain is mainly safety. Clinical trials return in Kliniska prövningar och läkemedelsutveckling.

title: Membrane structure
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Membrane lipids self-assemble into a sealed bilayer because of the hydrophobic effect. The plasma membrane mixes glycerophospholipids, sphingolipids and cholesterol.
The bilayer is a two-dimensional liquid: fast lateral diffusion, rare flip-flop. Tail length, double bonds, cholesterol and temperature set its fluidity.
The two leaflets differ (asymmetry): flippases keep PS inside; scramblases expose it as an “eat me” or “clot here” signal.
Proteins are integral (α-helices or β-barrels; predicted from hydropathy plots; extracted with detergents), lipid-anchored or peripheral. FRAP, cell fusion and freeze-fracture EM show a fluid mosaic with domains and fences.
Drug carriers use the same rules: lipid nanoparticles for RNA, PEG-liposomes for doxorubicin.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 10.
Image credits: credits

Let us go back to the red blood cell that squeezes through a capillary. Its membrane is a bilayer that forms and reseals by itself because water pushes the tails together. It is a liquid in its own plane, so it can bend and flow, but polar molecules and ions cannot cross its oily core, so it is a barrier. The cell tunes its fluidity with tail length, double bonds and cholesterol, and it keeps the two leaflets different with flippases; when a cell dies or a platelet is activated, scramblases expose PS as a signal. Proteins sit in the membrane in a few defined ways, and the rules of the bilayer, twenty hydrophobic residues for a helix, explain how we can predict them and how detergents take them out. FRAP, cell fusion and freeze-fracture are the evidence for this fluid mosaic, with domains such as the region fenced off by tight junctions. Finally, the same rules let us build drug carriers. The next lecture asks the question this one leaves open: if the bilayer blocks ions and sugars, how do they get across? The answer is transporters and pumps.

title: Study questions: ion channels and membrane potential
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Compare ion channels and transporters with respect to (a) rate, (b) how the solute crosses, (c) whether they can move a solute against its gradient. [ELO 2]






Model answer






Rate: channels pass up to about 10⁸ ions per second; transporters move about 10²–10⁴ molecules per second. (b) A channel is a water-filled pore; when open, ions stream through without the protein changing shape for each ion. A transporter binds the solute, changes shape (alternating access) and releases it on the other side; it is never open to both sides at once. (c) Channels only allow passive flow down the electrochemical gradient. Transporters can be active: coupled to ATP hydrolysis (pumps) or to the downhill flow of another solute, they can move a solute uphill.





2. Describe the structure of the K⁺ channel selectivity filter and explain how it lets K⁺ through but keeps Na⁺ out. [ELO 2]






Model answer





Four identical subunits surround a central pore. Near the outer end the pore narrows into the selectivity filter, about 1.2 nm long, lined by the backbone carbonyl oxygens of a conserved sequence (TVGYG). In water, each ion is surrounded by water oxygens; to enter the narrow filter it must lose this water, which costs energy. The carbonyl oxygens are held rigidly at the distance at which they replace the water around a K⁺ ion, so the energy is paid back. Na⁺ is smaller; the oxygens are too far away to replace its water, so dehydration is not compensated and Na⁺ does not enter. The structure was solved by X-ray crystallography (MacKinnon, KcsA, 1998).




3. Name the three main ways a channel can be gated. For each, give one example and say what opens it. [ELO 2]






Model answer





Voltage-gated: e.g. the voltage-gated Na⁺ channel of nerve and muscle; a helix with positive charges (the voltage sensor) moves outwards when the membrane depolarises and opens the gate. Ligand-gated: e.g. the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the nerve–muscle junction; binding of two acetylcholine molecules opens a cation pore. Mechanically gated: e.g. Piezo channels; tension in the membrane flattens the channel’s blades and opens the pore (Piezo2 in touch, Piezo1 in sensing blood flow).




4. Derive the Nernst equation from the Gibbs energy for moving one mole of an ion with charge \(z\) from outside to inside a cell. [ELO 2]






Model answer





Chemical part: \(\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q\) with \(\Delta G^\circ = 0\) (same ion on both sides) and \(Q = c_\text{in}/c_\text{out}\), so \(RT\ln(c_\text{in}/c_\text{out})\). Electrical part: moving \(z\) moles of charge through the membrane potential \(V = V_\text{in} - V_\text{out}\) costs \(zFV\). Total: \(\Delta G = RT\ln(c_\text{in}/c_\text{out}) + zFV\). At equilibrium there is no net flow, so \(\Delta G = 0\), which gives \[E = \frac{RT}{zF}\ln\frac{c_\text{out}}{c_\text{in}}.\]




5. Calculate the equilibrium potentials for K⁺ (inside 140 mM, outside 5 mM) and Cl⁻ (inside 10 mM, outside 110 mM) at 37 °C. Explain the sign of each. [ELO 2]






Model answer





\(E_\text{K} = 26.7 \times \ln(5/140) = 26.7 \times (-3.33) \approx\) −89 mV. K⁺ is higher inside and tends to leave; the inside must be negative to hold the positive ion back.
\(E_\text{Cl} = \frac{26.7}{-1} \times \ln(110/10) = -26.7 \times 2.40 \approx\) −64 mV. Cl⁻ is higher outside and tends to enter; because it is negative, a negative inside repels it, so equilibrium is reached at a negative potential.




6. Explain how the resting membrane potential arises. Include the roles of the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, K⁺ leak channels and large intracellular anions. [ELO 2]






Model answer





The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, building high K⁺ inside and high Na⁺ outside (it also contributes a few mV directly, because it is electrogenic). The resting membrane has many open K⁺ leak channels and few open Na⁺ channels. K⁺ flows out down its concentration gradient; the large anions inside (proteins, phosphates, organic molecules) cannot follow. Each K⁺ that leaves adds a positive charge outside and leaves a negative charge inside, building a thin layer of charge at the membrane. The voltage grows until the electrical pull balances the concentration push, close to \(E_\text{K}\). The small Na⁺ leak makes it a bit less negative (about −70 mV): the resting potential is a permeability-weighted average (Goldman). Very few ions need to move (fewer than 1 in 10 000 of the K⁺ ions), so concentrations hardly change.




7. Describe the four phases of an action potential and which channels cause each. [ELO 2]






Model answer






A stimulus depolarises the membrane to threshold (about −55 mV). 2. Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open; Na⁺ rushes in, depolarising the membrane further and opening more Na⁺ channels (positive feedback); the voltage rises towards \(E_\text{Na}\) (peak about +35 mV). 3. Na⁺ channels inactivate and slower voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ flows out and the voltage falls. 4. Undershoot towards \(E_\text{K}\) while K⁺ channels are still open; inactivated Na⁺ channels cannot yet reopen (refractory period), so the spike travels in one direction. The whole spike lasts about 1–2 ms and moves very few ions; the pump restores the gradients over time.





8. Describe the patch-clamp method. What is a gigaseal, and what does a single-channel recording show? [ELO 1] [ELO 2]






Model answer





A glass pipette with a tip about 1 µm wide, filled with salt solution and containing an electrode, is pressed against a cell, and gentle suction is applied. The membrane seals to the glass with a resistance above 1 GΩ (gigaseal), so no current leaks around the tip and the only current measured flows through channels in the membrane patch under the pipette. An amplifier holds the voltage constant (clamp) and measures the current. In the cell-attached configuration the cell stays intact. A single-channel recording shows the current jumping in square steps of a few pA between closed and fully open; open and closed times are random, and gating signals change the open probability. Developed by Neher and Sakmann (Nobel Prize 1991).




9. Explain how CFTR in airway epithelial cells keeps the airway surface wet, and why mucus becomes thick in cystic fibrosis. [ELO 2] [ELO 9]






Model answer





CFTR is a Cl⁻ channel in the apical membrane, opened by PKA phosphorylation and ATP binding. When open, Cl⁻ flows out into the airway lumen. Na⁺ follows between the cells (attracted by the negative charge), and water follows the salt by osmosis. This keeps a liquid layer under the mucus deep enough for the cilia to beat and move the mucus out of the lungs. In cystic fibrosis CFTR is missing or does not open, so little Cl⁻ and water are secreted; the liquid layer becomes thin, mucus becomes thick and sticky, cilia cannot clear it, and bacteria cause chronic infections.

title: Study questions: ion channels and membrane potential
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
10. [VG] A patient’s blood K⁺ rises from 5 mM to 10 mM (intracellular K⁺ stays at 140 mM). (a) Calculate the new \(E_\text{K}\). (b) Predict what happens to the resting potential of heart muscle cells and explain why. (c) Explain why this can be dangerous, using what you know about voltage-gated Na⁺ channels. [ELO 2]






Model answer






\(E_\text{K} = 26.7 \times \ln(10/140) = 26.7 \times (-2.64) \approx\) −70 mV (instead of −89 mV).
The resting membrane is mostly permeable to K⁺, so the resting potential follows \(E_\text{K}\): it becomes less negative (depolarised), roughly 15–20 mV.
A sustained depolarisation brings the membrane closer to threshold, so cells can fire too easily at first, but it also inactivates voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, which cannot recover while the membrane stays depolarised. With fewer available Na⁺ channels, action potentials become smaller and conduct more slowly, and the heart’s rhythm can fail (arrhythmia, in severe cases cardiac arrest). This is why blood K⁺ is monitored closely in kidney failure and when K⁺ is given intravenously.





11. [VG] In the sweat gland duct, CFTR reabsorbs Cl⁻ from sweat into the cell, while in the airways it secretes Cl⁻ out of the cell. (a) How can the same channel move Cl⁻ in opposite directions? (b) Explain why people with cystic fibrosis have salty sweat. [ELO 2] [ELO 9]






Model answer






A channel only lets ions flow down their electrochemical gradient; it has no direction of its own. The direction depends on the Cl⁻ concentrations and the membrane potential in each tissue. In airway cells, transporters load Cl⁻ into the cell above its equilibrium, so when CFTR opens, Cl⁻ flows out into the lumen. In the sweat duct, the sweat starts out with a high NaCl concentration (similar to plasma), so Cl⁻ flows from the lumen into the duct cells (with Na⁺ through Na⁺ channels) and is returned to the blood.
Without working CFTR in the duct, Cl⁻ (and therefore Na⁺) cannot be reabsorbed, so the sweat reaching the skin stays salty. The sweat test measures this: Cl⁻ ≥ 60 mmol/L indicates cystic fibrosis.





12. [VG] A new compound blocks pain in an animal model. You suspect it blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, like lidocaine. Design patch-clamp experiments to test (a) whether it blocks Na⁺ channels, (b) whether it acts from the inside or the outside of the membrane, and (c) whether, like lidocaine, it blocks more strongly when channels open often. [ELO 1] [ELO 2]






Model answer






Whole-cell recording from cells expressing the Na⁺ channel (e.g. cultured sensory neurons or a cell line expressing it). Depolarise with voltage steps and measure the inward Na⁺ current before and after adding the compound; a dose–response curve gives the IC₅₀. Controls: vehicle alone; a known blocker (tetrodotoxin or lidocaine); test other channels (e.g. K⁺ currents) to check specificity.
Use excised patches: in an inside-out patch, add the compound to the bath, which now faces the cytosolic side; in an outside-out patch, the bath faces the extracellular side. Block from one side only shows the site of action. A permanently charged version of the compound, which cannot cross the membrane, is a useful extra test.
Apply trains of depolarising pulses at low (e.g. 0.1 Hz) and high frequency (e.g. 10 Hz). If block builds up from pulse to pulse at high frequency (use-dependent block), the compound binds preferentially to open or inactivated channels, as lidocaine does. This property would let it block busy pain fibres more than normal nerves.

title: Quiz: a tour of the cell
text:
Short questions to check that you can use the map of the cell from the lecture. Try each on paper first, then open the hint, and only then the answer.

Q1. [ELO 1] Name three structures that a eukaryotic animal cell has and a bacterium does not.






Hint





Think of everything that is surrounded by its own membrane inside the cell.









Answer





Any three of: a nucleus with a double membrane (nuclear envelope), endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, endosomes and lysosomes, mitochondria, peroxisomes, and a cytoskeleton with microtubules organised by a centrosome. A bacterium has a plasma membrane, ribosomes and DNA in a nucleoid, but almost no internal membranes.




Q2. [ELO 1] Which of these spaces are on the same side of a membrane as the outside of the cell: cytosol, ER lumen, nucleoplasm, lysosome lumen, Golgi lumen?






Hint





Which compartments exchange material with the outside by vesicles that bud and fuse? Which are joined by open pores?









Answer





The ER lumen, the Golgi lumen and the lysosome lumen are topologically equivalent to the outside of the cell: vesicles carry material between them and the outside without crossing a membrane. The cytosol and the nucleoplasm form the other side; they are joined through nuclear pores.




Q3. [ELO 1] Put these in order from smallest to largest, and give a typical size for each: ribosome, mitochondrion (width), protein, nucleus, potassium ion, virus such as influenza.






Hint





Each step on the scale ladder was roughly a factor of 3–10.









Answer





Potassium ion (~0.3 nm) < protein (~5 nm) < ribosome (~25 nm) < influenza virus (~100 nm) < mitochondrion (~1 µm wide) < nucleus (~5–10 µm).




Q4. [ELO 1] A protein diffuses across a 10 µm cell in a few seconds. About how long would it take to diffuse 100 µm? What does this tell you about very long cells such as nerve cells?






Hint





Diffusion time grows with the square of the distance: \(t \approx x^2 / 6D\).









Answer





Ten times the distance means \(10^2 = 100\) times the time: a few hundred seconds, that is several minutes. Over a metre, the time becomes hundreds of years. So long cells such as nerve cells cannot rely on diffusion; they carry cargo with motor proteins along the cytoskeleton.




Q5. [ELO 5] A cell type is packed with rough ER and Golgi. What does the cell probably spend most of its effort on? Give one example of such a cell.






Hint





What does the rough ER make, and where do those proteins go?









Answer





It probably secretes large amounts of protein. The rough ER makes proteins for secretion and the Golgi modifies and sorts them. Examples: a pancreatic acinar cell (digestive enzymes) or a plasma cell (antibodies).




Q6. [ELO 1] A membrane receptor has a sugar chain on one domain. On which side of the plasma membrane do you expect to find that domain, and why?






Hint





Sugar chains are added in the lumen of the ER and Golgi. Follow the protein from the ER to the plasma membrane.









Answer





On the outside of the cell. The sugar chain is added while that domain faces the ER and Golgi lumen. Vesicles bud and fuse without the protein flipping, so the lumen-facing side ends up facing the outside of the cell.




Q7. [ELO 1] Give one advantage and one limitation of using HeLa cells to study a human protein.






Hint





Think of what a cell line is, and where HeLa came from.









Answer





Advantage: human cells that divide without limit, are cheap and easy to grow, image and perturb, and are used in many labs, so results can be compared. Limitation: HeLa cells are cancer cells with an abnormal genome (around 76–80 chromosomes) and an HPV infection that disables normal cell-cycle brakes; they grow flat on plastic, so they may not behave like a normal cell in a tissue. (Also acceptable: contamination of other cell lines, or the ethical questions about consent.)




Q8. [ELO 1] Electron microscopy of thin sections first showed the ER and ribosomes. Why was another method also needed to understand what lysosomes do?






Hint





What does a picture tell you, and what does it not tell you?









Answer





A micrograph shows where a structure is and what it looks like, but not what it does. Cell fractionation (breaking cells and separating their parts by centrifugation, then measuring enzyme activities in each fraction) showed that one fraction held digestive enzymes that work at acidic pH: the lysosomes.

section: About this lecture
text:
About this lecture
This is the first lecture of the course. It gives you a map of the cell that every later lecture uses.
After this lecture you can:

Name the main compartments of an animal cell and say in one sentence what each one does.
Explain topology: which spaces are on the cytosol side of a membrane and which are on the lumen side.
Give the size and number of the things inside a cell (ions, proteins, ribosomes, organelles, cells) to within a factor of ten.
Choose a model system (yeast, a cell line such as HeLa, an organoid) for a question, and say what it cannot tell you.

ELO 1 (parts of the cell, methods) and ELO 5 (organelles compared; this lecture is the first look).

Welcome to Cell Biology. This first lecture is a guided tour. We will not go deep into any one organelle today; every organelle you see here gets its own lecture later. The aim is a mental map that you can hang the rest of the course on. Keep three ideas in mind. First, the cell is divided into compartments by membranes, and the chemistry inside each compartment is different. Second, every membrane has two sides, and knowing which side is which, the topology, explains a lot of later material on protein sorting and vesicle traffic. Third, sizes and numbers matter: a protein is about five nanometres, a cell is about fifteen micrometres, and a cell holds billions of protein molecules. At the end we look at how we study cells, using model systems, and at HeLa cells: the most used human cells in research, and a story about consent that every biomedical scientist should know. This lecture belongs to ELO 1 and is the first step towards ELO 5.

You already think in molecules: DNA, proteins, enzymes, ΔG. This course moves you one level up: to compartments (where things are), machines (what moves and signals) and decisions (divide, move or die), and to disease when these go wrong.

The middle blocks are about signals and machines: how a cell senses its surroundings and how the cytoskeleton gives it shape and movement. Then come decisions: when to divide and when to die. title: A tour of the cell
section: The question: how does one small drop do everything at once?
text:
The question: how does one small drop do everything at once?


A cultured animal cell holds about 2 picolitres of water, and in it:

billions of protein molecules, many thousands of different kinds,
enzymes that make fats next to enzymes that burn them,
enzymes that digest proteins at pH 5, in a cell whose cytosol is pH 7.2,
DNA that must be copied once per division and never digested.

How does the cell keep incompatible chemistry apart, and still get every molecule to the place where it is needed?






Cultured endothelial cells. Blue: nucleus (DNA). Green: microtubules. Red: actin filaments.


Look at the image. These are cultured cells from a cow blood vessel, stained with three fluorescent dyes: blue for DNA in the nucleus, green for microtubules and red for actin filaments. Even with only three stains you can see order: the nucleus sits in the middle, microtubules spread out from near the nucleus, and actin lines the cell edge. Now the puzzle. Each cell is a tiny volume, about two picolitres, but inside it there are billions of protein molecules doing thousands of reactions at once. Some of these reactions would destroy each other if they were mixed. Digestive enzymes that work best at pH 5 would attack the cell’s own proteins. Fat synthesis and fat breakdown would cancel each other out. DNA must be kept safe and copied exactly once per cycle. The answer, which the rest of this lecture develops, has three parts: compartments separated by membranes, transport routes between the compartments, and a cytoskeleton that organises space. Keep this question in mind; we come back to it in the summary.

text:
Recap: prokaryote and eukaryote










Prokaryote (bacterium)
Eukaryote (animal cell)




DNA
in the cytosol (nucleoid)
inside a nucleus with a double membrane


Internal membranes
almost none
many: ER, Golgi, endosomes, lysosomes, mitochondria, …


Typical volume
~1 µm³

This is a recap of what you met in microbiology. A bacterium such as E. coli is about two micrometres long. It has a plasma membrane, usually a cell wall, ribosomes and its DNA in a region called the nucleoid, but no membrane around the DNA and almost no internal membranes. A eukaryotic cell is about a thousand times larger in volume. That is the key point on this slide: a bigger cell has a problem. Its surface is small compared with its volume, and molecules must travel further. Eukaryotes solve this with internal membranes, which add a large membrane area for reactions and divide the volume into compartments with different chemistry. Notice the mitochondria on the right: they are about the size of a bacterium. That is not a coincidence. Mitochondria come from a bacterium that was taken up by an ancestral cell, and they still have their own DNA and ribosomes. We come back to this in the mitochondria lecture.

title: A tour of the cell
section: A map of the animal cell
text:
A map of the animal cell


This is the map we use in the whole course, and the colours are fixed: every later lecture uses the same colour for the same organelle. Purple is the nucleus, teal the endoplasmic reticulum, orange the Golgi apparatus, red the mitochondria, green the endosomes and lysosomes, blue the peroxisomes, grey the cytoskeleton, and brown the plasma membrane. Start in the centre. The nucleus holds the DNA, surrounded by the nuclear envelope, which is two membranes with pores through them. The outer nuclear membrane continues into the endoplasmic reticulum, the ER. The rough ER has ribosomes on its surface and makes membrane proteins and proteins for secretion; the smooth ER makes lipids and stores calcium. Proteins go from the ER to the Golgi, which modifies and sorts them, and then on to the plasma membrane in secretory vesicles, or to lysosomes. Material taken in from outside goes to endosomes and then to lysosomes for digestion. Mitochondria make most of the ATP. The centrosome organises the microtubules. Everything else, the fluid between the organelles, is the cytosol. The picture is a simplification: a real cell has hundreds of mitochondria and a much larger ER.

This table is the text version of the map. Do not learn the percentages by heart; learn the pattern. About half of a typical cell is cytosol, and the cytosol is where proteins are made on free ribosomes and where much of metabolism happens, for example glycolysis. Each membrane-bound organelle has a special job, and each has its own lecture, shown in the right column. Notice that the amounts depend on what the cell does. A liver cell, which does a lot of metabolism, has many mitochondria, about a fifth of its volume. A pancreatic acinar cell, which secretes large amounts of digestive enzymes, is packed with rough ER. A plasma cell, which secretes antibodies, also has a lot of rough ER. So you can often guess what a cell does by looking at its organelles under an electron microscope, and the reverse is also true. Two jobs are worth noting now because they come back: mitochondria do not only make ATP, they also start one form of cell death; and the ER is the main calcium store of the cell, which matters for signalling.

title: A tour of the cell
section: Two sides of every membrane: topology
text:
Two sides of every membrane: topology


This is the most important idea of today, because it explains much of protein sorting and vesicle traffic later. Every membrane separates two spaces. Look at the colours. The light yellow space is the cytosol side: the cytosol itself and the inside of the nucleus, the nucleoplasm. These two are joined through nuclear pores, which are large open channels, so they count as one space. The light blue space is the lumen side: the inside of the ER, the gap between the two nuclear membranes, the Golgi, the vesicles, endosomes and lysosomes. The lumen side is, in topology, the same as the outside of the cell. Why? Because these compartments are connected to the outside by vesicles that bud from one membrane and fuse with another, without a molecule ever crossing a membrane. A protein secreted from the ER lumen reaches the outside without ever being in the cytosol. Mitochondria are the exception: their inner space, the matrix, is a third space of its own, a legacy of their bacterial origin. Peroxisomes, not shown here, also import their proteins from the cytosol.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Inside-out logic: a protein keeps its orientation
text:
Inside-out logic: a protein keeps its orientation


The part of a protein that is in the ER lumen ends up outside the cell.
This is why sugar chains (added in the ER and Golgi lumen) are found on the outer surface of the cell, and why receptors have their binding site outside.


Here is topology in action. A membrane protein is made in the ER membrane. One part of it faces the ER lumen, and in the lumen the cell adds sugar chains to it. The other part, the tail, faces the cytosol. Now follow it. A vesicle buds from the ER: the lumen side of the protein now faces the inside of the vesicle. The vesicle fuses with the Golgi: the lumen side faces the Golgi lumen. A new vesicle carries it to the plasma membrane and fuses: now the lumen side faces the outside of the cell. At no step does the protein flip, and at no step does any part of it cross a membrane. So the rule is simple: lumen side equals outside. This explains why all the sugar chains of the cell surface face outwards, and why a hormone receptor made in the ER has its hormone-binding part outside the cell and its signalling part in the cytosol. When we study receptors and protein sorting, you will use this rule again and again. It is also a common exam question.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: The scale ladder: from ion to cell
text:
The scale ladder: from ion to cell

Each step on the axis is a factor of 10. A cell is about 50,000× wider than an ion and about 3000× wider than a protein.

Cell biology covers about five orders of magnitude in size, so the axis is logarithmic: each tick is ten times the one before. An ion such as potassium is about a third of a nanometre across. A typical protein is about five nanometres. A ribosome, a large machine made of RNA and about eighty proteins, is about twenty-five nanometres. Many viruses, such as influenza or SARS coronavirus 2, are about a hundred nanometres. A bacterium and a mitochondrion are about one micrometre wide. The nucleus is a few micrometres, and a whole animal cell is ten to twenty micrometres. The bars at the bottom link to the next lecture. A light microscope cannot separate two objects closer than about two hundred nanometres, so with light you can see cells, nuclei and mitochondria, but not single ribosomes or proteins, unless you label them with a fluorescent tag. An electron microscope sees down to about a nanometre in a thin section of a cell. Remember these sizes: they let you check whether an answer is reasonable.

Rough values of the kind collected in BioNumbers (bionumbers.hms.harvard.edu) and Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo and Phillips). Diffusion time: t \approx x^2 / 6D with D \approx 5–10\ \mu\text{m}^2/\text{s} for a protein in cytoplasm.

These are numbers to remember as orders of magnitude, not exact values. A cell holds about one to ten billion protein molecules. Spread over a volume of a few picolitres, that is a protein concentration of a few hundred milligrams per millilitre: the cytoplasm is crowded, more like a gel than like water. Now diffusion. For a molecule that moves randomly, the time to travel a distance x grows with x squared: t is roughly x squared divided by six times the diffusion coefficient. A protein in cytoplasm has a diffusion coefficient of about five to ten square micrometres per second, so it crosses a ten-micrometre cell in a few seconds. That is fast enough for most signals. But because of the x squared, diffusion becomes useless over long distances: to diffuse one metre, from your spinal cord to your foot along a nerve axon, would take hundreds of years. This is why cells have motor proteins that carry cargo along the cytoskeleton, which you meet in the cytoskeleton block. Small molecules such as glucose diffuse about ten to a hundred times faster than proteins.

title: A tour of the cell
section: How do we know? Electron microscopy revealed the compartments
text:
How do we know? Electron microscopy revealed the compartments



Light microscopy (from the 1600s) showed cells and nuclei, but nothing smaller than ~0.2 µm.
1940s–1950s: the electron microscope and thin sections showed the ER, ribosomes, Golgi stacks and the inner structure of mitochondria.
At the same time, cell fractionation (breaking cells and separating parts by centrifugation) showed what each part does, for example lysosomes full of digestive enzymes.
Nobel Prize 1974: Claude, de Duve and Palade.

Lesson: one method shows where; another shows what it does. You need both.






Transmission electron micrograph of a human B lymphocyte. Large nucleus with dark chromatin; mitochondria with folded inner membranes in the cytoplasm. Scale bar 500 nm.


How do we know that the map is true? Until the 1940s, the light microscope was the main tool, and it cannot resolve anything smaller than about two hundred nanometres. Cells and nuclei were visible, and mitochondria as tiny dots, but the ER and ribosomes were invisible. The electron microscope uses electrons instead of light, and electrons have a much shorter wavelength, so it resolves structures down to about a nanometre. When researchers learned to cut cells into very thin sections, they suddenly saw the membranes inside cells: the ER, ribosomes, the Golgi stacks and the folded inner membrane of mitochondria. In the image you see a human B lymphocyte: the large nucleus with dark, condensed chromatin, and mitochondria with their folded inner membrane. But a picture shows where things are, not what they do. At the same time, others broke cells open and separated their parts by centrifugation, then measured enzymes in each fraction. This is how lysosomes and peroxisomes were discovered. Combining the two methods won the Nobel Prize in 1974. Microscopy and fractionation are the topics of the next two lectures.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Model systems: choose the simplest system that can answer the question
text:
Model systems: choose the simplest system that can answer the question










System

Cannot tell you




Bacteria (E. coli)

Budding yeast (S. cerevisiae)
eukaryote; divides in ~90 min; easy genetics

Organoids
