Yeast genetics found the genes for the cell cycle (Nobel 2001), vesicle traffic (2013) and autophagy (2016).






Budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae (DIC microscopy). Small buds are daughter cells growing out of the mother cells.


No single system answers every question, so cell biologists choose a model system. The rule is to use the simplest system that still has the feature you want to study. Bacteria are fast and simple but have no organelles. Budding yeast, the yeast used for baking and brewing, is the simplest common eukaryote: it has a nucleus, ER, Golgi and mitochondria, it divides in about ninety minutes, and its genes are easy to delete. Because most of the core machinery is shared with human cells, yeast genetics found the genes that control the cell cycle, the genes for vesicle traffic and the genes for autophagy, and each of these won a Nobel Prize. In the image you see yeast cells with buds; each bud is a new daughter cell. Human cell lines give human proteins in a dish. Organoids add three-dimensional tissue structure. Mice give a whole body. Each step up is closer to a patient but slower, more expensive and harder to control. In a VG question you may be asked to choose a system and to say what it cannot show.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Cell lines: HeLa, the first human cells that never stopped dividing
text:
Cell lines: HeLa, the first human cells that never stopped dividing



Normal human cells divide only about 40–60 times in culture, then stop.
A cell line divides without limit. Most come from tumours.
HeLa (1951) came from the cervical tumour of Henrietta Lacks. It was the first human cell line.
HeLa cells carry human papillomavirus 18 (HPV-18). Viral proteins switch off two brakes on cell division (you meet them in the cell-cycle and cancer lectures).
HeLa is not a normal cell: around 76–80 chromosomes instead of 46, and the number varies. And HeLa grows so well that it has contaminated many other cell lines, so labs now check the identity of their cells with a DNA test.







Living HeLa cells. Blue: nucleus. Green: microtubules. Red: mitochondria. Scale bar 10 µm.


Most cells taken from a human body divide a limited number of times in a dish, about forty to sixty times, and then stop. A cell line is a population of cells that can divide without limit. Almost all human cell lines come from tumours, because cancer cells have lost the normal limits on division. The first human cell line came from Henrietta Lacks, a thirty-one-year-old African American woman treated for cervical cancer at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore in 1951. Her cells, named HeLa from her name, grew faster than any human cells before them. We now know why. Her tumour was caused by human papillomavirus type 18, and viral proteins in HeLa cells switch off two key brakes on cell division, proteins called p53 and Rb, which you meet in the cell-cycle and cancer lectures. HeLa cells also have an abnormal genome, with about eighty chromosomes. In the image you see living HeLa cells with three fluorescent labels: nucleus, microtubules and mitochondria. Note the scale bar: these cells are about twenty to forty micrometres long when they spread on glass.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Organoids: tissue in a dish
text:
Organoids: tissue in a dish



An organoid is a small 3D structure that grows from stem cells in a gel, with the right growth factors.
The cells organise themselves: an intestinal organoid forms crypts and a lumen, with several cell types, like the real gut lining.
Organoids can be grown from one patient’s biopsy, so you can test drugs on that patient’s own cells.
Example: in cystic fibrosis, a patient’s intestinal organoids swell when a drug restores the faulty chloride channel (CFTR). The test helps choose a drug for that patient.







Intestinal organoid grown from Lgr5⁺ stem cells. The buds are crypt-like domains around a central lumen.


Cell lines grow as a flat layer on plastic, which is far from a real tissue. Organoids are a newer model, developed from about 2009. You take adult stem cells, for example from the base of an intestinal crypt, put them in a gel that mimics the material around cells in a tissue, and add the growth factors that the stem cells normally receive. The stem cells divide and organise themselves into a small three-dimensional structure with a central lumen and buds that look like crypts, with several cell types, much like the lining of the gut. The image shows such an intestinal organoid. Because organoids can be grown from a small biopsy, they can be made from one patient. A good example is cystic fibrosis, which is caused by a faulty chloride channel called CFTR. When a drug restores channel function in a patient’s intestinal organoids, chloride and water flow into the lumen and the organoids swell. The amount of swelling helps predict whether the drug will work in that patient. You meet ion channels in lecture six and cystic fibrosis again in the disease lectures.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Why it matters: HeLa cells changed medicine
text:
Why it matters: HeLa cells changed medicine


Polio vaccine: poliovirus grows in HeLa, so HeLa was mass-produced to test the Salk vaccine (1953–55).
HPV and cervical cancer: HPV-18 DNA in HeLa helped show that a virus causes cervical cancer (Nobel 2008), which led to the HPV vaccine.
Drug screening: cell lines like HeLa are the first test for thousands of drug candidates: does the compound kill cells, reach its target, change an organelle?


Here is why HeLa cells matter for medicine, and why we tie them back to the cell-line slide. Because HeLa cells were the first human cells that could be grown in large amounts, they became a tool for everything. In the early 1950s, poliovirus was found to grow in HeLa cells. A laboratory at the Tuskegee Institute mass-produced HeLa cells and sent them across the United States to test whether the Salk polio vaccine produced protective antibodies. In the 1980s, researchers found DNA from human papillomavirus type 18 in HeLa cells and in many other cervical cancers. This helped prove that a virus causes cervical cancer, work that won the Nobel Prize in 2008, and it led to the HPV vaccine that is now given to children, including in Sweden. HeLa cells have been used in more than a hundred thousand research papers. Today, cell lines are the first step of drug development: before any animal or human test, a drug candidate is tested on cells. You meet the later phases in the later programme course on clinical trials and drug development.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Why it matters: consent, then and now
text:
Why it matters: consent, then and now



In 1951 Henrietta Lacks was not asked whether her cells could be used. This was common practice at the time. She died the same year, aged 31.
Her family learned about HeLa decades later. Companies sold HeLa cells; the family received nothing.
2013: the HeLa genome was published without the family’s consent. It also says something about her relatives’ DNA. The US National Institutes of Health then agreed with the family on controlled access, with family members on the committee.
Today, in Sweden: research on human tissue needs ethical approval and, as a rule, informed consent. Samples in biobanks are protected by law.

Ask yourself: who should decide how cells from a patient are used, and who should benefit?






HeLa cells, DNA stained with the blue dye Hoechst 33258.


The science of HeLa cannot be separated from the person. Henrietta Lacks was a mother of five who was treated for cervical cancer in a segregated hospital ward in 1951. A sample of her tumour was taken during treatment and given to a research laboratory without her knowledge. This was common practice then, but that does not make it right, and her family did not learn about the cells for more than twenty years. When the HeLa genome sequence was published in 2013, it again happened without asking the family, even though a genome also reveals information about relatives. After discussions, the US National Institutes of Health agreed with the family that the data should be in controlled access, with family members helping to decide who can use it. In 2021 the World Health Organization honoured Henrietta Lacks, and in 2023 the family reached a settlement with a company that had sold HeLa cells. In Sweden today, research on human tissue needs approval from the Swedish Ethical Review Authority, informed consent is the rule, and biobank samples are protected by law. Treat this as a question for discussion, not a closed story.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Summary
text:
Summary

A eukaryotic cell is divided by membranes into compartments, each with its own chemistry and job: nucleus, ER, Golgi, endosomes and lysosomes, mitochondria, peroxisomes, and the cytosol between them.
Every membrane has two sides. The cytosol and nucleoplasm form one side; the lumen of the ER, Golgi, vesicles and lysosomes is topologically outside the cell. Mitochondria have a third space.
Sizes and numbers: protein ~5 nm, ribosome ~25 nm, cell 10–20 µm; 10⁹–10¹⁰ proteins per cell; diffusion is fast over a cell but useless over long distances.
We know this from microscopy (where) and fractionation (what), and we study cells in model systems (yeast, cell lines such as HeLa, organoids), each with its limits.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 1 and ch. 12 (first section).
Image credits

Let us return to the opening question: how does one small drop of cytoplasm do everything at once? The answer is compartments. Membranes divide the cell into spaces with different chemistry, such as the acidic lysosome and the calcium-rich ER, and vesicles carry material between the lumen-side compartments without crossing a membrane. Topology is the rule to remember: the lumen side equals the outside of the cell, and the cytosol side includes the nucleus. Sizes and numbers let you check your reasoning, and the diffusion numbers explain why a large cell needs a cytoskeleton and motors. Finally, every fact on today’s map came from methods: electron microscopy showed where structures are, fractionation showed what they do, and model systems let us test ideas. The next two lectures are about these methods: microscopy, and how to take cells apart and perturb them. If you want to read more, chapter one and the first section of chapter twelve of Molecular Biology of the Cell cover today’s material, but the slides and notes are enough for the exam.

title: Quiz: taking cells apart and perturbing them
text:
Short questions to check that you can choose and read the methods from the lecture. Try each on paper first, then open the hint, and only then the answer.

Q1. [ELO 1] Give one advantage of a cell line and one advantage of primary cells.






Hint





Think about how long each kind divides, and how close each is to the tissue.









Answer





Cell line: divides without limit, is cheap and easy to grow, and the same line can be used in many labs, so results are reproducible. Primary cells: come directly from the tissue, so they behave more like cells in the body (normal genome, normal regulation).




Q2. [ELO 1] In differential centrifugation, which comes down first, nuclei or ribosomes? Why?






Hint





Larger and denser particles sediment at lower force.









Answer





Nuclei, already at a low speed (about 1,000 g), because they are large and dense. Ribosomes are very small and need a very strong, long spin (well over 100,000 g).




Q3. [ELO 1] After a density gradient, fraction 4 contains the protein calnexin. What does that tell you, and why?






Hint





Calnexin is a marker protein.









Answer





Fraction 4 contains ER membranes, because calnexin is a marker protein found only in the ER. A new protein that appears in the same fractions as calnexin is probably also in the ER.




Q4. [ELO 1] In a western blot, why do you also stain for a loading control such as actin?






Hint





What if one lane simply got more sample?









Answer





To show that the same amount of protein was loaded in every lane. Only then does a weaker band of your protein mean less of that protein, not just less sample.




Q5. [ELO 1] What does immunoprecipitation give you that a western blot on a whole lysate does not?






Hint





What else comes down with the target protein?









Answer





It pulls out the target protein together with the proteins bound to it, so you can find its binding partners (for example by running the pulled-down material on a western blot or by mass spectrometry).




Q6. [ELO 1] In a flow cytometry dot plot, what is one dot, and what is a gate?






Hint





Flow cytometry measures single cells.









Answer





One dot is one cell. A gate is a region you draw on a plot so that only the cells inside it (for example lymphocytes, not debris) are analysed in the next plot.




Q7. [ELO 1] Match each tool to what it acts on: CRISPR knockout, RNAi, small-molecule inhibitor. (gene / mRNA / protein)






Hint





Follow the path from gene to active protein.









Answer





CRISPR knockout → gene (DNA). RNAi → mRNA. Inhibitor → protein (its activity).




Q8. [ELO 1] Removing protein X stops cell migration. Is X necessary or sufficient for migration? What experiment would test the other?






Hint





Removing tests one; adding tests the other.









Answer





X is necessary. To test whether it is sufficient, overexpress X (for example in cells that do not normally migrate) and see whether migration starts or increases.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: About this lecture
text:
About this lecture
Microscopy tells you where things are. This lecture is about the other half of cell biology: what things are, how many cells have them, and what happens if you change them.
After this lecture you can:

Say what cell culture gives you (primary cells, cell lines, organoids) and what it cannot tell you.
Explain how fractionation separates organelles, and how marker proteins show what is in each fraction.
Explain how antibodies are used to detect and pull out one protein (western blot, immunoprecipitation).
Read a flow cytometry dot plot and explain how cells are sorted.
Choose a perturbation (inhibitor, RNAi, CRISPR, overexpression) and the right controls to test whether a protein is needed for a process.

ELO 1: methods used to study cell biological processes.

In the microscopy lecture we looked at cells. Looking tells you where a protein is, but it does not tell you what the protein does. To answer that question, cell biologists do three kinds of things. They grow cells outside the body, so they have material to work with. They take cells apart, to find out which molecules belong to which compartment. And they change cells on purpose, by removing or adding a protein, and watch what happens. This lecture goes through these three steps. You have met some of the tools before: protein purification, SDS-PAGE and PCR from biochemistry. Here we use them on whole cells. Several of these methods also come back in the laboratory part of the course, so this lecture is also your preparation for the labs. At the end we see how the same methods are used to find new drugs and to make a living cancer therapy.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: The question: one protein, four questions
text:
The question: one protein, four questions


You have found a new protein, X. Immunofluorescence shows it in the cytoplasm.
To understand it, you need four more answers:

Which compartment is it really in? (fractionation)
How much is there, and does the amount change? (western blot)
Which cells in a mixed population have it? (flow cytometry)
Is it needed for anything? (perturbation)

And for all of these you need cells to work on. (cell culture)






HeLa cells stained with antibodies: microtubules, mitochondria (HSP60), nucleoli (fibrillarin) and DNA.


Here is a typical situation. Someone has made an antibody against a new protein, X, and the image shows it somewhere in the cytoplasm. That is a start, but a fluorescence image has limits. Two compartments can look the same at two hundred nanometres resolution, so you cannot be sure which one X is in. An image is also hard to quantify: is there more X after a treatment, or is the staining just brighter? An image shows a few cells; you may want to know the fraction of cells in a whole blood sample that carry X. And above all, seeing X tells you nothing about what X does. Each of these questions has its own standard method, and those methods are the topic of this lecture. Keep protein X in mind; we come back to it in a worked example near the end.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Cell culture: primary cells and cell lines
text:
Cell culture: primary cells and cell lines



Cells are grown in a sterile dish or flask, in a medium with salts, glucose, amino acids and growth factors, at 37 °C.
Primary cells come straight from a tissue. They behave like the tissue, but divide only a limited number of times.
Cell lines divide without limit (they are immortal), usually because they come from a tumour or carry an immortalising gene. HeLa, from the tour of the cell, is the classic example.
Trade-off: cell lines are easy and reproducible; primary cells are closer to the body.







Living HeLa cells in a culture flask (phase contrast).





A sterile bench (biosafety cabinet) for cell culture work.


Cell culture means growing cells outside the body. The cells sit in a plastic dish or flask, covered by a liquid medium that gives them what the blood would: salts, glucose, amino acids, vitamins and growth factors, usually from serum. They are kept at body temperature in an incubator. All work is done on a sterile bench, because bacteria and fungi grow much faster than human cells. There are two main kinds of cultured cells. Primary cells are taken directly from a tissue, for example skin fibroblasts or blood cells. They are close to the real tissue but stop dividing after a limited number of divisions, so you must keep getting new ones. Cell lines have become immortal, either because they come from a tumour, like HeLa, or because an immortalising gene was added. They are cheap, grow fast and every lab can use the same line, which makes results comparable. The price is that a cell line has adapted to life on plastic and is often genetically abnormal.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Stem cells, 3D culture and organoids
text:
Stem cells, 3D culture and organoids



Cells on flat plastic lose much of their normal shape and behaviour.
3D culture: cells grow in a soft gel that mimics the extracellular matrix.
Organoids: stem cells in a gel organise themselves into a small, simple version of an organ, with several cell types in roughly the right places.
Made from adult stem cells (e.g. gut) or from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells), which can be made from a patient’s skin or blood.
Use: study a patient’s own cells, and test drugs on them.







A small-intestine organoid. Green: E-cadherin at cell–cell contacts; red: the signalling protein AKT; blue: nuclei.


A cell spread flat on hard plastic is not in its natural situation. In a tissue, cells touch neighbours on all sides, sit on a soft extracellular matrix, and have a top and a bottom. One way closer to the body is 3D culture in a soft gel. Organoids take this a step further. If you put intestinal stem cells into such a gel with the right growth factors, they divide and organise themselves into a small hollow structure with crypts and villus-like regions and several cell types, like a tiny gut. Organoids can also be made from induced pluripotent stem cells, which are made by reprogramming ordinary adult cells, such as skin cells, back to a stem-cell state. This means you can grow organoids from a particular patient. A well-known use is cystic fibrosis: gut organoids from a patient swell when the chloride channel works, so you can test which drug works for that patient’s mutation. You will meet that channel in the ion channels lecture.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Is the culture what you think it is?
text:
Is the culture what you think it is?
Two classic problems, both easy to miss:








Problem
Why it matters
How labs check




Wrong cells (misidentified cell line)
Hundreds of published “cell lines” turned out to be another line, often HeLa. Results are then about the wrong tissue.
DNA fingerprint (STR profile) compared with a reference database


Hidden bacteria (Mycoplasma)
Tiny bacteria without a cell wall. Not visible in the microscope, not killed by common antibiotics; they change the cells’ metabolism and gene expression.
Regular PCR test of the culture



Lesson: a result from cultured cells is only as good as the cells. Good laboratory practice includes checking them.

Two problems have caused a lot of wrong results in cell biology, and both are invisible. The first is the wrong cells. Because HeLa grows so well, a few HeLa cells carried over into another culture can take it over within weeks. Many lines that were thought to come from, for example, breast or prostate tissue were later shown to be HeLa or another line. Today journals often ask for proof of identity, a DNA fingerprint based on short tandem repeats, which is compared with the database for that line. The second problem is Mycoplasma, a group of very small bacteria without a cell wall. Because they lack a wall, the usual penicillin-type antibiotics do not kill them, and because they are so small, the culture still looks clear. Yet they change how the cells behave. Labs therefore test their cultures regularly, usually with PCR. The general lesson fits the lab part of this course: you must be able to trust your material before you can trust your result.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Taking cells apart: homogenisation and centrifugation
text:
Taking cells apart: homogenisation and centrifugation


First break the cells gently (homogenisation), so organelles stay intact.
Then spin at increasing speed and time. Large, dense particles pellet first; small ones need stronger force.


To find out which compartment a protein belongs to, you can take the cell apart and separate its organelles. First the cells are broken open gently, for example by pushing them through a narrow gap, in a buffer that keeps the organelles intact. This is called homogenisation, and the result is a homogenate. Then comes differential centrifugation. A short, slow spin pellets the biggest and heaviest particles: nuclei and unbroken cells. The liquid on top, the supernatant, is spun again, faster and longer. Now mitochondria, lysosomes and peroxisomes form a pellet. A still stronger spin pellets small membrane pieces called microsomes, which are mostly bits of ER and Golgi that closed into little vesicles. After the strongest spin, what stays in the supernatant is the cytosol with its soluble proteins. The g-values and times in the figure are typical numbers; every lab adjusts them. This approach earned Albert Claude, Christian de Duve and George Palade a Nobel Prize in 1974; de Duve found lysosomes and peroxisomes this way.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it
Taking cells apart and perturbing them

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Density gradients and marker proteins
text:
Density gradients and marker proteins








Differential spins give mixtures. For better separation, spin through a gradient (e.g. sucrose): each organelle stops where its density matches.
Which fraction holds which organelle? Use marker proteins known to sit in one organelle only. If protein X runs with the ER marker, X is probably in the ER.









Differential centrifugation is quick but crude: each pellet is a mixture. A cleaner separation uses a density gradient. A tube is filled with a sugar solution that is light at the top and dense at the bottom. The homogenate goes on top, and during a long spin in an ultracentrifuge each organelle moves down until it reaches the layer that has the same density as itself, and stops there. Afterwards the tube is emptied in small fractions from top to bottom. But the fractions are not labelled, so how do you know what is in each one? You run each fraction on a western blot, which comes in two slides, and stain for marker proteins: proteins that are known to live in only one organelle. In the figure, GM130 marks the Golgi, calnexin the ER, TOM20 mitochondria and catalase peroxisomes. Then you stain for your protein X. If X appears in the same fractions as calnexin, it is probably an ER protein. Real gradients overlap more than this clean figure shows.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Antibodies as tools
text:
Antibodies as tools


An antibody binds one small patch, the epitope, on one protein. That makes it a tag-free “probe” for a protein.
Immunoprecipitation (IP): antibody on beads pulls the target, and the proteins bound to it, out of a cell lysate.
The same antibody, with a fluorophore, gives the immunofluorescence images from the microscopy lecture.


Antibodies are the most used tool in cell biology, because they recognise one protein among thousands. An antibody of the IgG type has two identical binding sites, each of which fits a small patch on the target, the epitope, typically five to ten amino acids or a small surface. In immunofluorescence, which you saw in the microscopy lecture, the antibody carries a fluorophore so you can see where the target is. In immunoprecipitation, the antibody is attached to small beads. You mix the beads with a cell lysate, the target binds, you spin the beads down and wash away everything else. What remains is the target protein together with any proteins that were bound to it. That is how you find the partners of a protein. Everything depends on the antibody being specific. A bad antibody also binds other proteins, and then every result is wrong. A good control is to use cells where the target gene has been knocked out: the signal should disappear.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Western blot: which protein, how much
text:
Western blot: which protein, how much








Recap: SDS-PAGE separates proteins by size. Proteins are then transferred to a membrane, and one protein is found with an antibody.
Band position = size (check it!). Band strength = amount, compared between lanes.
Always include a loading control (a protein that should not change).









You know SDS-PAGE from biochemistry: proteins are coated with a negative detergent and pulled through a gel by an electric field, so small proteins move fastest. A western blot adds two steps. First the separated proteins are moved from the gel onto a thin membrane by a second electric current, where they stick. Then the membrane is incubated with a primary antibody against your protein, and a secondary antibody that binds the first one and carries an enzyme. The enzyme turns a substrate into light, and you see a band. The position of the band tells you the size, which is a good check that the antibody found the right protein. The strength of the band tells you roughly how much protein there is, compared between lanes. In lane three of the figure there is less protein X, for example after the gene was knocked down. To compare lanes fairly you also stain a loading control, a protein such as actin or tubulin whose amount should be the same everywhere, to show that the same amount of material was loaded.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Flow cytometry: measuring thousands of single cells
text:
Flow cytometry: measuring thousands of single cells








Cells pass a laser one at a time, thousands per second. Scatter gives size (forward) and granularity (side); fluorescence tells which labelled molecules each cell carries.
FACS (cell sorting): droplets with a wanted cell get a charge and are deflected into a tube.









A western blot measures the average of millions of cells ground up together. Often you want to know about single cells instead: what fraction of the cells carry protein X, and do they carry a lot or a little? Flow cytometry does this. Cells, labelled with fluorescent antibodies, are made into a suspension and pushed through a narrow stream, squeezed by sheath fluid so that they pass a laser one by one. For each cell, detectors record how much light is scattered forwards, which tells about size, how much is scattered sideways, which tells about internal granularity, and how much fluorescence comes out in each colour. A modern machine measures tens of thousands of cells per second and a dozen or more colours. A cell sorter, called FACS for fluorescence-activated cell sorting, goes one step further: the stream breaks into droplets, a droplet that contains a wanted cell gets an electric charge, and electric plates steer it into a collection tube. So you can collect, for example, only the cells that carry X, and keep them alive.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Reading a dot plot: gating
text:
Reading a dot plot: gating


Each dot is one cell. First gate on scatter to keep the cells you want (here lymphocytes) and drop debris.
Then plot two fluorescent markers: four quadrants, four kinds of cell. Report the percentage in each. Try it: the gating game.


The results of flow cytometry are shown as dot plots, where every dot is one cell. Analysis is done in steps called gating. In panel A, forward scatter is plotted against side scatter for a blood sample. Small, smooth lymphocytes form one cloud, granulocytes with many granules sit higher, and monocytes between. Debris and dead cells sit in the low corner. We draw a gate, a boundary, around the lymphocytes, and from now on look only at those cells. In panel B the same lymphocytes are plotted by two fluorescent antibodies: one against CD4 and one against CD8, two surface proteins that mark two kinds of T cell. The plot falls into four quadrants. Cells with only CD4 are helper T cells, cells with only CD8 are cytotoxic T cells, cells with neither are mostly B cells and NK cells here, and very few have both. The result is reported as percentages. In HIV infection, for instance, the CD4 percentage falls over time, and this is how it is measured in the clinic. These data are simulated, but typical.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Changing cells on purpose: four tools
text:
Changing cells on purpose: four tools

Each tool acts at a different step from gene to activity, and each has its own speed, strength and pitfalls.

So far we have described cells. Now we change them. You can interfere at each step from gene to working protein, and the figure arranges the four common tools along that path. CRISPR knockout cuts the gene itself, so the cell can never make the protein again; it is all-or-none and permanent, but it takes weeks to make a cell line, and a cell may adapt to the loss over that time. RNA interference destroys the messenger RNA with a short matching RNA; the protein drops, usually not to zero, for a few days. Overexpression adds extra copies of the gene, so the cell makes more protein than normal; this tests whether the protein is sufficient to cause an effect. Finally, small-molecule inhibitors, which are drugs, block the protein directly. They act within minutes, can be washed out, and you can vary the dose, but most inhibitors also hit other proteins, called off-targets. Because each tool has different weaknesses, a strong conclusion usually uses two different tools that give the same answer.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: CRISPR–Cas9: knocking out a gene
text:
CRISPR–Cas9: knocking out a gene


Cas9 cuts DNA where a guide RNA matches. The quick repair often adds or removes a few letters: the reading frame shifts, and no working protein is made.
A bacterial defence against viruses, turned into a tool by Emmanuelle Charpentier (partly at Umeå University) and Jennifer Doudna: Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020.


CRISPR-Cas9 comes from bacteria, where it is an immune system against viruses: the bacterium stores short pieces of viral DNA and uses them to guide the Cas9 enzyme to cut the virus. Researchers turned this into a tool. Cas9 is given a guide RNA whose sequence matches the gene you want to target, and it cuts both DNA strands at that place. The cell cannot leave a broken chromosome, so it repairs it, usually by simply joining the ends again. This repair is fast but sloppy: it often adds or deletes a few base pairs. If the change is not a multiple of three, the reading frame shifts, the ribosome soon meets a stop codon, and no working protein is made. That is a knockout. You know reading frames and stop codons from molecular biology, so you can see why this works. Emmanuelle Charpentier did part of her key work on CRISPR at Umeå University, and she and Jennifer Doudna received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. CRISPR is now also used in medicine, which you may meet in later courses.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: How do we know? Necessary, sufficient, and controls
text:
How do we know? Necessary, sufficient, and controls


Necessary: remove X → the process stops (knockout, knockdown, inhibitor). Sufficient: add X → the process starts or increases (overexpression).
Controls: a non-targeting guide or RNA; rescue (put back X and the effect disappears); a second, independent tool.


This slide is the logic behind every experiment in this lecture. Imagine you observe that cells with more protein X divide faster. Three stories fit this observation. X may drive division. Dividing cells may simply make more X, so the arrow goes the other way. Or a third factor, such as a growth signal, may raise both, and X does nothing at all. Observation alone cannot tell these apart. You must change X and keep everything else the same. If removing X stops division, X is necessary. If adding X causes division, X is sufficient. Many proteins are necessary but not sufficient. Controls make the result believable. A control guide RNA or RNA that targets nothing shows that the treatment itself does no harm. A rescue experiment, where you put back a version of X that the tool cannot hit, should bring the process back; if it does, the effect really came from losing X and not from an off-target. And a second tool that acts in a different way, giving the same result, makes the conclusion much stronger.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Worked example: is protein X needed for cell division?
text:
Worked example: is protein X needed for cell division?








Step
Choice
Why




Cells
A human cell line that divides well (e.g. HeLa or RPE1)
Easy to grow, many divisions to measure


Perturbation 1
RNAi against X, and a non-targeting control RNA
Fast; partial loss is fine for a first test


Check
Western blot for X, with a loading control
Did X actually go down?


Readout
Count cells over 4 days; flow cytometry of DNA content (cell-cycle phase)
Do cells divide less? Where do they stop?


Perturbation 2
CRISPR knockout, plus a rescue with X put back
Independent tool; rules out off-targets


Location
Fractionation or immunofluorescence
Where does X act?



Conclusion only if both tools agree and the rescue works.

Let us put the methods together on protein X. Suppose we want to know whether X is needed for cell division. We pick a human cell line that divides well. As a first, quick test we use RNA interference against X, side by side with a control RNA that targets nothing. Before we look at the cells we check with a western blot that X really went down, with a loading control in every lane; a perturbation that did not work tells you nothing. The readout is the number of cells over a few days, and flow cytometry of DNA content, which tells us in which phase of the cell cycle the cells get stuck; you will understand that readout fully in the cell-cycle lectures. If division slows, we confirm with a second tool, a CRISPR knockout, and do a rescue by adding back X. Finally we ask where X is, by fractionation or imaging. Only when the independent tools agree and the rescue works do we write that X is needed for division. This is the kind of reasoning the VG exam questions ask for.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Single-cell omics: a census of cells
text:
Single-cell omics: a census of cells


Each cell is put in its own droplet with a barcode; all its mRNAs are sequenced and counted.
Cells with similar mRNA sit together on a map: cell types, and sometimes new ones.
Cell atlases (e.g. the Human Cell Atlas) aim to map every cell type in the body.


Flow cytometry measures a dozen proteins per cell. Single-cell RNA sequencing goes much wider: it measures thousands of messenger RNAs in each of thousands of cells. A tissue is broken into single cells, and each cell is captured in a tiny droplet together with a bead that carries a unique DNA barcode. Inside the droplet, the cell’s mRNAs are copied and tagged with that barcode, so after sequencing every read can be traced back to its cell. The result is a large table of cells by genes. A computer then places cells with similar expression close together on a map, and groups of cells appear: T cells, B cells, macrophages, epithelial cells, and sometimes a small group that nobody had described before. International projects such as the Human Cell Atlas use this to make a reference map of all cell types in the human body. One cell type found this way was the ionocyte in the airways, a rare cell with very high levels of the cystic fibrosis channel CFTR. For this course, the main idea is enough: the same principle as flow cytometry, many single cells, but measuring the whole transcriptome.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Why it matters: finding drugs in cultured cells
text:
Why it matters: finding drugs in cultured cells



High-content screening: thousands of compounds, each in its own well with cultured cells; an automated microscope images every well.
A computer scores each well: did cells stop dividing, die, change shape, move a protein?
Example: monastrol was found in such a screen for compounds that block mitosis. It inhibits the motor protein kinesin-5, which builds the mitotic spindle.
Hits from screens are the first step of drug development, long before animals or patients.







Preparing a 384-well plate for a high-throughput screen.


Everything in this lecture comes together in drug discovery. In a high-content screen, cultured cells are grown in plates with 384 or more small wells. Each well gets a different compound from a library of many thousands. After a day or two, the cells are fixed and stained, and an automated microscope takes images of every well. Software then measures many features per cell: number of cells, nucleus size, cell shape, where a fluorescent protein sits. Compounds that cause the change you are looking for are called hits. A classic example is monastrol. In a screen for compounds that arrest cells in mitosis, researchers found a small molecule that gave cells a single round spindle instead of the normal two-poled one. It turned out to inhibit kinesin-5, a motor protein that pushes the spindle poles apart; you will meet motor proteins in the cytoskeleton lectures. Kinesin-5 inhibitors were later tested as cancer drugs. A hit like this is only the first step; the later programme course on clinical trials and drug development covers the long road from hit to medicine.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Why it matters: CAR-T cells, a living drug
text:
Why it matters: CAR-T cells, a living drug


A patient’s own T cells are given a new receptor, a CAR, that recognises a protein on cancer cells (here CD19 on B-cell leukaemia).
Every step uses this lecture: cell culture to grow them, flow cytometry to check them.


The second example is a therapy that is itself a cultured cell. CAR-T therapy treats some leukaemias and lymphomas that come from B cells. Blood is taken from the patient and the T cells are isolated. A gene for a chimeric antigen receptor, a CAR, is added. The outside part of the CAR comes from an antibody and binds CD19, a protein on the surface of B cells; the inside part gives the T cell its “go” signal. The modified T cells are grown in culture for one to two weeks until there are enough of them. Before they are given back, they are checked by flow cytometry: what percentage carry the CAR, and are they the right kind of cells? Then they are infused into the same patient, where they find and kill the cancer B cells. So cell culture, antibodies and flow cytometry, three methods from this lecture, are part of making the medicine. You will learn how T cells recognise and kill their targets in the later immunology course.

title: Taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Cell culture gives material to work on: cell lines are easy and reproducible, primary cells and organoids are closer to the body. Check identity and contamination.
Fractionation (differential and density-gradient centrifugation) separates organelles; marker proteins show what is in each fraction.
Antibodies find one protein: western blot (size and amount), immunoprecipitation (partners), immunofluorescence (location).
Flow cytometry measures many single cells; gating picks populations; FACS sorts them.
Perturbations (inhibitor, RNAi, CRISPR, overexpression) test whether a protein is necessary or sufficient; controls and a second tool make the conclusion strong.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 8.
Image credits

To sum up. Cell culture is the basis: cell lines for convenience, primary cells and organoids for realism, and always a check that your cells are what you think. Fractionation separates organelles by size and density, and marker proteins tell you which fraction is which. Antibodies are the most used tool: in a western blot they report size and amount, in immunoprecipitation they pull out a protein and its partners, and in immunofluorescence they show where it is. Flow cytometry turns this into single-cell numbers, and a sorter can collect living cells of one kind. Finally, to learn what a protein does you must change it, with an inhibitor, RNA interference, CRISPR or overexpression, and think carefully about necessary versus sufficient and about controls. These methods return in every later lecture, in the “How do we know?” slides, and in the lab part of the course.

title: Study questions: taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. [ELO 1] Describe the difference between primary cells, cell lines and organoids. Give one research question for which each is the best choice.






Model answer






Primary cells are taken directly from a tissue and divide a limited number of times. Best when you need normal behaviour, e.g. how freshly isolated T cells respond to a signal.
Cell lines divide without limit (usually from a tumour or immortalised). Best for large, repeated or reproducible experiments, e.g. a screen of many compounds, or a standard microscopy experiment.
Organoids are 3D structures grown from stem cells that contain several cell types of an organ. Best when tissue organisation or a patient’s own cells matter, e.g. testing which drug works on gut organoids from a patient with cystic fibrosis.





2. [ELO 1] Explain why a researcher must check (a) the identity of a cell line and (b) whether the culture contains Mycoplasma. How is each checked?






Model answer






Many cell lines have been taken over by other lines (often HeLa), so experiments may be done on the wrong cell type. Identity is checked with a DNA fingerprint (STR profile) compared with a reference. (b) Mycoplasma are tiny bacteria without a cell wall; they are invisible in the microscope and not killed by common antibiotics, but they change the cells’ metabolism and gene expression. They are detected with a PCR test.





3. [ELO 1] Describe how you would separate nuclei, mitochondria and cytosol from a liver homogenate by differential centrifugation. Explain the principle.






Model answer





Break the cells gently in an isotonic buffer (homogenisation). Spin at low speed (around 1,000 g, ~10 min): nuclei pellet. Spin the supernatant faster (around 10,000–20,000 g): mitochondria (with lysosomes and peroxisomes) pellet. After a very strong spin (>100,000 g), which pellets microsomes and ribosomes, the remaining supernatant is the cytosol. Principle: larger and denser particles sediment faster, so increasing force and time pellets smaller and smaller particles.




4. [ELO 1] What is a marker protein, and why is it needed in a fractionation experiment?






Model answer





A marker protein is a protein known to be found in only one organelle (e.g. calnexin for ER, TOM20 for mitochondria). Fractions are not labelled and are never completely pure, so staining each fraction for markers (by western blot) shows which organelle is in which fraction and how pure it is. A new protein that follows one marker probably lives in that organelle.




5. [ELO 1] Describe the steps of a western blot, and say what the position and the intensity of a band tell you.






Model answer





Proteins in a cell lysate are separated by size with SDS-PAGE, transferred to a membrane, and the membrane is incubated with a primary antibody against the target and a secondary antibody with an enzyme that produces light (or a fluorophore). The position shows the size of the protein (checks that the right protein was detected); the intensity, compared between lanes and normalised to a loading control, shows the relative amount.




6. [ELO 1] Explain how a flow cytometer measures cells, and what forward scatter, side scatter and fluorescence tell you. How does a cell sorter collect one kind of cell?






Model answer





Cells in suspension are lined up by sheath fluid and pass a laser one at a time. Forward scatter relates to cell size, side scatter to internal granularity, and fluorescence in each colour to how much of a labelled molecule (antibody or fluorescent protein) the cell carries. In a sorter (FACS) the stream breaks into droplets; a droplet containing a wanted cell is given an electric charge and deflected by charged plates into a collection tube.




7. [ELO 1] Compare RNAi knockdown and CRISPR knockout: what each acts on, how complete and how lasting the effect is, and one pitfall of each.






Model answer





RNAi acts on the mRNA: the protein drops partly (often 70–90 %) for a few days; pitfall: incomplete loss and off-target effects on similar mRNAs. CRISPR acts on the gene: the cut, repaired with small insertions or deletions, shifts the reading frame, giving a complete and permanent loss; pitfall: it takes weeks to make a knockout line, so cells may adapt (compensate), and the guide can cut elsewhere (off-targets).




8. [ELO 1] Explain the difference between a correlation and a causal effect, using an example from cell biology. Which kind of experiment shows a causal effect?






Model answer





Example: cells with more protein X divide faster. This correlation may mean X drives division, that dividing cells make more X, or that a third factor (a growth signal) raises both. A perturbation experiment shows causation: change X (remove or add it) while keeping everything else the same, with proper controls, and see whether division changes.

title: Study questions: taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
9. [ELO 1] [VG] A student treats cells with siRNA against protein Y and finds that the cells die. The student concludes that Y is needed for survival. List three things that could make this conclusion wrong, and describe the experiments that would rule each of them out.






Model answer






The treatment itself kills cells (transfection is toxic). Control: a non-targeting control siRNA handled the same way.
Y was not actually reduced, or the effect came from another protein (off-target). Controls: western blot for Y with a loading control; use a second siRNA with a different sequence, or a CRISPR knockout; do a rescue by expressing a version of Y that the siRNA cannot target: if the cells now survive, the effect was due to losing Y.
The result only holds for this cell line (e.g. a cancer line that depends on Y). Test another cell type, ideally primary cells. A strong answer also notes that “needed for survival” means necessary, and says nothing about how Y acts.





10. [ELO 1] [VG] You want to know whether a newly found protein Z is in mitochondria or in peroxisomes, two organelles of similar size. Design an experiment using fractionation, and say how you would interpret the result. Name one weakness and one complementary method.






Model answer





Homogenise cells gently, remove nuclei with a low-speed spin, then separate the organelles on a density gradient (peroxisomes are denser than mitochondria). Collect fractions and run a western blot of each fraction for Z, a mitochondrial marker (e.g. TOM20) and a peroxisome marker (e.g. catalase). If the Z profile follows TOM20, Z is mitochondrial; if it follows catalase, peroxisomal. Weakness: fractions overlap and organelles can break or stick together, so the result is a distribution, not proof; Z could also be in both. Complementary method: immunofluorescence of Z together with a marker for each organelle (co-localisation), ideally with super-resolution, or a GFP-tagged Z in living cells.




11. [ELO 1] [VG] A drug kills a leukaemia cell line in a dish at low concentration. Explain why this is not enough to say that the drug will work in patients, using at least three differences between a cell line in culture and cancer cells in a body. Suggest one better model.






Model answer





Differences: (1) a cell line has adapted to culture and may have extra mutations; patients’ tumours vary between people; (2) in a dish the drug reaches the cells directly, while in the body it must be absorbed, distributed and not broken down too fast (pharmacokinetics); (3) the body has normal cells that may also be harmed (toxicity), and the dish has none; (4) a tumour has a microenvironment (blood vessels, immune cells, stroma) that culture lacks. Better models: primary cells or organoids from patients, followed by animal studies, before clinical trials, the topic of the later course on drug development.

title: Study questions: taking cells apart and perturbing them
section: Explore
text:
Explore
A simulated blood sample (white blood cells after the red cells were removed), stained with antibodies against CD4 and CD8. Plot 1 shows every event by forward and side scatter; plot 2 shows only the events inside your gate, by CD4 and CD8 fluorescence, with quadrant lines and the percentage in each quadrant. Drag the corners of the gate or the whole gate, or press Draw a new gate and draw around a cloud. Drag the orange point to move the quadrant lines. Check my gate compares your result with the true composition of the sample (which a real experiment never tells you). The numbers are illustrative but of the right kind for human blood.



E1. [ELO 1] Start with the healthy donor and the start gate. Which clouds in plot 1 are lymphocytes, monocytes, granulocytes and debris (use what you know about size and granularity, then tick “show the true cell types” to check)? Read the four quadrant percentages, then press Check my gate. What is wrong with the start gate, and in which direction does it push the CD4 T-cell percentage? Fix the gate and check again.
E2. [ELO 1] With a good lymphocyte gate, move the vertical (CD4) line far to the left, to about \(10^1\). What happens to the percentages, and why? How do you decide where a quadrant line belongs in a real experiment?
E3. [ELO 1] [VG] Predict first. HIV infects and kills CD4 T cells. Before you switch to Untreated HIV infection, predict how plot 2 and the CD4/CD8 ratio will change. Then switch, gate properly and report the four percentages and the ratio. Now go back to the start gate (Reset gate): how wrong would the CD4 percentage be, and why is this error worse than in the healthy donor?
E4. [ELO 1] [VG] A colleague draws a very small gate around the centre of the lymphocyte cloud (about a quarter of the lymphocytes). The gate is 100 % pure. Is the result wrong, or only less precise? When could a tight gate give a biased result?






Solutions





E1. Debris is the small, low-scatter cloud in the corner (low FSC and SSC). Lymphocytes are small and smooth (low FSC, low SSC), monocytes larger with a little more side scatter, and granulocytes large and very granular (high SSC). The start gate is too big: besides about 1175 lymphocytes it holds about 280 monocytes and a few granulocytes and debris particles (purity 80 %). Monocytes carry a little CD4, so with the quadrant line at \(10^2\) they land in the CD4+ quadrant: the start gate reports 54 % “CD4 T cells” against a true 46 %, and a CD4/CD8 ratio of 2.7 against a true 1.8. A gate drawn tightly around the lymphocyte cloud (FSC about 220–450, SSC below about 200) gives 45 % CD4, 25 % CD8, 28 % neither and 2 % both, within a point of the truth.
E2. The CD4-negative cells (CD8 T cells, B and NK cells) are not at zero: they have some background fluorescence (autofluorescence and some non-specific antibody binding), spread around about \(10^{0.75}\). A line at \(10^1\) cuts through this cloud, so part of the CD8 T cells move into “both” (from 2 % to about 7 %) and part of the double-negative cells move into “CD4” (from 45 % to 50 %); the CD4/CD8 ratio goes from 1.8 to 2.4. A quadrant line belongs in the gap between the negative and the positive cloud, and in a real experiment its position is set with controls: unstained cells, cells stained with only one antibody, or “fluorescence-minus-one” controls (all antibodies except one).
E3. Expected: far fewer cells in the lower-right (CD4) quadrant, more in the upper-left (CD8), and a CD4/CD8 ratio well below 1 (healthy is about 1–3). With a good gate: CD4 about 16 %, CD8 about 54 %, neither about 28 %, both about 2 %; ratio about 0.3. With the start gate the CD4 value is about 33 %: double the truth, because the about 290 monocytes are now counted next to only about 155 real CD4 T cells. The fewer real CD4 T cells there are, the larger the relative error from contaminating cells, which is exactly the situation in which the clinic needs an accurate number. (Clinics also report the absolute CD4 count per µL of blood, using counting beads.)
E4. Mostly only less precise: if the cells in the centre of the cloud are a random sample of all lymphocytes, the percentages are right on average but have a larger random error, because fewer cells are counted (with about 330 cells the demo gives 48 % CD4 and 24 % CD8 instead of 46 % and 25 %). A tight gate becomes biased when the cells it leaves out differ from those it keeps. For example, activated or dividing lymphocytes are larger (higher FSC) and would be cut off at the edge of the cloud, so a study of activated cells would undercount them. That is why gates follow the shape of the whole population and are checked with backgating.

title: Explore a real HeLa cell
text:
The cell map in the lecture is a cartoon. This is the real thing: one slice through a HeLa cell, imaged by electron microscopy. The slice runs parallel to the culture dish, through the nucleus. It covers 48 × 26 µm; each pixel is 12 nm. The coloured outlines mark the organelles.
How to use it. Drag to move; zoom with the mouse wheel, by pinching, or with the + / − buttons (⤢ shows the whole slice). The scale bar updates as you zoom. Tick the layers on and off. title: Explore a real HeLa cell
section: Tasks
text:
Tasks
E1. [ELO 1] Zoom in on a mitochondrion until the scale bar shows 200 nm or 500 nm. How wide is it? Now look at the dark grains in the cytoplasm around it (ribosomes, about 25 nm). Which of the two could a light microscope (limit about 200 nm) show as separate objects, and which not?
E2. [ELO 5] Find the Golgi apparatus (switch off all layers except Golgi to find it, then switch everything back on). What lies close to it? Why does it make sense that the Golgi sits next to the nucleus and the centrosome?
E3. [ELO 5] Look along the edge of the nucleus and at the ER around it. Find a place where you can see that the nuclear envelope is two membranes. Can you find a mitochondrion that an ER tube touches?
E4. [VG] [ELO 1] Mitochondria, ER and the centrosome seem to lie inside the nucleus in this picture. Use what you know about the nuclear envelope to explain what you are really seeing, and say how you could check it with the same dataset.
E5. [ELO 1, 5] Switch to Find the organelle and play one round. Aim for at least 8 of 10 on the first try. Which organelles were hardest, and what feature finally gave them away?






Solutions





E1. Most mitochondria in this slice are about 0.3–0.6 µm wide (measured on the outlines: median about 0.4 µm) and up to a few µm long, so they are above the 200 nm limit: a light microscope shows them as separate objects (but not their cristae). Ribosomes are about 25 nm, eight times below the limit: in a light microscope they would merge into a uniform haze. This is why the inside of organelles was unknown until electron microscopy.
E2. The Golgi is a stack of curved, parallel membranes just to the right of the nucleus, with small vesicles around it. Close by are the nucleus and the ER around it; the centrosome lies about 8 µm to the left, inside the fold of the nucleus (in 3D the two are probably closer than in this single plane). Proteins leave the ER, which is continuous with the nuclear envelope, in vesicles and travel only a short way to the Golgi. The centrosome organises the microtubules, and the Golgi is held near it by microtubules and motor proteins; from there vesicles travel out along microtubules to the cell surface (lectures on the Golgi and on microtubules).
E3. At high zoom the edge of the nucleus shows two thin dark lines with a narrow light gap between them, interrupted where nuclear pores are. In several places ER tubes continue from the outer nuclear membrane. ER tubes touching mitochondria are common in this cell (look at the red outlines with teal outlines right next to them): these are ER–mitochondria contact sites, where lipids and Ca²⁺ pass between the organelles (lecture: organelles compared).
E4. The cytoplasm is not inside the nucleus. The nuclear envelope is a closed double membrane, and the nucleus here has a deep fold (invagination): cytoplasm reaches into it like a finger pushed into a balloon. A slice through the fold shows a ring of nucleus with cytoplasm in the middle; the nuclear envelope runs all around the inner patch too. To check: look at neighbouring planes of the same 3D volume (for example in the OpenOrganelle viewer). Going up or down through the cell, the inner patch should connect to the main cytoplasm, which shows that it is a fold and not a separate compartment. A single 2D section can mislead; 3D data answers the question.
E5. Your own answer. Typical difficulties: the centrosome (tiny: look for the cartwheel-like ring of nine triplets near the Golgi), the nucleolus (no membrane: look for the dense, evenly grey patch inside the nucleus), the lipid droplet (round, evenly grey, with no membrane line) and telling endosomes and lysosomes from ER or mitochondria (no cristae, round, often dark and dense or full of small vesicles).

title: Study questions: a tour of the cell
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. [ELO 1] Draw a simple animal cell and label the plasma membrane, nucleus, nuclear envelope, rough ER, Golgi apparatus, a mitochondrion, a lysosome and the cytosol. Give one function for each labelled part.






Model answer






Plasma membrane: barrier between cell and outside; controls what enters and leaves.
Nucleus: stores the DNA; transcription happens here.
Nuclear envelope: two membranes with pores; separates nucleoplasm from cytosol but lets molecules pass through pores. The outer membrane continues into the ER.
Rough ER: has ribosomes on its surface; makes membrane proteins and proteins for secretion.
Golgi apparatus: modifies proteins (adds and trims sugar chains) and sorts them to their destination.
Mitochondrion: makes most of the ATP by oxidative phosphorylation.
Lysosome: digests material at about pH 5.
Cytosol: the fluid between organelles; protein synthesis on free ribosomes and much of metabolism (for example glycolysis).





2. [ELO 1] List three differences between a prokaryotic and a eukaryotic cell. Why is it an advantage for a large cell to have internal membranes?






Model answer





Differences: eukaryotes have a nucleus with a nuclear envelope (prokaryote DNA lies in the cytosol); eukaryotes have membrane-bound organelles (ER, Golgi, mitochondria, lysosomes); eukaryotic cells are about 1000 times larger in volume; eukaryotes have an extensive cytoskeleton with motor proteins. Advantage: internal membranes give more membrane area for membrane-bound reactions, and they divide the cell into compartments with different chemistry (for example acidic lysosomes, calcium-rich ER), so incompatible reactions can run at the same time.




3. [ELO 1] Explain what is meant by the lumen of an organelle. Which compartments are topologically equivalent to the outside of the cell, and why?






Model answer





The lumen is the space inside a membrane-bound organelle, on the opposite side of its membrane from the cytosol. The lumens of the ER, the nuclear envelope (the gap between its two membranes), the Golgi, transport vesicles, endosomes and lysosomes are topologically equivalent to the outside of the cell. Material moves between them, and to and from the outside, by vesicles that bud from one membrane and fuse with another, so it never crosses a membrane and never enters the cytosol.




4. [ELO 1] The nucleoplasm is surrounded by two membranes, yet it is said to be on the same side as the cytosol. Explain.






Model answer





The nuclear envelope has nuclear pores: large channels that join the nucleoplasm and the cytosol. Molecules move between them through the pores without crossing a lipid bilayer. The space between the two nuclear membranes, however, is continuous with the ER lumen and is on the lumen side.




5. [ELO 1] Give typical sizes (order of magnitude) for: a protein, a ribosome, a virus, a bacterium, a nucleus and an animal cell. Which of these can you resolve in a light microscope without special methods?






Model answer





Protein ~5 nm; ribosome ~25 nm; virus ~100 nm; bacterium ~1–2 µm; nucleus ~5–10 µm; animal cell ~10–20 µm. The light microscope resolves objects larger than about 0.2 µm, so the bacterium, nucleus and cell can be resolved (and mitochondria, about 1 µm wide). Proteins, ribosomes and most viruses are too small to resolve; single molecules can only be detected if they carry a fluorescent label.




6. [ELO 1] A mammalian cell contains about \(10^9\)–\(10^{10}\) protein molecules in a volume of a few picolitres. What does this mean for the physical state of the cytoplasm, and how fast does a typical protein move across the cell?






Model answer





The protein concentration is a few hundred mg/mL, so the cytoplasm is crowded: more like a gel than a dilute solution. A typical protein diffuses with \(D \approx 5\)–\(10\ \mu\text{m}^2/\text{s}\) in cytoplasm; with \(t \approx x^2/6D\) it crosses a 10 µm cell in a few seconds.




7. [ELO 5] Compare the mitochondrion and the lysosome: number of membranes, main function, and the chemistry of the inner space.






Model answer





Mitochondrion: two membranes (outer and folded inner membrane); main function ATP production by oxidative phosphorylation (also involved in starting apoptosis); the matrix is a separate space with its own DNA and ribosomes, not part of the lumen side. Lysosome: one membrane; digests proteins, lipids and other material; acidic lumen (pH about 4.5–5) full of digestive enzymes; part of the lumen side (reached by vesicles from endosomes).




8. [ELO 1] What is a cell line? Give two reasons why HeLa cells became so widely used, and two reasons to be careful when interpreting results from them.






Model answer





A cell line is a population of cells that divides without limit in culture; normal cells stop after about 40–60 divisions. HeLa became widely used because it was the first human cell line (1951), it grows fast and robustly, and it can be shipped and shared, for example to test the polio vaccine. Reasons for caution: HeLa cells are cancer cells with an abnormal genome (around 76–80 chromosomes) and HPV-18 proteins that disable cell-cycle brakes; they grow flat on plastic, not in a tissue; and HeLa has contaminated many other cell lines, so the identity of a cell line must be checked with a DNA test.

title: Study questions: a tour of the cell
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
9. [ELO 1] [VG] A membrane protein has its N-terminus in the ER lumen and its C-terminus in the cytosol. Predict the orientation of the protein (a) in the membrane of a transport vesicle, (b) in the Golgi membrane and (c) in the plasma membrane. A researcher adds an antibody against the N-terminus to living, intact cells. Will the antibody bind? Explain.






Model answer






In the vesicle, the N-terminus faces the vesicle lumen, the C-terminus the cytosol. (b) In the Golgi, the N-terminus faces the Golgi lumen. (c) In the plasma membrane, the N-terminus faces the outside of the cell. The orientation never changes because vesicles bud and fuse without the protein flipping, and the lumen side is topologically equivalent to the outside. The antibody will bind on living cells, because the N-terminus is exposed on the cell surface and an antibody cannot cross the plasma membrane. An antibody against the C-terminus would not bind to intact cells; it would bind only after the membrane is made permeable (for example with a detergent). This is a standard experiment to determine membrane topology.





10. [ELO 1] [VG] You want to know whether a drug that is toxic to the liver damages mitochondria. You can use HeLa cells, budding yeast or organoids grown from human liver cells. Choose a system, justify your choice, and name one thing your system cannot tell you. Suggest a first experiment.






Model answer





A good answer chooses and justifies, and names a limitation. For example: human liver organoids are the best first choice because they are human, contain liver-like cells that metabolise drugs as the liver does (many liver toxins become toxic only after liver enzymes modify them), and can be grown from several donors. Limitation: no blood supply, immune system or other organs, so they cannot show effects that depend on the whole body (for example inflammation, or drug levels in blood). HeLa cells are easier but are cancer cells that may not metabolise the drug like liver cells and rely less on mitochondria. Yeast is good for finding which genes make cells sensitive, but is not human and has a cell wall that may block the drug. First experiment: treat organoids with a range of drug concentrations and an untreated control, then measure mitochondrial function (for example with a dye whose uptake depends on the mitochondrial membrane potential, viewed by fluorescence microscopy) and cell survival, with replicate cultures.




11. [ELO 1] [VG] In a textbook from 1950, the cytoplasm of a cell is described as “a structureless gel with some granules”. Explain, with reference to sizes and methods, why scientists at that time could not see most of the structures on today’s cell map, and which two methods changed this.






Model answer





The light microscope cannot resolve structures closer than about 0.2 µm. Ribosomes (~25 nm), ER membranes (a bilayer is ~5 nm thick, ER tubes ~50–100 nm across) and the inner structure of mitochondria are below this limit, and unstained membranes give little contrast. So the cytoplasm looked structureless, with mitochondria as small granules. Two methods changed this: electron microscopy of thin sections (resolution down to about a nanometre), which showed the ER, ribosomes, Golgi stacks and cristae; and cell fractionation by centrifugation, which separated the parts and showed what each did (for example lysosomes with digestive enzymes). Combining the two gave the modern map.
