title: Glossary
section: The cell and how we study it
text:
The cell and how we study it

A tour of the cell
See A tour of the cell.
Cytosol: the fluid part of the cell between the organelles, where free ribosomes make proteins and much of metabolism takes place.
Cytoplasm: everything inside the plasma membrane except the nucleus: the cytosol plus the organelles.
Organelle: a membrane-bound compartment inside a eukaryotic cell with its own job, such as the ER or a mitochondrion.
Lumen: the space inside a membrane-bound organelle, on the other side of its membrane from the cytosol.
Topology (membrane): which side of a membrane a space or a part of a protein lies on; the lumen of the ER, Golgi, vesicles and lysosomes is topologically equivalent to the outside of the cell.
Nuclear envelope: the two membranes around the nucleus, crossed by nuclear pores; the outer membrane continues into the ER.
Nuclear pore: a large protein channel in the nuclear envelope that joins the nucleoplasm to the cytosol.
Endoplasmic reticulum (ER): a network of membrane sheets and tubes that makes membrane and secreted proteins (rough ER) and lipids (smooth ER), and stores Ca²⁺.
Golgi apparatus: a stack of flattened membrane compartments that modifies proteins from the ER, for example by adding sugar chains, and sorts them to their destinations.
Lysosome: an acidic organelle (pH about 5) full of digestive enzymes that breaks down material taken up by the cell or from the cell itself.
Model system: a simpler organism or cell type (yeast, a cell line, an organoid) chosen because it answers a question more easily than a human body can.
Informed consent: a person’s voluntary agreement, after being told the purpose and risks, to let their tissue or data be used in research.
Cell fractionation: breaking cells open and separating their parts, usually by centrifugation, to find out what each part does.


Seeing cells: microscopy
See Seeing cells: microscopy.
Resolution: the smallest distance at which two points can still be seen as two separate points.
Magnification: how much larger the image is than the object; it adds no detail beyond the resolution limit.
Numerical aperture, NA: how wide a cone of light an objective collects; a higher NA gives better resolution.
Phase-contrast microscopy: turns small delays of light in dense cell parts into differences in brightness, so living unstained cells become visible.
Differential interference contrast, DIC: shows steep changes in optical path as light and shadow, so cells look three-dimensional.
Fluorophore: a molecule that absorbs light of one wavelength and emits light of a longer wavelength.
Stokes shift: the difference in wavelength between a fluorophore’s excitation peak and emission peak.
Dichroic mirror: a mirror that reflects light below a certain wavelength and lets longer wavelengths pass; it separates excitation light from emitted light.
Immunofluorescence: labelling a protein in fixed, permeabilised cells with antibodies coupled, directly or through a secondary antibody, to a fluorophore.
Green fluorescent protein, GFP: a jellyfish protein that forms its own fluorescent group, used as a genetic tag to see proteins in living cells.
Fusion protein: one protein chain made from two genes joined in the same reading frame, for example a protein of interest joined to GFP.
Confocal microscopy: fluorescence microscopy in which a pinhole blocks out-of-focus light, giving a sharp optical section of a thick sample.
Photobleaching: the permanent loss of fluorescence when a fluorophore is destroyed by repeated excitation.
Super-resolution microscopy: light-microscopy methods, such as STED and PALM/STORM, that resolve details below the ~200 nm limit.
Transmission electron microscopy, TEM: electrons pass through an ultrathin, heavy-metal-stained section, showing structures inside the cell at about 1–2 nm.
Scanning electron microscopy, SEM: images the 3D surface of a metal-coated sample by scanning it with a fine electron beam.
Cryo-electron microscopy, cryo-EM: electron microscopy of rapidly frozen samples in glass-like ice; averaging many images of one protein gives its 3D structure.


Taking cells apart and perturbing them
Cell line: a population of cells that has been made immortal and can be grown in culture without limit.
Primary cells: cells taken directly from a tissue, which divide only a limited number of times in culture.
Organoid: a small 3D structure grown from stem cells that contains several cell types of an organ, arranged roughly as in the tissue.
Mycoplasma: very small bacteria without a cell wall that often contaminate cell cultures unnoticed and change how the cells behave.
Differential centrifugation: separating cell components by spinning at increasing speeds, so larger and denser particles form a pellet first.
Density-gradient centrifugation: separating particles by spinning them through a solution that gets denser towards the bottom, so each stops at its own density.
Marker protein: a protein known to be found in only one organelle, used to identify that organelle in a fraction.
Epitope: the small part of a target molecule that an antibody binds.
Western blot: separates proteins by size, transfers them to a membrane and detects one protein with antibodies.
Immunoprecipitation: using an antibody on beads to pull a protein, and the proteins bound to it, out of a cell lysate.
Flow cytometry: measuring light scatter and fluorescence of single cells as they pass a laser one at a time.
Gating: choosing a region in a flow cytometry plot so that only one population of cells is analysed further.
RNA interference, RNAi: lowering the amount of a protein with a short double-stranded RNA that leads to the matching mRNA being cut.
Knockout: disabling a gene completely, for example by a CRISPR-Cas9 cut that causes a frameshift.

title: Glossary
section: Membranes and transport
text:
Membranes and transport

Membrane structure
See Membrane structure.
Amphipathic: describes a molecule with one part that likes water (polar) and one part that avoids water (hydrophobic).
Hydrophobic effect: the tendency of non-polar groups to gather together in water, driven mainly by the rise in entropy of the water molecules they release.
Lipid bilayer: two layers of lipid molecules with their tails facing inwards, forming the basic sealed structure of every cell membrane.
Membrane fluidity: how easily lipids and proteins move within the plane of a membrane, set by tail length, double bonds, cholesterol and temperature.
Flip-flop: movement of a lipid from one leaflet of the bilayer to the other, which is very rare without the help of enzymes.
Flippase: an ATP-driven enzyme that moves specific lipids, such as phosphatidylserine, from the outer to the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
Scramblase: a membrane protein that, when switched on, lets lipids move in both directions between leaflets without using energy, so their asymmetry is lost.
Lipid raft: a proposed small, short-lived membrane domain rich in sphingolipids and cholesterol that may gather certain proteins.
Integral membrane protein: a protein with parts embedded in the hydrophobic core of the bilayer, which can be released only with a detergent.
GPI anchor: a glycolipid attached to the end of a protein that holds the protein on the outer surface of the plasma membrane.
Hydropathy plot: a graph of average hydrophobicity along a protein sequence, used to predict transmembrane α-helices.
Detergent: a small amphipathic molecule with one tail that forms micelles and can dissolve membranes to extract membrane proteins.
FRAP: fluorescence recovery after photobleaching; a laser bleaches a small spot and you measure how fast fluorescent molecules diffuse back in.
Freeze-fracture electron microscopy: splitting a frozen membrane between its two leaflets, which shows the integral proteins as particles in a metal replica.
Glycocalyx: the coat of sugar chains on glycoproteins, glycolipids and proteoglycans that covers the outside of the cell.
Lipid nanoparticle (LNP): a small particle of ionisable lipid, helper phospholipid, cholesterol and PEG-lipid that carries RNA into cells.


Transporters and pumps
See Transporters and pumps.
Simple diffusion: movement of a molecule straight through the lipid bilayer, down its concentration gradient, without help from a protein.
Passive transport: movement of a solute down its (electro)chemical gradient (ΔG < 0); it needs no energy input but may need a transport protein as a path.
Active transport: movement of a solute against its (electro)chemical gradient (ΔG > 0), driven by ATP hydrolysis or by another gradient.
Electrochemical gradient: the combined driving force on an ion from its concentration difference and from the voltage across the membrane.
Transporter (carrier): a membrane protein that binds a specific solute and changes shape to move it across the membrane, one or a few molecules per cycle.
Alternating access: the mechanism by which a transporter’s binding site faces first one side of the membrane and then the other, never both at once.
Uniport: transport of a single kind of solute by a transporter, always down its gradient (e.g. GLUT1).
Symport: coupled transport of two different solutes in the same direction by one transporter (e.g. SGLT1: 2 Na⁺ + 1 glucose).
Antiport: coupled transport of two different solutes in opposite directions by one transporter (e.g. the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger).
Secondary active transport: uphill transport of a solute driven by the downhill flow of another ion, usually Na⁺ or H⁺, whose gradient was made by a pump.
Na⁺/K⁺ pump (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase): a P-type pump in all animal cells that uses one ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ into the cell.
P-type pump: an ATP-driven pump that phosphorylates itself on an aspartate during each transport cycle (e.g. the Na⁺/K⁺ pump and the Ca²⁺ pumps).
ABC transporter: a pump with two ATP-binding cassettes that uses ATP to move substrates across a membrane; in human cells mostly exporters of lipids, toxins and drugs.
P-glycoprotein (ABCB1): an ABC exporter that pumps many hydrophobic drugs out of cells, causing multidrug resistance in cancer and limiting drug uptake into the gut and brain.
Aquaporin: a water channel that lets water, but not ions or H⁺, cross the membrane rapidly by osmosis.
SGLT2 inhibitor (gliflozin): a drug that blocks the kidney Na⁺–glucose symporter SGLT2, so glucose leaves in the urine; used in type 2 diabetes, heart failure and kidney disease.


Ion channels and membrane potential
See Ion channels and membrane potential.
Ion channel: a membrane protein that forms a water-filled pore through which specific ions flow rapidly down their electrochemical gradient when the channel is open.
Selectivity filter: the narrowest part of a channel pore, whose lining atoms decide which ion can pass; in K⁺ channels it is lined by backbone carbonyl oxygens.
Gating: the switching of a channel between closed and open states in response to a signal such as voltage, a bound ligand or mechanical force.
Voltage sensor: a transmembrane helix carrying positive charges that moves when the membrane potential changes, and so opens or closes a voltage-gated channel.
Equilibrium (Nernst) potential: the membrane potential at which an ion’s concentration and electrical forces balance, so its net flow through open channels is zero.
Nernst equation: \(E = \frac{RT}{zF}\ln\frac{c_\text{out}}{c_\text{in}}\), which gives the equilibrium potential of an ion from its concentrations and charge.
Resting membrane potential: the steady voltage across the plasma membrane of an unstimulated cell, about −70 mV, set mainly by open K⁺ leak channels.
Depolarisation: a change of the membrane potential towards less negative values.
Action potential: a brief, all-or-none electrical signal in which voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and then voltage-gated K⁺ channels restore the resting potential.
Refractory period: the short time after an action potential when inactivated Na⁺ channels cannot reopen, so a new action potential cannot start.
Patch clamp: a glass pipette sealed tightly onto a membrane records the tiny currents through single ion channels or a whole cell.
CFTR: an ATP- and phosphorylation-gated Cl⁻ channel in epithelial cells whose loss of function causes cystic fibrosis.
CFTR potentiator: a drug, such as ivacaftor, that increases the time a CFTR channel at the cell surface spends open.
CFTR corrector: a drug, such as elexacaftor or tezacaftor, that helps misfolded CFTR fold and leave the ER so that it reaches the plasma membrane.

section: About this lecture

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: The question: every cell is a small battery
text:
The question: every cell is a small battery


Put a fine electrode into almost any animal cell: the inside is about 70 mV more negative than the outside.
The membrane is only 5 nm thick, so the electric field across it is huge: about 14 million volts per metre.
Where does the voltage come from? How can a protein pore pass K⁺ but not the smaller Na⁺? And why does a child with cystic fibrosis taste salty?


If you push a very fine glass electrode into a cell and compare it with a second electrode in the fluid outside, the voltmeter reads about minus 70 millivolts. The inside is negative. That sounds small, a twentieth of a torch battery. But the membrane is only about 5 nanometres thick. Seventy millivolts across five nanometres is about fourteen million volts per metre, an electric field strong enough to move charged parts of proteins inside the membrane. Look also at the ion concentrations: potassium is about thirty times higher inside, sodium more than ten times higher outside. You saw in the transport lecture that the sodium-potassium pump builds these gradients. Today we connect the gradients to the voltage. Three puzzles guide the lecture. First, where does the voltage come from? Second, a potassium channel lets potassium through ten thousand times better than sodium, although sodium is the smaller ion. How? Third, an old European saying warned that a child who tastes salty when kissed will die young. We now know this is cystic fibrosis, a disease of one chloride channel.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Channels and transporters: two ways across
text:
Channels and transporters: two ways across
Recap: the bilayer stops ions; the Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to keep K⁺ high inside and Na⁺ high outside.

A channel is fast because nothing has to change shape for each ion. It can only let ions flow down their electrochemical gradient: passive transport.

In the transport lecture you met transporters. A transporter binds its solute, changes shape, and releases the solute on the other side. It is never open to both sides at the same time, which is why it can couple the movement of one solute to ATP or to another gradient, and pump uphill. The price is speed: each cycle needs a shape change, so a transporter moves a hundred to ten thousand molecules per second. A channel is different. When it is open, it is a water-filled pore through the membrane, and ions stream through one after another, up to a hundred million per second. That is close to the speed of free diffusion. But a channel can never pump: ions only go downhill, from high to low electrochemical potential. Channels have two more properties. They are selective: most let only one kind of ion through, for example potassium, sodium, calcium or chloride. And they are gated: they switch between open and closed, and the cell controls the switch. Rate, selectivity and gating are the three words to remember.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: How do we know? The structure of a K⁺ channel
text:
How do we know? The structure of a K⁺ channel







KcsA, a bacterial K⁺ channel (PDB 1K4C). Two of the four subunits are shown. K⁺ ions (purple) and water (red) sit in the selectivity filter, sites S1–S4.


1998: Roderick MacKinnon’s group solved the first atomic structure of an ion channel by X-ray crystallography: KcsA from the bacterium Streptomyces.
Four identical subunits form a ring around a central pore, like the staves of a barrel.
Most of the pore is wide and lined with water. Only a short part near the outside, the selectivity filter (about 1.2 nm long), is narrow.
The filter is lined by backbone carbonyl oxygens (C=O) of the sequence TVGYG, the same in K⁺ channels from bacteria to humans.
Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2003 (MacKinnon, with Peter Agre for water channels).



For decades, physiologists knew from electrical measurements that potassium channels were very selective and very fast, and they could not explain how both were possible. The answer came from a structure. Roderick MacKinnon chose a simple potassium channel from a soil bacterium, KcsA, because it could be made in large amounts and crystallised. In 1998 his group solved the structure by X-ray crystallography. The image shows two of the four identical subunits; the other two, in front and behind, are removed so you can see into the pore. Each subunit has two long helices that cross the membrane. The four subunits make a ring, and the pore runs down the middle. Most of the pore is wide and full of water. Near the outer end it narrows into the selectivity filter. Here, the protein backbone, not the side chains, points its carbonyl oxygen atoms into the pore. The filter sequence, threonine, valine, glycine, tyrosine, glycine, is conserved in potassium channels of bacteria, plants and humans. You can see four ion sites, with potassium ions and water molecules alternating. MacKinnon shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: The selectivity filter: why K⁺ passes and Na⁺ does not
text:
The selectivity filter: why K⁺ passes and Na⁺ does not


In water, every ion is wrapped in a shell of water molecules. To enter the narrow filter, the ion must lose its water, which costs energy.
For K⁺ (radius 0.13 nm), the filter’s carbonyl oxygens sit exactly where the water oxygens were: the energy is paid back.
Na⁺ is smaller (0.10 nm). The rigid filter cannot close in on it, so losing water is not paid back. Na⁺ stays out: about 1 in 10 000 ions that pass is Na⁺.


Here is the solution to the puzzle. An ion in water is never naked. Water molecules turn their partly negative oxygen atoms towards a positive ion and hold it tightly. Pulling these water molecules off costs a lot of energy. The selectivity filter is too narrow for an ion with its water shell, so an ion can only enter if it gives up its water. For potassium, the filter offers a perfect replacement. The carbonyl oxygens of the protein backbone are held by the rigid structure at the same distance from the ion as the water oxygens were. The potassium ion trades water oxygens for protein oxygens and hardly notices the change. Sodium is smaller. In water its shell is tighter. In the filter, the oxygens are too far away to touch it, and the filter is too stiff to close in. So for sodium, entering the filter means losing water without getting anything back. That costs too much, and sodium stays out. Speed comes from the same structure: two potassium ions sit in the filter at a time, and they repel each other, so one pushes the next one through.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Gating: three ways to open a channel
text:
Gating: three ways to open a channel


Voltage-gated: positive charges in a voltage-sensor helix are pulled by the membrane field. When the inside becomes less negative, the sensor moves and opens the gate.
Ligand-gated: a molecule binds and opens the pore. Two acetylcholine molecules open the receptor on a muscle cell; Na⁺ flows in.
Mechanically gated: tension in the membrane opens Piezo, a large three-bladed channel (Nobel Prize 2021, Patapoutian). Piezo2 lets you feel touch.


Most channels are closed most of the time and open only for a few milliseconds when they get a signal. There are three main kinds of signal. Voltage-gated channels have a voltage sensor: a helix that crosses the membrane and carries a positive charge at every third amino acid. At rest, the negative inside pulls these charges inwards. When the membrane depolarises, that is, the inside becomes less negative, the sensor moves outwards and pulls the gate open. Voltage-gated sodium channels in nerve and muscle open this way. Ligand-gated channels open when a molecule binds. The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the junction between nerve and muscle is a ring of five subunits; when two acetylcholine molecules bind, the pore opens and lets sodium and potassium through, mostly sodium in. Mechanically gated channels respond to force. The Piezo channels have three long blades that sit in the membrane; when the membrane is stretched, the blades flatten and the central pore opens. Piezo2 in skin nerve endings makes touch possible, and Piezo1 senses blood flow in vessels. You will meet more ligand-gated channels in the signalling lectures.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Two forces on an ion: the electrochemical gradient
text:
Two forces on an ion: the electrochemical gradient


Concentration: more K⁺ inside than outside pushes K⁺ out.
Voltage: a negative inside pulls positive ions in (and pushes negative ions out).
Together they make the electrochemical gradient. The ion flows until the two forces are equal: the equilibrium potential of that ion.


An ion feels two forces at once. The first is the concentration gradient, which you know from diffusion: potassium is about thirty times more concentrated inside, so potassium ions that find an open channel tend to leave. The second is the electrical force. Potassium is positive, and a negative inside pulls it back. The sum of these two is called the electrochemical gradient. Imagine you open only potassium channels. Potassium starts to flow out. Each ion that leaves takes a positive charge with it and leaves a negative charge behind, so the inside becomes more negative, and the electrical pull back grows. At some voltage the two forces balance. Ions still cross in both directions, but as many go in as come out, so there is no net flow. That voltage is the equilibrium potential of potassium, written E sub K. For potassium it is about minus 90 millivolts. Every ion has its own equilibrium potential, set by its own concentrations. On the next slide we calculate it from Gibbs energy.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: The Nernst equation from ΔG
text:
The Nernst equation from ΔG
You know \Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q. Move 1 mol of ion from outside to inside:

Same ion on both sides, so \Delta G^\circ = 0 and Q = c_\text{in}/c_\text{out}. Chemical part: \;RT \ln \dfrac{c_\text{in}}{c_\text{out}}
Moving charge z across the membrane potential V = V_\text{in} - V_\text{out} adds electrical work: \;zFV
Total: \quad \Delta G = RT \ln \dfrac{c_\text{in}}{c_\text{out}} + zFV
At equilibrium \Delta G = 0. Solve for V:

E_\text{ion} = \frac{RT}{zF}\,\ln\frac{c_\text{out}}{c_\text{in}}
R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, T = 310 K (37 °C), F = 96 485 C mol⁻¹, so RT/F \approx 26.7 mV. In base-10 logarithm: E \approx \dfrac{61.5\text{ mV}}{z}\,\log_{10}\dfrac{c_\text{out}}{c_\text{in}}: 61.5 mV per tenfold gradient for a +1 ion.

You already know this from chemistry, so we only need three steps. Take one mole of an ion and move it from outside to inside. The chemical part of the Gibbs energy is RT ln Q, where Q is the inside concentration over the outside concentration; delta G zero is zero because the ion is the same chemical on both sides. The new part is electrical. Moving a mole of charge z through a voltage V costs z times F times V, where F, the Faraday constant, is the charge of one mole of electrons, about 96 thousand coulombs. Add the two. If delta G is negative, the ion flows in by itself; if positive, it flows out. At equilibrium, delta G is zero, and solving for V gives the Nernst equation. Notice the shape: the equilibrium potential depends only on the ratio of the concentrations and the charge of the ion. At body temperature RT over F is about 26.7 millivolts. A handy rule: for a singly charged ion, each tenfold concentration difference gives about 61.5 millivolts. The sign of z matters: for chloride, z is minus one, and for calcium, plus two.

E_\text{K} ≈ −89 mV: K⁺ would stop flowing out when the inside is 89 mV negative.
E_\text{Na} ≈ +67 mV: Na⁺ would keep flowing in until the inside is 67 mV positive.
The resting cell (−70 mV) is close to E_\text{K} and far from E_\text{Na}. So at rest K⁺ leaks out slowly, and Na⁺ is pulled in strongly whenever a Na⁺ channel opens.

Typical mammalian values; concentrations differ between cell types.

Let us put in numbers. Potassium: inside 140 millimolar, outside 5. The ratio out over in is 0.036; its natural log is about minus 3.3; times 26.7 gives minus 89 millivolts. Sodium: inside 12, outside 145. The ratio is about 12, the log is 2.5, so plus 67 millivolts. Sodium is in equilibrium only when the inside is strongly positive. Chloride has a negative charge, so we divide by minus one, and E for chloride is about minus 64, close to the resting potential. Calcium has a huge gradient, twenty thousand fold, and a charge of two, which gives about plus 130 millivolts. Now compare each number with the real resting potential, minus 70. The difference between the membrane potential and E tells you the driving force. For potassium the difference is small, so potassium leaks out slowly. For sodium the difference is about 140 millivolts, so the moment a sodium channel opens, sodium rushes in. For calcium the driving force is even bigger. This driving force is the energy store that channels spend. The exact concentrations vary between cells, so treat these as typical values.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: How the resting potential arises
text:
How the resting potential arises


Pump: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP) builds and keeps the gradients.
Leak: the resting membrane has many open K⁺ leak channels, few open Na⁺ channels. K⁺ leaves; the large negative molecules inside cannot follow.
Charge: the thin layer of extra charge at the membrane is the membrane potential. Concentrations hardly change.


Put the pieces together. Step one: the sodium-potassium pump, from the transport lecture, uses ATP to move three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in. This builds the gradients. The pump itself makes the inside only a few millivolts more negative, because it moves more positive charge out than in, but that is not the main source of the voltage. Step two: the resting membrane contains potassium leak channels, which are open most of the time. Potassium ions flow out down their concentration gradient. Their partners inside, mostly negatively charged proteins, phosphates and other organic molecules, are too large and cannot follow. Step three: every potassium ion that leaves adds one positive charge outside and leaves one negative charge inside. These charges collect in a thin layer on both faces of the membrane, and the voltage builds up until it stops further net potassium loss, close to E K. Surprisingly few ions are needed: in a typical cell, fewer than one potassium ion in ten thousand has to leave. So the voltage changes quickly, but the concentrations stay almost the same.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: The voltage follows the most open channels
text:
The voltage follows the most open channels


At rest the membrane is mostly permeable to K⁺, so the resting potential (about −70 mV) lies close to E_\text{K}, pulled a little towards E_\text{Na} by a small Na⁺ leak.
This weighted average is the Goldman equation. Learn the idea, not the formula: more open channels for an ion = voltage closer to that ion’s E.
Open many Na⁺ channels, and the voltage swings towards E_\text{Na}. That is the action potential.
Change the K⁺ outside, and the resting potential changes: high blood K⁺ is dangerous for the heart.


If only potassium channels were open, the membrane potential would sit exactly at E K, minus 89. Real resting membranes also let through a little sodium and some chloride. The membrane potential then becomes a kind of weighted average of the equilibrium potentials, where the weights are the permeabilities, that is, how many channels for each ion are open. This is the Goldman equation. We will not use its formula, but the idea is powerful. At rest, potassium dominates, so the resting potential is close to E K, a bit less negative because of the small sodium leak. If the cell suddenly opens many sodium channels, sodium dominates and the voltage swings towards E Na. That is what happens in an action potential, next slide. The same idea explains a clinical fact. If potassium in the blood rises, E K becomes less negative, the resting potential of heart muscle cells moves up, and the heart’s rhythm can fail. Doctors watch blood potassium carefully for this reason. You will meet the heart in detail in the course on organ structure and function.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: The action potential in one slide
text:
The action potential in one slide

An all-or-none spike of about 1 ms: voltage-gated Na⁺ in, then voltage-gated K⁺ out. Na⁺ channel inactivation makes a short refractory period, so the signal only travels forwards along an axon. Only a tiny number of ions move; the pump restores the gradients later.

Nerve and muscle cells use the voltage to send fast signals. Follow the numbers. One: something, for example a synaptic input, makes the membrane less negative. If it reaches the threshold, about minus 55 millivolts, enough voltage-gated sodium channels open to start a positive feedback loop. Two: sodium rushes in, which depolarises the membrane more, which opens more sodium channels. Within half a millisecond the voltage swings to about plus 35, towards E Na. Three: the sodium channels inactivate. A part of the channel on the inside plugs the pore, even though the voltage is still positive. At the same time, slower voltage-gated potassium channels open. Potassium flows out, and the voltage falls. Four: because many potassium channels are still open, the voltage briefly goes below the resting level, towards E K. Inactivated sodium channels cannot reopen until the membrane has been negative for a while, so a second spike cannot start at once. This refractory period makes the spike travel in one direction along an axon. The whole spike moves very few ions. The full neuroscience comes in the course on organ structure and function.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: How do we know? Patch clamp
text:
How do we know? Patch clamp



A glass pipette (left, blue-grey) sealed onto a neuron in a brain slice (hippocampus), seen by DIC microscopy.







Press a polished glass pipette onto a cell and apply gentle suction. The glass seals to the membrane so tightly (gigaseal) that the only current is through channels in the patch under the tip.
Cell-attached recording: the cell stays intact; you measure currents of a few picoamperes.



How could anyone see one channel? Erwin Neher and Bert Sakmann solved this in the late 1970s with patch clamp. You pull a glass tube into a fine pipette with a tip about one micrometre wide, fill it with salt solution and put a wire inside. Under a microscope you press the tip against a cell, as in the photograph, and suck gently. The membrane seals to the glass with an electrical resistance of more than a gigaohm, a billion ohms. Because almost no current can leak around the seal, any current you measure must flow through the few channels in the small patch of membrane under the tip. A sensitive amplifier holds the voltage constant, the clamp, and measures the tiny current. This configuration, with the cell still intact, is called cell-attached. You can also tear the patch off to study the inside face, or break the patch to record from the whole cell, the whole-cell configuration used in most drug tests today. Neher and Sakmann received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1991.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Watching one protein open and close
text:
Watching one protein open and close

Single-channel recording (inside-out patch) of BK channels, a Ca²⁺-activated K⁺ channel. Dashed lines: 0, 1, 2 or 3 channels open. Each step is the current through one channel.

The current jumps in square steps: a channel is either fully open or closed. No half-open state.
One step of 2 pA = 2 × 10⁻¹² C/s ÷ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C ≈ 12 million ions per second through one protein.
Open times are random, milliseconds long. Gating signals change the probability of being open, not the size of the step.


This is what patch clamp gives you. The trace shows the current through a patch that contains three potassium channels. The current does not change smoothly. It jumps between fixed levels: zero, one, two or three channels open. Each jump is one protein molecule changing its shape. This was the first time anyone had watched a single protein molecule work, in real time. Let us calculate what a step means. A current of two picoamperes is two times ten to the minus twelve coulombs per second. Divide by the charge of one ion, 1.6 times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs, and you get about twelve million ions per second through one channel, the high rate we promised on the channel slide. Notice also that each channel opens and closes at random. A gating signal, such as voltage or a ligand, does not open a channel halfway. It changes the probability that the channel is open. When you record from a whole cell with thousands of channels, these random steps add up to the smooth currents seen in textbooks. Drug companies use automated patch clamp to test thousands of compounds on channels.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Channels in non-excitable cells: CFTR moves salt and water
text:
Channels in non-excitable cells: CFTR moves salt and water




CFTR is a Cl⁻ channel in the apical (top) membrane of epithelia: airways, gut, pancreas, sweat glands. It opens when phosphorylated by protein kinase A and when it binds ATP.
Cells cannot pump water. They secrete salt (Cl⁻ through CFTR, Na⁺ between the cells), and water follows by osmosis. This keeps the airway surface wet, so cilia can clear mucus.







Human CFTR, cryo-EM (PDB 5UAK).


Channels are not only for nerves. Here is one in an epithelium, a sheet of cells that lines the airways, gut and glands. The airway surface is covered by a thin liquid layer, with mucus on top. Cilia beat in the liquid and move the mucus, with trapped dust and bacteria, up and out of the lungs. Cells cannot pump water directly. Instead they move salt, and water follows by osmosis, partly through water channels. The key protein is CFTR, a chloride channel in the apical membrane, the side that faces the airway. When the cell is stimulated, protein kinase A phosphorylates CFTR, ATP binds, and the channel opens. Chloride flows out into the airway, down its electrochemical gradient. Sodium follows between the cells, attracted by the negative charge, and water follows the salt. The structure on the right, solved by cryo-EM, shows the two membrane domains on top and the two ATP-binding domains below, in the cytosol. CFTR belongs to the family of ABC transporters, but it evolved into a channel. In cystic fibrosis, this channel is missing or broken, the liquid layer dries out, and mucus becomes thick.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Ca²⁺ channels: making a signal
text:
Ca²⁺ channels: making a signal


Pumps keep cytosolic Ca²⁺ 10 000 times lower than outside and in the ER. Opening a few Ca²⁺ channels therefore makes a large, fast rise.
Ca²⁺ binds proteins that change shape and act: neurotransmitter release, muscle contraction, insulin secretion, gene expression.
Channels in the plasma membrane (voltage- or ligand-gated) and in the ER membrane (opened by second messengers). More in the signalling lectures.


Calcium is special. Cells keep free calcium in the cytosol extremely low, about 100 nanomolar, while outside the cell and inside the ER lumen it is around a millimolar or more: a gradient of ten thousand times. Pumps in the plasma membrane and in the ER membrane work all the time to keep it so. Because the resting level is so low, opening even a few calcium channels raises cytosolic calcium ten- or a hundred-fold within milliseconds. Calcium then binds proteins such as calmodulin or synaptotagmin, which change shape and switch on a process. In a nerve terminal, voltage-gated calcium channels open when the action potential arrives, and calcium triggers the release of neurotransmitter. In muscle, calcium triggers contraction. In pancreatic beta cells, it triggers insulin secretion. Calcium can also be released from the ER through channels that open when a second messenger binds. So here a channel is not used to make a voltage, but to make a chemical signal. You will meet these pathways again in the signalling lectures and in the lecture comparing organelles. Calcium-channel blockers are common drugs for high blood pressure.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Why it matters: cystic fibrosis and drugs matched to the defect
text:
Why it matters: cystic fibrosis and drugs matched to the defect




Cystic fibrosis: both copies of the CFTR gene mutated. Thick mucus, lung infections, blocked pancreas.
F508del: one amino acid missing; CFTR misfolds in the ER and is degraded (the ER lecture). Carried by about 9 in 10 patients.



G551D: CFTR reaches the surface, but the gate does not open.
Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (one combination, approved 2019): two correctors plus a potentiator. Lung function improves markedly.



Cystic fibrosis is one of the most common severe inherited diseases in people of European descent. It is recessive: both copies of the CFTR gene carry a mutation. Without working CFTR, the airway liquid layer becomes thin, mucus is thick and sticky, and bacteria grow in the lungs; the pancreas ducts also block. More than two thousand mutations are known, but they fall into a few types of molecular defect, and that is the key to treatment. The most common, F508del, deletes one phenylalanine. The protein folds badly in the ER, quality control recognises it, and it is degraded, so almost none reaches the surface. You will learn this quality control in the ER lecture. Drugs called correctors, such as elexacaftor and tezacaftor, bind the protein while it folds and help it reach the membrane. Another mutation, G551D, gives a protein that reaches the membrane but rarely opens. A potentiator, ivacaftor, binds CFTR and holds the gate open longer. Since F508del protein that reaches the surface also gates poorly, the combination of two correctors and a potentiator works for most patients. You will meet drug development like this in Kliniska prövningar och läkemedelsutveckling.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Why it matters: salty sweat, and blocking Na⁺ channels
text:
Why it matters: salty sweat, and blocking Na⁺ channels




Lidocaine (local anaesthetic, dentist) crosses the membrane, then blocks the Na⁺ channel pore from inside. No action potentials in pain fibres.
Tetrodotoxin from pufferfish plugs the outer mouth. It blocks all nerve signals: deadly.







Sweat test: Cl⁻ in sweat ≥ 60 mmol/L means cystic fibrosis.





Pufferfish (Takifugu). Its toxin is made by bacteria.


Two more examples link this lecture to the clinic. First, the sweat test. In the sweat gland duct, CFTR normally takes chloride back from the sweat into the body, and sodium follows, so sweat on the skin is only a little salty. Without CFTR the salt stays in the sweat. A sweat test collects sweat from the arm, and a chloride level of 60 millimoles per litre or more indicates cystic fibrosis; this is the old saying about the salty kiss. Second, sodium channels as drug targets. If voltage-gated sodium channels cannot open, no action potential can start. Lidocaine, the local anaesthetic used by dentists, crosses the membrane in its uncharged form, becomes charged inside the cell and binds inside the pore. It binds best to channels that open often, so active pain fibres are blocked first. Tetrodotoxin, from the pufferfish, is a toxin that plugs the outer mouth of the sodium channel. A tiny amount stops nerve signals to the breathing muscles. Disease mechanisms like these return in Sjukdomslära, and the development of channel drugs in Kliniska prövningar och läkemedelsutveckling.

title: Ion channels and membrane potential
section: Summary
text:
Summary

Channels are open pores: fast (up to 10⁸ ions/s), selective and gated (voltage, ligand, mechanical force). Transporters are slower but can pump.
The K⁺ channel filter selects K⁺ over the smaller Na⁺ because its carbonyl oxygens replace the water shell of K⁺ exactly, but not of Na⁺.
Each ion has an equilibrium potential from \Delta G = RT\ln(c_\text{in}/c_\text{out}) + zFV = 0: the Nernst equation. E_\text{K} ≈ −89 mV, E_\text{Na} ≈ +67 mV.
The resting potential (≈ −70 mV) comes from the pump’s gradients plus open K⁺ leak channels, so it lies near E_\text{K}. Opening Na⁺ channels gives the action potential. Patch clamp shows single channels opening and closing.
Channels work in all cells: CFTR drives salt and water secretion, Ca²⁺ channels make signals. Drugs match the defect: CFTR correctors and potentiators, lidocaine on Na⁺ channels.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 11.
Image credits: credits

Five take-home points. First, channels are pores that let ions flow down their electrochemical gradient, very fast, and they are selective and gated; transporters are slower but can couple to energy and pump. Second, selectivity comes from structure: the potassium channel filter replaces the water around a potassium ion with protein oxygens at exactly the right distance, which does not work for the smaller sodium ion. Third, the Nernst equation is just Gibbs energy with an electrical term; set delta G to zero and you get the equilibrium potential, which you should be able to calculate. Fourth, the resting potential arises because the pump makes the gradients and the resting membrane is mainly permeable to potassium; when sodium channels open, the voltage swings towards E Na, which is the action potential. Patch clamp lets us record a single channel. Fifth, all cells use channels: CFTR for salt and water secretion, calcium channels for signals. Knowing the exact molecular defect lets us choose the drug. Next we leave the plasma membrane and follow proteins into the compartments of the cell.

title: Quiz: ion channels and membrane potential
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture Ion channels and membrane potential. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. A membrane protein moves 500 molecules of glucose per second. Another moves 10 million K⁺ ions per second. Which is a channel and which is a transporter? Give one more property that tells them apart. [ELO 2]






Hint





Does the protein change shape for every molecule, or is it an open pore?









Answer





The glucose mover is a transporter (10²–10⁴ per second: it binds, changes shape and releases each molecule). The K⁺ mover is a channel (up to 10⁸ ions per second through an open pore). Other differences: a transporter is never open to both sides at once and can be coupled to ATP or another gradient to move a solute uphill; a channel only lets ions flow down their electrochemical gradient.




Q2. Na⁺ is smaller than K⁺. Why can it not pass through the K⁺ channel’s selectivity filter? [ELO 2]






Hint





What does an ion have to lose before it enters the narrow filter, and what does the filter give back?









Answer





To enter the narrow filter, an ion must lose its shell of water, which costs energy. For K⁺, the filter’s backbone carbonyl oxygens sit at the same distance as the water oxygens did, so the cost is paid back. Na⁺ is smaller; the rigid filter cannot close in on it, so the oxygens are too far away to replace its water. Losing water without being paid back costs too much, so Na⁺ stays out.




Q3. Match each channel to how it is opened: (a) voltage-gated Na⁺ channel, (b) nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, (c) Piezo2. Gating types: ligand, mechanical force, voltage. [ELO 2]






Hint





One has a charged sensor helix, one binds a transmitter, one responds to stretch of the membrane.









Answer






voltage: positive charges in a sensor helix move when the membrane depolarises. (b) ligand: two acetylcholine molecules bind and open the pore. (c) mechanical force: membrane tension pulls on its blades; Piezo2 senses touch.





Q4. Use the Nernst equation (\(E = \frac{61.5\text{ mV}}{z}\log_{10}\frac{c_\text{out}}{c_\text{in}}\) at 37 °C) to calculate \(E_\text{K}\) if K⁺ is 150 mM inside and 15 mM outside. [ELO 2]






Hint





The ratio out/in is 0.1. What is log₁₀(0.1)?









Answer





\(E_\text{K} = 61.5 \times \log_{10}(15/150) = 61.5 \times (-1) =\) −61.5 mV. A tenfold gradient of a singly charged ion gives about 61.5 mV. The sign is negative because K⁺ is higher inside: the inside must be negative to hold K⁺ back.




Q5. The resting membrane potential of a cell is −70 mV, \(E_\text{K}\) is −89 mV and \(E_\text{Na}\) is +67 mV. Why is the resting potential so much closer to \(E_\text{K}\) than to \(E_\text{Na}\)? [ELO 2]






Hint





Which channels are open at rest?









Answer





At rest, many K⁺ leak channels are open and very few Na⁺ channels. The membrane potential is a weighted average of the equilibrium potentials, weighted by permeability (the Goldman idea). K⁺ dominates, so the potential lies near \(E_\text{K}\), pulled a little towards \(E_\text{Na}\) by the small Na⁺ leak.




Q6. During an action potential, why does the voltage fall again after the peak, and why can a second action potential not start immediately? [ELO 2]






Hint





Two things happen to two kinds of voltage-gated channels after the peak.









Answer





The voltage-gated Na⁺ channels inactivate (a part of the channel plugs the pore from inside), and slower voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, so K⁺ flows out and the voltage falls towards \(E_\text{K}\). Inactivated Na⁺ channels cannot reopen until the membrane has been negative for a short time: the refractory period. This also makes the signal travel in only one direction along an axon.




Q7. In a cell-attached patch-clamp recording, the current jumps between 0 and −2 pA and never stays in between. What does this tell you, and about how many ions per second pass through the channel when it is open? (Charge of one ion: 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.) [ELO 1] [ELO 2]






Hint





1 A = 1 C/s. Divide the current by the charge of one ion.









Answer





The square steps show one channel switching between fully open and fully closed; there is no half-open state. 2 × 10⁻¹² C/s ÷ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C ≈ 1.25 × 10⁷, about 12 million ions per second through one protein molecule.




Q8. Two patients have cystic fibrosis. Patient A is homozygous for G551D, patient B for F508del. Ivacaftor alone helps A a lot but B very little. Explain. [ELO 2] [ELO 9]






Hint





Where is the CFTR protein in each patient, and what does a potentiator do?









Answer





G551D CFTR reaches the plasma membrane but its gate rarely opens. Ivacaftor is a potentiator: it increases the time the channel is open, so it fixes this defect. F508del CFTR misfolds in the ER and is degraded, so almost none reaches the surface; a potentiator has nothing to act on. Patient B needs correctors (elexacaftor, tezacaftor) to help the protein fold and reach the membrane, plus the potentiator, because rescued F508del also gates poorly.

title: Study questions: membrane structure
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Explain, using \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\), why phospholipids in water form a bilayer by themselves. Why does a bilayer form closed compartments rather than flat sheets with edges? [ELO 2]






Model answer





Phospholipids are amphipathic: a polar head and two hydrophobic tails. Water cannot hydrogen-bond to a hydrocarbon tail, so the water molecules around a tail are held in an ordered cage, which lowers the entropy of the water. When the tails come together inside a bilayer, this water is released and its entropy rises (\(\Delta S > 0\)). \(\Delta H\) is small, so \(-T\Delta S\) dominates and \(\Delta G < 0\): assembly is spontaneous. This is the hydrophobic effect. At the edge of a flat sheet the tails would be exposed to water again, which is unfavourable, so a bilayer closes on itself into a sealed compartment (and small tears reseal).




2. Name the three main classes of membrane lipid. For each, give one example and one feature of its structure that matters for the membrane. [ELO 2]






Model answer






Glycerophospholipids, e.g. phosphatidylcholine (PC) or phosphatidylserine (PS): glycerol backbone with two fatty-acid tails (often one unsaturated, kinked) and a phosphate-linked head; PS carries a net negative charge.
Sphingolipids, e.g. sphingomyelin or glycolipids: sphingosine backbone; long, saturated tails that pack tightly; glycolipids carry sugars and sit only in the outer leaflet.
Sterols: cholesterol, a small, rigid ring structure with an OH head; it regulates fluidity and makes the membrane less leaky. It is abundant in the plasma membrane (about one per phospholipid).





3. Describe the movements a phospholipid molecule makes in a bilayer, and explain why one of them is very rare. [ELO 2]






Model answer





A lipid diffuses laterally within its leaflet (it swaps places with a neighbour about 10⁷ times per second and moves about 2 µm per second), it rotates about its long axis, and its tails flex. Flip-flop, moving to the other leaflet, is very rare (about once a month for a phospholipid on its own), because the polar, often charged head group would have to pass through the hydrophobic core of about 3 nm, which costs a lot of energy. Cells use enzymes (flippases, scramblases) when lipids must move between leaflets.




4. List four factors that change membrane fluidity and say in which direction each one acts. How do bacteria respond when the temperature falls? [ELO 2]






Model answer






Shorter tails: less contact between tails, more fluid.
More cis double bonds (unsaturation): kinks prevent tight packing, more fluid.
Higher temperature: more fluid (below a transition temperature a pure bilayer becomes a gel).
Cholesterol: at 37 °C less fluid (stiffens tails near the heads); at low temperature it prevents the gel state. It acts as a buffer.

When the temperature falls, bacteria make more unsaturated (and shorter) fatty acids, so their membrane stays fluid enough for membrane proteins to work.




5. What is meant by lipid asymmetry in the plasma membrane? Explain how cells maintain it, and give two situations where it is lost on purpose. [ELO 2]






Model answer





The two leaflets have different lipids: the outer leaflet is rich in PC, sphingomyelin and glycolipids, the inner leaflet in PS, PE and PI. Asymmetry is set up when lipids are made (on the cytosolic face of the ER) and moved, and maintained because flip-flop is slow and flippases (P-type ATPases) use ATP to move PS and PE back to the inner leaflet. It is lost when scramblases are switched on, which move lipids both ways without energy: (1) in apoptosis, caspases switch the flippase off and a scramblase on, so PS on the surface acts as an “eat me” signal for phagocytes; (2) in activated platelets, Ca²⁺ switches on a scramblase, and the exposed PS forms a surface on which clotting factors assemble.




6. Draw a bilayer and show the main ways in which proteins can be associated with a membrane. Say how each kind can be removed from the membrane in the laboratory. [ELO 2]






Model answer





Sketch should show:

Integral, single-pass: one α-helix crossing the bilayer.
Integral, multi-pass: several α-helices (e.g. seven), or a β-barrel (in outer membranes of bacteria, mitochondria and chloroplasts).
Lipid-anchored: on the cytosolic side through a covalently attached fatty acid (myristoyl, palmitoyl) or prenyl group; on the outside through a GPI anchor.
Peripheral: bound non-covalently to head groups or to the exposed part of an integral protein.

Removal: integral (and in practice lipid-anchored) proteins need a detergent that dissolves the bilayer (GPI-anchored proteins can also be cut off by a phospholipase). Peripheral proteins come off with high salt or a change in pH, which break non-covalent contacts while the membrane stays intact.




7. Why do the parts of membrane proteins that cross the bilayer form either α-helices or β-barrels? About how many amino acids does a transmembrane α-helix need, and why? [ELO 2]






Model answer





Every peptide bond has polar C=O and N–H groups. In water these bond to water, but inside the bilayer there is no water, so they must bond to each other. In an α-helix each backbone group bonds to another within the same helix, and the side chains point outwards, where hydrophobic side chains contact the lipid tails. A single β-strand cannot satisfy its backbone, but in a β-barrel each strand bonds to its two neighbours and the sheet closes on itself. A helix rises 0.15 nm per residue, so about 20 hydrophobic amino acids (20 × 0.15 nm = 3 nm) span the hydrophobic core of about 3 nm.




8. Explain how a hydropathy plot is made and how you read it. Give one limitation. [ELO 2]






Model answer





Each amino acid has a hydropathy score (e.g. Kyte–Doolittle: Ile +4.5, Arg −4.5). A window of about 19 residues slides along the sequence; the average score of the window is plotted at its central position. A broad peak of about 20 residues above a threshold (about +1.6 for this window) predicts a transmembrane α-helix; the number of peaks predicts the number of crossings (e.g. seven for a G-protein-coupled receptor). Limitations: it misses β-barrels (short strands alternating polar and non-polar); helices with polar residues (e.g. lining a pore) can fall below the threshold; an ER signal sequence gives a peak too; and it does not show which side of the membrane each loop is on. Predictions must be tested.




9. Describe the Frye–Edidin cell-fusion experiment and FRAP. What does each show about membrane proteins? [ELO 1] [ELO 2]






Model answer





Frye–Edidin (1970): a mouse cell and a human cell were fused (with a virus) into one hybrid cell. Mouse surface proteins were labelled with a green-fluorescent antibody and human proteins with a red one. At first each colour covered half the cell; after about 40 min at 37 °C the colours were completely mixed, but not at low temperature, and not prevented by blocking protein synthesis or ATP production. So membrane proteins diffuse laterally in a fluid bilayer.
FRAP: a fluorescent membrane protein (e.g. a GFP fusion) is bleached in a small spot with a strong laser; fluorescence recovers as unbleached molecules diffuse in. The rate of recovery gives the diffusion coefficient; the part that does not recover is the immobile fraction, held by the cytoskeleton or other proteins. FRAP measures mobility in living cells and shows that many proteins move more slowly than lipids.




10. Explain the principle of freeze-fracture electron microscopy and what it showed about the structure of membranes. [ELO 1] [ELO 2]






Model answer





Cells are frozen rapidly and cracked with a cold knife. The fracture runs between the two leaflets of the bilayer, where only weak contacts hold the tail ends together, exposing the inner faces of each half (the P face, cytosolic half, and the E face, outer half). The faces are shadowed with platinum from an angle, the biological material is removed, and the metal replica is examined in a TEM. Pure lipid bilayers give smooth faces, but cell membranes show many intramembrane particles (about 8–10 nm); their number rises with the protein content of the membrane, so they are integral proteins that cross the bilayer. This supported the fluid mosaic model (proteins embedded in a lipid bilayer), rather than a model in which proteins only coat the surface.




11. What is the glycocalyx? Use the ABO blood groups to explain how a small difference in the glycocalyx can matter clinically. [ELO 2]






Model answer





The glycocalyx is the coat of carbohydrate on the outside of the plasma membrane: sugar chains on glycoproteins, glycolipids and proteoglycans. Sugars are added in the ER and Golgi lumen, so they always face the outside. It protects the cell, holds water and takes part in cell recognition. On red blood cells, a sugar chain ends in the H antigen (galactose with fucose). One gene encodes a Golgi glycosyltransferase: the A form adds N-acetylgalactosamine, the B form adds galactose, the O form is inactive (H only). People make antibodies against the A or B sugar they lack (a type A person has anti-B). If a type A patient receives type B blood, the anti-B antibodies bind the donor red cells and destroy them (a haemolytic transfusion reaction). One sugar at the tip of a chain decides compatibility.

title: Study questions: membrane structure
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
12. [VG] An E. coli culture is moved from 37 °C to 15 °C. (a) Predict what happens to the fatty-acid composition of its membrane over the next hours, and explain why this is needed. (b) A mutant cannot make unsaturated fatty acids unless they are added to the medium. Predict how the mutant behaves at 15 °C without added fatty acids, and design an experiment that tests your explanation using one method from the lecture. [ELO 2]






Model answer






At lower temperature the bilayer becomes less fluid and may approach a gel state. Membrane proteins (transporters, enzymes of the respiratory chain) need a fluid membrane to change shape and diffuse, and a gel membrane can also become leaky at phase boundaries. The bacteria respond by making a higher proportion of unsaturated (cis-kinked) and somewhat shorter fatty acids, restoring fluidity (homeoviscous adaptation). E. coli has no cholesterol, so it cannot use a sterol buffer.
The mutant cannot raise unsaturation, so its membrane becomes too ordered at 15 °C: expect slow or no growth, poor transport of nutrients and possibly leakiness; adding an unsaturated fatty acid (e.g. oleic acid) to the medium should rescue growth.

Experiment: measure membrane fluidity directly with FRAP. Label membranes with a fluorescent lipid probe (or express a GFP-tagged membrane protein), bleach a spot and measure recovery at 15 °C in wild-type cells, in the mutant without oleic acid and in the mutant with oleic acid. Prediction: slower recovery (smaller diffusion coefficient) in the mutant without oleic acid, restored by oleic acid, and the growth defect should track the fluidity. Fatty-acid analysis (gas chromatography of extracted lipids) would confirm the composition. Controls: same probe concentration, same temperature, and bleaching settings kept constant.




13. [VG] A lab expresses a new protein X fused to GFP in cultured epithelial cells grown as a sealed layer. X–GFP is found only on the apical surface. (a) Explain how X could stay apical even though the membrane is fluid. (b) The lab adds a drug that opens tight junctions, and after one hour X–GFP is on the basolateral surface too. A FRAP experiment before the drug shows full, fast recovery of a bleached spot on the apical surface. Explain both results together. (c) Suggest one experiment that tests whether X is held in place by the cortical cytoskeleton instead. [ELO 2]






Model answer






The tight junction forms a ring around each cell near its apical end. Besides sealing the space between cells, it acts as a fence: integral membrane proteins (and outer-leaflet lipids) cannot diffuse past it. If X is delivered to the apical membrane, it stays in the apical domain even though it diffuses freely within that domain.
The FRAP result shows that X is mobile within the apical membrane: it is not anchored, it diffuses. So the only thing keeping it apical was the fence. When the drug opens the tight junctions, the fence is lost and X diffuses into the basolateral membrane. Both results fit “free diffusion inside a fenced domain”.
Disrupt actin with a drug such as latrunculin or cytochalasin (with tight junctions intact) and repeat FRAP: if X were held by the cortical cytoskeleton, its immobile fraction would fall or its diffusion would speed up after actin disruption. Since X already recovers fully and fast, the prediction is little change. Controls: confirm actin is disrupted (phalloidin staining) and that the junctions stay closed (e.g. electrical resistance across the cell layer).





14. [VG] Compare liposomal doxorubicin (Doxil) and an mRNA lipid nanoparticle. For each, explain how the lipid composition serves its task, and explain why Doxil reduces damage to the heart. Why is the EPR effect not a full explanation of how Doxil works in patients? [ELO 2] [ELO 9]






Model answer





Doxil must keep a small drug inside for days and release it slowly. It is a liposome (aqueous core, one bilayer) of saturated phospholipid plus cholesterol, so the bilayer is rigid and not leaky; doxorubicin is loaded into the core with a gradient and crystallises there. A PEG coat hides the liposome from phagocytes, so it circulates for days. mRNA LNP must carry a large, negative RNA and release it into the cytosol. Its ionisable lipid is positive at low pH (binds RNA during manufacture; disrupts the acidic endosome membrane so RNA escapes) but nearly neutral at pH 7.4 (less toxic in blood). DSPC and cholesterol give structure, and a small amount of PEG-lipid controls particle size and stops aggregation; it is shed in the body, so the particle can be taken up (patisiran binds ApoE and enters liver cells through the LDL receptor).
Heart: free doxorubicin is a small molecule that leaves the blood everywhere, including through heart capillaries, and the high peak level damages heart muscle. Heart capillaries have a continuous, tight endothelium, so 90 nm liposomes stay in the blood there, and the free-drug peak is low, so cardiotoxicity falls.
EPR caveat: the enhanced permeability and retention effect (leaky tumour vessels, poor lymph drainage) was shown mainly in fast-growing mouse tumours. Human tumours vary a lot in leakiness, and in trials Doxil gave similar survival to free doxorubicin. So its main proven benefit is a different side-effect profile (less heart damage, but hand–foot syndrome in skin), not a much larger dose in the tumour.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: The question: how does sugar get from your gut into your blood?
text:
The question: how does sugar get from your gut into your blood?







Small intestine (rat), stained section. The finger-like villi are covered by one layer of epithelial cells.


After a meal, the gut takes up hundreds of grams of glucose a day.
Glucose is polar: it barely crosses a lipid bilayer.
It must cross two membranes: into the epithelial cell from the gut, and out again on the blood side.
Between meals the cell still takes up glucose when the gut has less glucose than the blood: uphill.
And every one of your cells keeps Na⁺ low and K⁺ high inside, the opposite of the blood. A resting cell spends about a quarter of its ATP on this.

How, and why?


Look at the picture. This is a section through the small intestine of a rat, stained with dyes. The finger-like folds are villi, and each villus is covered by a single layer of epithelial cells. Everything you absorb from food must pass through these cells: in through the membrane facing the gut, and out through the membrane facing the blood. Glucose is a polar molecule with many hydroxyl groups, so it hardly enters a lipid bilayer at all. Still, your gut absorbs it very efficiently, even towards the end of digestion when there is less glucose in the gut than in the blood. That means the cell can move glucose uphill, against its gradient. At the same time, every cell in your body keeps sodium low and potassium high inside, the reverse of the blood, and spends a large part of its ATP to do so. By the end of the lecture you will see that these two puzzles have the same answer: the sodium gradient made by one pump drives the uptake of glucose.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: What crosses a pure lipid bilayer?
text:
What crosses a pure lipid bilayer?


The middle of the bilayer is hydrophobic. A molecule must leave water and dissolve in oil to cross.
Small and hydrophobic (O₂, CO₂, steroid hormones, many drugs): fast. Small polar (water, urea): slower. Glucose: very slow. Ions: practically never, because they carry a charge and a shell of water.
So a cell needs membrane transport proteins: they make up about 15–30 % of the membrane proteins in a cell.


Imagine an artificial membrane made only of lipid, with no proteins, and ask what gets through. The answer depends on two things: size and how well the molecule dissolves in oil. Small hydrophobic molecules such as oxygen, carbon dioxide and nitrogen cross very fast, and so do steroid hormones and many drugs. This is why most drugs taken as tablets are designed to be fairly small and fairly lipophilic. Small uncharged polar molecules such as water, urea and glycerol also cross, more slowly. Larger polar molecules such as glucose cross very slowly, far too slowly for a cell’s needs. Ions almost never cross: a sodium ion carries a charge and holds a shell of water molecules, and pulling it into the oily core costs a great deal of energy. A pure bilayer lets water through about a billion times faster than sodium or potassium. So the bilayer is a barrier, and the cell controls traffic with proteins. In a typical cell, roughly 15 to 30 percent of membrane proteins are transport proteins, which shows how important this job is.
