These differences are not equilibrium. Ions leak all the time, and pumps work all the time to restore them. Stop the pumps and the gradients run down.
Gradients store energy, like water behind a dam. Cells use them to drive transport and to send electrical signals (the ion-channels lecture).


This table is worth learning, because almost everything in the next two lectures follows from it. Typical values for a mammalian cell: sodium is about 12 millimolar inside and 145 outside. Potassium is the reverse: about 140 inside and 5 outside. Free calcium in the cytosol is extremely low, about 100 nanomolar, ten thousand times lower than outside. Chloride is low inside. The cytosol is slightly more acidic than blood. Inside the cell, the positive charge of potassium is balanced mostly by large negatively charged molecules, proteins, nucleic acids and phosphorylated metabolites, which cannot leave. The key word is steady state, not equilibrium. Ions leak slowly across the membrane all the time, down their gradients, and pumps keep putting them back. If you poison the pumps, for example by blocking ATP production, the gradients slowly disappear and the cell swells and dies. Why keep these gradients? Because a gradient is stored energy. Today we see how cells spend the sodium gradient to move other molecules. In the ion-channels lecture you will see how the same gradients create the membrane potential and nerve signals.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Recap: ΔG decides the direction
text:
Recap: ΔG decides the direction

For an uncharged solute moving from outside to inside, at 37 °C:
\Delta G = RT \ln\frac{c_\text{in}}{c_\text{out}} \qquad (RT \approx 2.6\ \text{kJ/mol})

Passive transport: down the gradient, \Delta G < 0. A 10-fold gradient is worth about 5.9 kJ/mol.
Active transport: up the gradient, \Delta G > 0, so it must be coupled to a reaction with a larger negative ΔG. ATP hydrolysis in a cell gives about −50 kJ/mol.
For an ion, the membrane voltage adds an electrical term: the electrochemical gradient (the ion-channels lecture).


This is a recap from chemistry, applied to a membrane. Moving one mole of an uncharged solute from outside to inside changes free energy by RT times the natural log of the inside concentration over the outside concentration. If the inside is lower, the log is negative, ΔG is negative, and the movement can happen by itself, provided there is a path. That is passive transport, also called facilitated diffusion when a protein provides the path. If the inside is higher, ΔG is positive: the cell must pay. At body temperature RT is about 2.6 kilojoules per mole, so each tenfold difference in concentration is worth about 5.9 kilojoules per mole. Hydrolysis of ATP under cell conditions releases about 50 kilojoules per mole, enough to pump against large gradients. A pump couples the two reactions in one protein, so the total ΔG is negative. For ions there is one more term: the voltage across the membrane pushes or pulls charges. The sum is the electrochemical gradient, and we leave the electrical part to the ion-channels lecture, where it gives the Nernst equation.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Two kinds of transport protein: transporters and channels
text:
Two kinds of transport protein: transporters and channels

A channel is a gated hole: fast, but only downhill. A transporter (also called a carrier) binds its solute and changes shape: slower, but it can be coupled to energy and move things uphill.

Membrane transport proteins come in two kinds. A channel forms a water-filled pore. When it is open, ions flow through it in single file, down their electrochemical gradient, at rates up to a hundred million ions per second. A channel cannot push anything uphill, because the pore is open to both sides at the same time. Channels open and close in response to signals, called gating, and they are the topic of the next lecture. A transporter works differently. It binds its solute at a specific site, like an enzyme binds its substrate, and then changes shape so that the site faces the other side. Each cycle moves one or a few molecules, so transporters are much slower, about a hundred to ten thousand molecules per second. But because each cycle is a defined series of shape changes, it can be linked to another event, such as ATP hydrolysis or the movement of a sodium ion. That is how transporters do active transport. Remember the rule: channels are fast and passive; transporters are slow, specific, saturable, and can be active.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: How a transporter works: alternating access
text:
How a transporter works: alternating access








The binding site faces out, then in, never both at once.
One cycle can run in either direction. With no energy input, net flow goes down the gradient (passive).
Example: GLUT1, the glucose uniporter of red blood cells and the blood–brain barrier.







Human GLUT1 (PDB 4PYP), side view. Its 12 membrane helices form two halves (blue, red) around the sugar site.


How does a transporter move a molecule without ever making a hole in the membrane? The answer is alternating access. In step one the transporter is open to the outside, and its binding site is empty. A glucose molecule binds. The protein then closes behind it, so for a moment the glucose is trapped inside the protein, closed to both sides. Then the protein opens to the inside and the glucose leaves into the cytosol. Finally the empty transporter flips back. Nothing in this cycle has a preferred direction, so if glucose is higher inside, the same cycle runs the other way. Net flow is always down the gradient. This is passive transport, but much faster and more specific than diffusion through lipid. The structure on the right is the real protein, GLUT1, solved by X-ray crystallography in 2014. It has twelve helices crossing the membrane, arranged as two bundles, and the sugar binds between them. The two halves rock against each other like a seesaw to open one side and close the other. GLUT1 supplies glucose to red blood cells and to the brain.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: How do we know? Uptake assays show that transporters saturate
text:
How do we know? Uptake assays show that transporters saturate


Diffusion through lipid rises linearly with concentration. Transport by a protein reaches a maximum (Vmax): all binding sites are busy. Km = concentration at half-maximal rate.
Transporters are specific: GLUT1 takes D-glucose, not its mirror image L-glucose. They can be competed by similar molecules and blocked by inhibitors.


How do we know that a protein is involved at all? Here is the classic experiment, and you can do it in a teaching lab. Cells, for example red blood cells, are given glucose labelled with a radioactive atom such as tritium, or with a fluorescent tag. After a short time, say thirty seconds, uptake is stopped by washing with ice-cold buffer, and the label inside the cells is measured. Repeat at many concentrations and plot the initial rate against concentration. If glucose simply diffused through lipid, the rate would rise in a straight line. Instead the curve bends and reaches a plateau. You know this shape from enzyme kinetics: it is the Michaelis–Menten curve. The plateau, Vmax, is reached when all transporter molecules are busy. Km is the concentration that gives half of Vmax, a measure of affinity. Two more results point to a protein. The transporter is stereospecific: it moves D-glucose, the natural form, but hardly L-glucose, which has the same size and polarity. And similar sugars compete for uptake, just as competitive inhibitors do for an enzyme.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Three ways to couple: uniport, symport, antiport
text:
Three ways to couple: uniport, symport, antiport


Uniport: one solute, passive (GLUT).
Symport (co-transport): two solutes cross in the same direction. Example: SGLT1 carries 2 Na⁺ + 1 glucose into gut cells.
Antiport (exchange): two solutes cross in opposite directions. Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger: 3 Na⁺ in, 1 Ca²⁺ out. Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger: 1 Na⁺ in, 1 H⁺ out (controls cytosolic pH).


Transporters are classified by how many solutes they move and in which direction. A uniporter moves one kind of molecule, like GLUT. It can only move it downhill. A symporter binds two different solutes and moves them together, in the same direction. The transporter only completes its cycle when both are bound, so the two movements are tightly coupled. In SGLT1, two sodium ions and one glucose molecule enter together. An antiporter, or exchanger, moves two solutes in opposite directions: it takes one in and carries the other out in the same cycle. The sodium–calcium exchanger lets three sodium ions in and pushes one calcium ion out; it is important in heart muscle. The sodium–proton exchanger lets one sodium in and pushes one proton out, which protects the cytosol from becoming acidic. The important point: in symport and antiport, one solute can go downhill and pay for the other going uphill. Notice that in all three examples, sodium enters the cell. That is not a coincidence, as the next slide shows.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Secondary active transport: the Na⁺ gradient is a battery
text:
Secondary active transport: the Na⁺ gradient is a battery


Primary active transport uses ATP directly (a pump). Secondary active transport uses a gradient that a pump made.
Na⁺ flowing in releases energy: about −13 kJ/mol (concentration plus voltage). With 2 Na⁺ per glucose, SGLT1 can in theory concentrate glucose more than 10 000-fold.
Animal cells use Na⁺; bacteria, plants and fungi mostly use an H⁺ gradient.


Now we can solve the opening puzzle. The sodium–potassium pump, on the left, spends ATP to push sodium out. That keeps sodium about ten times higher outside than inside. In addition, the inside of the cell is electrically negative, which pulls positive sodium ions inwards. So sodium entering the cell is strongly downhill: about minus thirteen kilojoules per mole, about half from the concentration difference and half from the voltage. A symporter or antiporter can use this downhill flow to drive a second solute uphill. This is secondary active transport: no ATP is used by the transporter itself, but the energy came from ATP spent earlier by the pump. Think of the pump as charging a battery and the other transporters as devices running on it. Because SGLT1 couples two sodium ions to each glucose, it has twice that energy available and can, in theory, concentrate glucose more than ten thousand times. If you poison the pump, the battery runs down and glucose uptake stops too. Bacteria and plants do the same with a proton gradient instead of sodium.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Primary active transport: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump
text:
Primary active transport: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump


A P-type ATPase: it phosphorylates itself on an aspartate, and this switches its shape from inward-open to outward-open.
3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP. It uses about a quarter of a resting cell’s ATP, and much more in nerve cells.
Found in every animal cell. Discovered by Jens Skou in crab nerves in 1957 (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1997).


Here is the battery charger. The sodium–potassium pump, also called the sodium–potassium ATPase, is a P-type pump: P for phosphorylation. Follow the cycle. In state one, the binding sites face the cytosol, where sodium is relatively low, but the sites have a high affinity for sodium, so three sodium ions bind. That triggers the pump to transfer the phosphate of ATP to one of its own aspartate residues. The phosphorylated pump changes shape: the sites now face the outside, and their affinity for sodium drops, so the three sodium ions are released, even though sodium outside is high. In this shape the sites bind two potassium ions from the outside. Potassium binding triggers removal of the phosphate, the pump flips back, and potassium is released into the cytosol. Each cycle uses one ATP. Because three positive charges go out and only two come in, the pump also makes a small electrical current: it is electrogenic. This single protein uses roughly a quarter of the ATP of a resting cell, and in the brain a much larger share. Jens Skou found it in crab nerves in 1957.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: How do we know? Rebuild the pump, and block it
text:
How do we know? Rebuild the pump, and block it


Reconstitution: purify the pump, put it into liposomes (artificial lipid vesicles), add ATP: Na⁺ and K⁺ move in a 3 : 2 ratio. No other protein is needed.
Inhibitors: ouabain (an arrow poison) and digoxin block the pump only from the outside. Resealed red-cell membranes (“ghosts”) showed that ATP and Na⁺ must be inside, K⁺ outside.


Two classic approaches prove that one protein does all of this. The first is reconstitution. You dissolve membranes with a mild detergent, purify the pump protein, and mix it with lipids. When the detergent is removed, the lipids form closed vesicles, liposomes, with pumps in their membranes. The pumps insert in both orientations, but only those whose ATP-binding part faces the outside can use ATP added to the outside. Those pumps move sodium into the liposome and potassium out, three to two. Since the liposome contains nothing but lipid and pump, the pump alone is sufficient. The second approach uses inhibitors. Ouabain, a plant toxin once used on arrow tips, binds the pump and stops it. Researchers made red blood cell ghosts: they let the cells swell until the haemoglobin leaked out, then resealed the empty membranes with chosen solutions inside. Ouabain worked only when it was outside; the pump needed ATP and sodium inside and potassium outside. That told us the pump’s orientation in the membrane. Digoxin, a heart drug from the foxglove plant, binds the same site.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Other pumps: Ca²⁺ pumps, V-type and F-type
text:
Other pumps: Ca²⁺ pumps, V-type and F-type


Ca²⁺ pumps (P-type) keep cytosolic Ca²⁺ at about 100 nM: out of the cell (PMCA) and into the ER (SERCA). A brief rise in Ca²⁺ is a signal (the signalling lectures).
V-type H⁺ pump acidifies lysosomes (pH 4.5–5), endosomes and secretory vesicles (the lysosome lecture).
F-type ATP synthase looks like a V-type pump but runs backwards: H⁺ flowing down its gradient makes ATP (the mitochondria lecture).


The sodium–potassium pump is not alone. Calcium pumps are also P-type pumps, with the same phosphorylation cycle. One kind in the plasma membrane pushes calcium out of the cell. Another, SERCA, pumps calcium into the endoplasmic reticulum, so the ER lumen holds thousands of times more calcium than the cytosol. Because cytosolic calcium is kept so low, opening a calcium channel for a moment makes a large relative rise, which the cell uses as a signal for muscle contraction, secretion and much more. A second family, the V-type pumps, are large rotating machines that pump protons into lysosomes, endosomes and secretory vesicles. That makes the lysosome acidic, around pH 4.5 to 5, which its digestive enzymes need. A third family, the F-type ATPases, is built like the V-type but works in reverse. In the inner membrane of mitochondria, protons flow back into the matrix through the ATP synthase, and this flow turns a rotor that makes ATP from ADP and phosphate. Any pump can in principle run backwards if the gradient is steep enough. You meet both again in the organelle lectures.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: ABC transporters: ATP-powered exporters
text:
ABC transporters: ATP-powered exporters


Two membrane halves plus two ATP-binding cassettes (hence “ABC”). ATP binding brings the cassettes together and flips the transporter to face outward; hydrolysis resets it.
The largest transporter family: humans have about 48 ABC genes. In our cells most are exporters: lipids, bile salts, toxins and drugs.
P-glycoprotein (ABCB1) pumps many different hydrophobic drugs out of cells. The CFTR chloride channel is an unusual member (the ion-channels lecture).


The third big family of ATP-driven pumps is the ABC transporters, named after their ATP-binding cassettes. Each ABC transporter has two halves that cross the membrane, and two cassettes in the cytosol that bind ATP. Follow the cartoon. In the inward-facing state the cassettes are apart and a cavity opens towards the cytosol and the inner half of the membrane. A hydrophobic molecule, often coming from inside the membrane itself, enters the cavity. Two ATP molecules then bind between the cassettes and glue them together. This pulls the membrane halves into an outward-facing shape, and the substrate is released outside. Hydrolysis of ATP lets the cassettes separate, and the transporter resets. Bacteria use ABC transporters to import nutrients, but in human cells nearly all of them export. They move lipids between membrane leaflets, bile salts out of liver cells, and toxins and drugs out of cells. One of them, P-glycoprotein, is famous for having a large, greasy binding cavity that accepts many unrelated drugs. We come back to it at the end. CFTR, the protein defective in cystic fibrosis, belongs to this family but works as a channel.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Transcellular transport: from gut to blood
text:
Transcellular transport: from gut to blood




Apical (gut side): SGLT1 brings glucose in, uphill. Basolateral (blood side): GLUT2 lets it out, downhill; the Na⁺/K⁺ pump removes the Na⁺.
Tight junctions seal the gaps between cells and keep apical and basolateral proteins apart.



Microvilli on a human gut epithelial cell (TEM). Scale bar 100 nm. They enlarge the apical surface many times.


Now we put the pieces together in an epithelium. An epithelial cell is polarised: its apical membrane faces the gut and its basolateral membrane faces the blood, and the two membranes carry different proteins. The apical side is folded into thousands of microvilli, shown in the electron micrograph, which increase the surface area. In the apical membrane, SGLT1 couples glucose entry to sodium entry, so glucose builds up inside the cell even when the gut contains little. In the basolateral membrane, GLUT2, a uniporter, lets glucose leave down its gradient into the blood. The sodium that came in with the glucose is pumped out on the basolateral side by the sodium–potassium pump, which keeps the battery charged. Tight junctions seal the spaces between neighbouring cells, so glucose cannot leak back, and they act as a fence that keeps apical and basolateral proteins in their own membrane. The same design works in the proximal tubule of the kidney, which takes back glucose, amino acids and salt from the urine. Oral rehydration solution, sugar and salt in water, uses SGLT1 to save the lives of children with severe diarrhoea.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Water: aquaporins
text:
Water: aquaporins



Aquaporin seen from outside the cell: four subunits, each with its own water pore (space-filling model, PDB 1FQY).


Water crosses lipid slowly. Kidney, red cells and glands need it fast.
Aquaporins are water channels: about a billion water molecules per second per pore, in single file.
They exclude ions, even H⁺, so they do not destroy gradients.
Water always moves passively, by osmosis: towards the side with more dissolved particles. Cells move water by moving solutes.
AQP2 in the kidney collecting duct is inserted into the membrane when the hormone vasopressin signals; this concentrates the urine. Peter Agre, Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2003.



One last passenger: water. Water does cross a lipid bilayer, but slowly. Cells that move a lot of water, such as kidney tubule cells, red blood cells and gland cells, add channels for it: aquaporins. Peter Agre found the first one in red blood cells. His team put its RNA into frog eggs, which normally take up very little water; in a dilute solution the eggs with aquaporin swelled and burst within minutes. Each aquaporin has four subunits, and each subunit has its own narrow pore, as you see in this view from outside the cell. Water passes in single file at up to a billion molecules per second. A clever feature of the pore stops protons, which could otherwise hop along a chain of water molecules; so aquaporins carry water without letting the proton gradient leak. Note that no pump moves water. Water always follows solutes by osmosis, so cells move water by moving salt first. In the kidney, the hormone vasopressin makes collecting-duct cells insert aquaporin 2 into their apical membrane, which lets water return to the blood and concentrates the urine. You meet this in the course on organs and tissues.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Why it matters: SGLT2 inhibitors in diabetes and heart failure
text:
Why it matters: SGLT2 inhibitors in diabetes and heart failure


The kidneys filter about 180 g of glucose a day; SGLT2 in the proximal tubule takes back about 90 %, SGLT1 the rest. Above a blood glucose of about 10 mM the transporters saturate and glucose appears in urine.
Gliflozins (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) block SGLT2: glucose and some Na⁺ leave in the urine, and blood glucose falls in type 2 diabetes.
In large trials they also reduced heart failure and slowed kidney disease, even in people without diabetes. Exactly why is still studied.


Here the symporter from the gut slide becomes a drug target. The kidneys filter your blood plasma, about 180 litres a day, and with it about 180 grams of glucose. The proximal tubule takes nearly all of it back. The first part of the tubule uses SGLT2, a sodium–glucose symporter with one sodium per glucose, which takes about ninety percent; SGLT1 further along takes the rest. Basolateral GLUT2 lets glucose return to the blood, as in the gut. Remember saturation: when blood glucose is above about ten millimolar, the transporters are full and glucose spills into the urine. That is why untreated diabetes gives sweet urine. Gliflozins block SGLT2. The story started with phlorizin, a natural compound from apple tree bark known since the nineteenth century to cause glucose in the urine. A person on a gliflozin loses tens of grams of glucose a day in the urine, and blood glucose falls. Surprisingly, large clinical trials showed that these drugs also protect the heart and kidneys, even in people without diabetes. The mechanism is still debated. You meet trials like these in the course on clinical trials and drug development.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Why it matters: pumps as drug targets and drug barriers
text:
Why it matters: pumps as drug targets and drug barriers



Digoxin (from foxglove) blocks the Na⁺/K⁺ pump in heart muscle. Less Na⁺ gradient → the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger removes less Ca²⁺ → more Ca²⁺ → stronger contraction. Used in heart failure and atrial fibrillation; the safe dose range is narrow.
P-glycoprotein (ABCB1) pumps chemotherapy drugs out of cancer cells: multidrug resistance. In the gut, liver, kidney and blood–brain barrier it pumps drugs back out, which limits oral absorption and keeps many drugs out of the brain.
A tablet must cross the gut epithelium: by diffusion through lipid (small, lipophilic drugs) or on a transporter, while escaping P-glycoprotein. More in drug development (Kliniska prövningar och läkemedelsutveckling).



P-glycoprotein (mouse, PDB 3G5U). Lines: outer (blue) and inner (red) face of the membrane.


Foxglove, Digitalis. Its leaves contain digitalis glycosides.


Two more examples of transport and medicine. Foxglove extracts were used for heart failure as early as 1785, by William Withering in England. The active compounds are digitalis glycosides, such as digoxin; digoxin itself is mostly made from a related species, the woolly foxglove. They bind the sodium–potassium pump from outside, as ouabain does. In heart muscle a partly blocked pump lets sodium rise a little inside. The smaller sodium gradient means the sodium–calcium exchanger removes less calcium, more calcium is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and each beat is stronger. The difference between a helpful and a toxic dose is small, so levels are monitored. The second example is P-glycoprotein, the ABC exporter from earlier. Cancer cells that make a lot of it pump out many unrelated chemotherapy drugs, which is called multidrug resistance. In healthy tissue it sits on the gut side of intestinal cells and in brain capillaries, where it pumps drugs back out. The diarrhoea drug loperamide, an opioid, does not reach the brain because P-glycoprotein removes it. Drug developers test early whether a candidate is a P-glycoprotein substrate.

title: Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps
section: Summary
text:
Summary

A lipid bilayer lets small hydrophobic molecules through but blocks ions and most polar molecules; transport proteins give them a path.
Passive transport goes down the gradient (ΔG < 0); active transport goes up and must be coupled to ATP or to another gradient. Cells keep large, non-equilibrium gradients of Na⁺, K⁺ and Ca²⁺.
Channels are fast pores, always passive. Transporters bind their solute, work by alternating access, saturate like enzymes, and can be uniporters, symporters or antiporters.
Pumps use ATP directly: P-type (Na⁺/K⁺ pump, 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in; Ca²⁺ pumps), V-type (acidify organelles), ABC (export, including drugs); the F-type ATP synthase runs in reverse. The Na⁺ gradient drives secondary active transport.
Epithelia move solutes across the cell with different transporters on the apical and basolateral sides; drugs such as gliflozins and digoxin act on transporters, and P-glycoprotein pumps drugs away.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 11.
Image credits: credits

Five take-home points. First, the bilayer is a barrier to ions and polar molecules; only small hydrophobic molecules, and water slowly, cross on their own. Second, ΔG tells you whether transport can be passive, and cells keep large gradients of sodium, potassium and calcium that are not at equilibrium; they cost energy to maintain and are a store of energy to use. Third, transporters and channels are different machines: channels are fast and only passive, transporters bind their solute, alternate between outward-open and inward-open shapes, saturate like enzymes and can couple two solutes. Fourth, primary active transport uses ATP directly in P-type, V-type and ABC pumps, while secondary active transport spends the sodium gradient made by the sodium–potassium pump. Fifth, an epithelium combines these proteins on two sides of a cell to move glucose from gut to blood, and many drugs act on transporters or are limited by them. Next lecture: ion channels, where the same gradients produce the membrane potential.

title: Quiz: moving molecules across membranes
text:
Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture Moving molecules across membranes: transporters and pumps. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

Q1. Rank these by how fast they cross a pure lipid bilayer (no proteins), fastest first: glucose, O₂, Na⁺, water. [ELO 2]






Hint





Two things matter: size, and how well the molecule dissolves in the oily middle of the bilayer. A charge is the biggest obstacle.









Answer





O₂ > water > glucose > Na⁺. O₂ is small and hydrophobic and crosses fast. Water is small and uncharged, so it crosses, but more slowly. Glucose is larger and polar and crosses very slowly. Na⁺ is charged and surrounded by water molecules, so it practically does not cross (about 10⁹ times slower than water).




Q2. Na⁺ is about 12 mM inside a cell and 145 mM outside. K⁺ is about 140 mM inside and 5 mM outside. If you block all ATP production in a cell, what happens to these concentrations over time, and why? [ELO 2]






Hint





Are the gradients at equilibrium, or are they kept up by work?









Answer





The gradients run down: Na⁺ slowly rises inside and K⁺ falls. The gradients are a steady state, not an equilibrium: ions leak through the membrane all the time, and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to put them back. Without ATP the pump stops, but the leak continues.




Q3. Using \(\Delta G = RT\ln(c_\text{in}/c_\text{out})\) with \(RT \approx 2.6\) kJ/mol, estimate ΔG for moving glucose into a cell when glucose is 5 mM outside and 0.5 mM inside. Is this passive or active transport? [ELO 2]






Hint





\(\ln(0.1) \approx -2.3\).









Answer





\(\Delta G \approx 2.6 \times \ln(0.5/5) = 2.6 \times (-2.3) \approx -6\) kJ/mol. ΔG is negative, so glucose moves downhill: passive transport, for example by a GLUT uniporter. No energy input is needed.




Q4. You measure the initial rate of uptake of a radiolabelled amino acid into cells at many concentrations. The rate rises and then levels off at high concentration. What does this tell you about how the amino acid enters, and what do Vmax and Km mean here? [ELO 2]






Hint





Compare with Michaelis–Menten kinetics of an enzyme. What would simple diffusion through lipid look like?









Answer





Saturation means a transporter with a limited number of binding sites carries the amino acid; diffusion through lipid would rise linearly without a maximum. Vmax is the rate when all transporters are busy (it depends on how many transporters there are). Km is the concentration that gives half of Vmax; a low Km means high affinity.




Q5. Classify each as uniport, symport or antiport, and as passive, primary active or secondary active: (a) GLUT1; (b) SGLT1; (c) the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger; (d) the Na⁺/K⁺ pump. [ELO 2]






Hint





Does the protein use ATP itself? Does it move one solute or two, and in which directions?









Answer






GLUT1: uniport, passive. (b) SGLT1: symport (2 Na⁺ + 1 glucose, both inwards), secondary active. (c) Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger: antiport (Na⁺ in, Ca²⁺ out), secondary active. (d) Na⁺/K⁺ pump: antiport (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in), primary active: it hydrolyses ATP itself (P-type pump).





Q6. Why is the Na⁺/K⁺ pump called a P-type pump, and how many ions does it move per ATP? [ELO 2]






Hint





Where does the phosphate of ATP go during the cycle?









Answer





During its cycle the pump phosphorylates itself on an aspartate; this switches it from the inward-open to the outward-open shape. P stands for phosphorylation. Per ATP it moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in. One net positive charge leaves per cycle, so the pump is electrogenic.




Q7. In a gut epithelial cell, which transporter sits in the apical membrane and which in the basolateral membrane to absorb glucose? Why must they be in different membranes? [ELO 2]






Hint





One brings glucose into the cell uphill; the other lets it out downhill. What would happen if both were on the same side?









Answer





Apical: SGLT1 (Na⁺–glucose symporter), which takes glucose into the cell even against its gradient. Basolateral: GLUT2 (uniporter), which lets glucose leave down its gradient into the blood, plus the Na⁺/K⁺ pump to remove the Na⁺. If both transporters were on the same side, glucose would just go in and out on that side, and there would be no net movement across the cell. Tight junctions keep the two sets of proteins apart and seal the gaps between cells.




Q8. Gliflozins block SGLT2. What happens to glucose in the urine of a patient taking one, and why does this lower blood glucose? [ELO 2] [ELO 9]






Hint





Where in the body is SGLT2, and what does it normally do with filtered glucose?









Answer





SGLT2 in the proximal tubule of the kidney normally takes back about 90 % of the glucose filtered from the blood. When it is blocked, much of that glucose (tens of grams a day) stays in the tubule and leaves in the urine. The body loses glucose, so blood glucose falls. Some Na⁺ is lost too, because SGLT2 is a Na⁺–glucose symporter.

title: Study questions: seeing cells (microscopy)
section: G-level questions
text:
G-level questions
1. Explain the difference between magnification and resolution. Why can a light microscope not separate two objects that are 50 nm apart, however much it magnifies? [ELO 1]






Model answer





Magnification is how much bigger the image is than the object. Resolution is the smallest distance at which two points can still be seen as two. Light is a wave, so a lens turns each point of the sample into a small blur spot. When two points are closer than about \(0.61\,\lambda/\mathrm{NA}\), their blur spots merge into one. With visible light (about 500 nm) and the best objectives (NA about 1.4) this limit is about 200 nm. Two objects 50 nm apart give one blob, and magnifying the blob more adds no detail.




2. Describe how a phase-contrast microscope and a DIC microscope make living, unstained cells visible. Why is staining with dyes usually not an option for living cells? [ELO 1]






Model answer





Unstained cells absorb almost no light, but dense structures (nucleus, membranes) have a higher refractive index and slow light down (phase shift). Phase contrast converts these phase shifts into differences in brightness. DIC uses polarised light to turn gradients in optical path into light and shadow, so edges look three-dimensional. Most dyes for bright-field microscopy need the cells to be fixed and often sectioned, and many dyes are toxic, so stained cells are dead.




3. Draw and label the light path in an epifluorescence microscope with a filter cube for a green fluorophore. State what each filter and the dichroic mirror does. [ELO 1]






Model answer





Lamp → excitation filter (passes only blue light that excites the fluorophore) → dichroic mirror (reflects blue light down through the objective onto the sample) → fluorophore absorbs blue and emits green → green light goes back up through the objective → passes through the dichroic mirror (it transmits longer wavelengths) → emission filter (passes green, blocks stray blue) → camera or eye. The design works because of the Stokes shift: emitted light has a longer wavelength than the excitation light.




4. Describe the steps of indirect immunofluorescence to show where tubulin is in cultured cells. Why do we use a secondary antibody? [ELO 1] [ELO 6]






Model answer






Fix the cells (e.g. formaldehyde) so proteins are cross-linked and stay in place. 2. Permeabilise the membranes with a mild detergent so antibodies can enter. 3. Block free binding sites (e.g. with serum proteins) to reduce background. 4. Add the primary antibody against tubulin (e.g. made in mouse), wash. 5. Add a fluorescent secondary antibody against mouse antibodies, wash. 6. Often add a DNA dye (DAPI), mount and image. The secondary antibody amplifies the signal (several secondaries bind each primary), and one labelled secondary can be used with many different primaries from the same species.





5. What is GFP, why was it so useful for cell biology, and how is a GFP fusion protein made? [ELO 1] [ELO 6]






Model answer





GFP is the green fluorescent protein from the jellyfish Aequorea victoria. Its chain of 238 amino acids folds into a barrel and forms its fluorescent group by itself (it needs only oxygen), so the gene works in any cell. To make a fusion protein you join the coding sequence of the protein of interest to the GFP coding sequence in the same reading frame, without a stop codon between them, and introduce the DNA into cells. The cell makes one chain, protein–GFP, so you can see where the protein is in a living cell and follow it over time. Mutants of GFP and proteins from corals give other colours, so several proteins can be followed at once.




6. Explain how a confocal microscope gives sharper images of thick samples than a wide-field fluorescence microscope. What is the cost? [ELO 1]






Model answer





In wide-field fluorescence the whole depth of the sample is lit, so out-of-focus light adds haze. A confocal microscope focuses a laser spot in the sample and places a pinhole in front of the detector at the point where light from the focal plane is focused. Light from other depths is out of focus at the pinhole and mostly blocked. The spot is scanned to build the image. This gives a thin optical section (about 0.5–1 µm), and a stack of sections gives a 3D image. Costs: it is slower (point by point), and the sample receives more light, so there is more photobleaching and phototoxicity.




7. Name two problems you meet when you film living fluorescent cells for many hours, and one way to reduce each. [ELO 1]






Model answer





Photobleaching: fluorophores are destroyed by repeated excitation, so the signal fades. Phototoxicity: excited fluorophores make reactive oxygen species that damage the cell, so it may behave abnormally or die. Both are reduced by using less light (lower intensity, shorter exposures, fewer time points, a more sensitive camera) and gentler methods such as spinning-disk confocal or light-sheet microscopy, which light less of the sample. The cells must also be kept at 37 °C with the right CO₂ and medium.




8. Compare TEM and SEM: how is the image made, what does each show, and why can neither be used on living cells? [ELO 1]






Model answer





TEM: electrons pass through an ultrathin section (about 50–100 nm) stained with heavy metals; areas that scatter electrons look dark. It shows internal structure (membranes, organelles, ribosomes) at about 1–2 nm. SEM: a fine beam scans a metal-coated sample, and electrons knocked out of the surface are detected. It shows the 3D surface at a few nm. Both work in a vacuum, so samples are fixed and dried (and for TEM embedded and cut), which kills the cells.




9. What is single-particle cryo-EM? Explain why averaging many images is needed and what the result is. [ELO 1]






Model answer





A purified protein or complex is frozen so quickly that water forms glass-like ice, keeping the molecules in their native, hydrated shape without stain. Only a low electron dose can be used, so each image of a single molecule is very noisy. A computer finds tens of thousands to millions of particle images, sorts them by viewing angle and averages them, so noise cancels and the signal remains. The 2D views are combined into a 3D density map, often at better than 0.3 nm, into which an atomic model is built.

title: Study questions: seeing cells (microscopy)
section: VG-style questions
text:
VG-style questions
10. [VG] A research group makes a GFP fusion of a newly discovered protein, P. In living cells, P–GFP is spread evenly through the cytosol. But immunofluorescence with an antibody against P in fixed cells shows P on mitochondria. Give two possible explanations, and propose an experiment to decide between them. [ELO 1]






Model answer





Possible explanations:

The GFP tag disturbs targeting. If P has a mitochondrial targeting signal at its N-terminus and GFP was fused there, the signal may be hidden; or the fusion is overexpressed so much that the import machinery is saturated and the excess stays in the cytosol.
The antibody is not specific. It may bind another, mitochondrial protein, so the immunofluorescence result is wrong.
(Also acceptable) Fixation artefact: soluble proteins can be extracted or moved during fixation and permeabilisation.

Experiments: put GFP at the other end of P and express it at low level (e.g. from the gene’s own promoter, or by tagging the endogenous gene with CRISPR); check if it then goes to mitochondria (co-stain with a mitochondrial marker). Test the antibody on cells lacking P (knockout or knockdown): if mitochondria are still stained, the antibody is not specific. Biochemistry can add independent evidence: fractionate cells and test which fraction contains P on a western blot (next lecture).




11. [VG] You want to know (a) how often vesicles carrying a GFP-tagged cargo move along microtubules in living cells, and (b) whether the cargo sits inside the vesicle or on its outer membrane. Design an imaging approach for each part, and explain why one method cannot answer both. [ELO 1] [ELO 6]






Model answer






Live-cell fluorescence imaging of the GFP-cargo, ideally with microtubules labelled in a second colour (e.g. a red fluorescent tubulin fusion), using a fast, gentle method (spinning-disk confocal or light-sheet) and short exposures to limit bleaching and phototoxicity. Track vesicles over time and count runs along microtubules. Control: a drug that depolymerises microtubules should stop the directed runs.
A vesicle is about 50–100 nm across, below the 200 nm light limit, so inside versus outside cannot be decided with ordinary light microscopy. Use immuno-electron microscopy: fix cells, label the cargo (anti-GFP antibody with gold particles) on thin sections, and see whether the gold is in the lumen or on the cytosolic face of the vesicle membrane. Cryo-electron tomography or super-resolution would also help.

One method cannot do both because live imaging needs light microscopy (low resolution, living cells), while the nanometre question needs EM (high resolution, but dead or frozen cells). Combining them on the same cells is called correlative light and electron microscopy (CLEM).




12. [VG] Explain why the SARS-CoV-2 spike in the mRNA COVID-19 vaccines carries two extra prolines (the “2P” spike), and why cryo-EM was a good method to check this design quickly. [ELO 1]






Model answer





The spike is a fusion protein: it starts in a compact prefusion shape and, when it fuses the viral and cell membranes, S1 is lost and S2 refolds into a long postfusion rod. Many protective (neutralising) antibodies recognise the prefusion shape, but a spike made on its own can flip to the postfusion form. Two prolines, which are stiff, placed at a hinge in S2 block this refolding and keep the prefusion shape, so the immune system sees the right target. The idea came from structures of related coronavirus spikes (MERS, SARS). Cryo-EM was ideal because the spike is a large, flexible, glycosylated membrane-protein trimer that is hard to crystallise; cryo-EM needs only a small amount of purified protein, no crystals, and keeps it in a near-native state. In early 2020 a cryo-EM structure confirmed within weeks that the SARS-CoV-2 2P spike holds the prefusion shape.

title: Study questions: seeing cells (microscopy)
section: Explore
text:
Explore
Two glowing points (for example two fluorescent molecules) seen through a microscope. The lens turns each point into a blur spot with faint rings (an Airy pattern); the camera sees the sum of the two spots. The graph below the image shows the brightness along the line through both points: the dashed curves are the two single spots, the solid curve is what the camera records. Change the distance \(d\) between the points (slider, or drag on the image), the wavelength \(\lambda\) and the numerical aperture NA, or switch to electrons. The readout gives the Rayleigh limit \(0.61\,\lambda/\mathrm{NA}\) and the depth of the dip between the two peaks.



E1. Start with green light (520 nm) and the oil objective (NA 1.4), \(d = 300\) nm. Move the points slowly together. At what distance does the readout say you reach the Rayleigh limit? Check it with the formula. How deep is the dip there, and at about what distance does the dip disappear completely? [ELO 1]
E2. Set \(d = 250\) nm. Try the three objectives: dry 10× (NA 0.25), dry 40× (NA 0.65) and oil 100× (NA 1.4). Which of them separate the two points? What is the limit for each? [ELO 1]
E3. [VG] Predict first, then check. Keep \(d = 250\) nm and NA 1.4. Will the two points be resolved in red light (650 nm)? In blue light (450 nm)? Then explain why a light microscope cannot be improved much further by choosing a shorter wavelength or a better lens. [ELO 1]
E4. [VG] Switch to Electrons (TEM). The wavelength is about 100 000 times shorter than green light. What is the limit with a 10 mrad aperture, and why is it much larger than the wavelength? Why do electron micrographs of cells still show only about 1–2 nm detail? [ELO 1]






Solutions





E1. The limit is \(0.61 \times 520 / 1.4 \approx 227\) nm. At that distance the first dark ring of one spot falls on the centre of the other, and the solid curve has a dip of about 26 % between the two peaks: just enough to see two spots. Closer, the dip becomes shallower and disappears at about 175 nm (about \(0.47\,\lambda/\mathrm{NA}\), the Sparrow limit); below that the camera records one blob, and no magnification can split it again.
E2. The limits are about 1270 nm (NA 0.25), 490 nm (NA 0.65) and 227 nm (NA 1.4). Only the oil objective separates points 250 nm apart. A lens with a higher NA collects light from a wider cone, which makes the blur spot smaller.
E3. Red light: limit \(0.61 \times 650 / 1.4 \approx 283\) nm, larger than 250 nm, so not resolved (a faint dip only). Blue light: \(0.61 \times 450 / 1.4 \approx 196\) nm, so resolved. Shorter wavelengths help, but visible light stops at about 400 nm (shorter UV light damages cells and is absorbed by glass). NA \(= n \sin\theta\) cannot exceed the refractive index of the oil and glass (about 1.5), because \(\sin\theta \le 1\). So the limit for a light microscope stays near 200 nm. Super-resolution methods get around it by making neighbouring molecules glow at different times, not by a better lens.
E4. \(0.61 \times 0.0037 / 0.01 \approx 0.23\) nm. The limit is about 60 times the wavelength because electron lenses have large errors (aberrations), so only electrons travelling at a very small angle can be used: the NA is about 0.01 instead of 1.4. In cells, the sample sets the limit: the section is fixed, stained with heavy metals and about 50–100 nm thick, and the stain grains and the overlapping material in the section blur the detail to about 1–2 nm. Purified proteins imaged frozen (cryo-EM) get much closer to the lens limit.

Credits: 15 ECTS
Education level: First cycle
Main fields of study: Molecular Biology; Biomedical Sciences (both first cycle, less than 60 credits of first-cycle courses as entry requirements)
Grading scale: Three-grade scale (U / G / VG)
Responsible department: Department of Molecular Biology
Established: by PRBMT, 2025-10-27
Validity: 2027-01-18 and until further notice
First run: spring 2027, 18 January to 24 March 2027, on campus in Umeå, taught in English





Theory. Fundamental theory in modern molecular cell biology. This site covers this module.
PPT: Working Life and Career. Oral presentations, seminar discussions, problem solving, a poster on a biomedical problem for a commissioning party, and projects as a working method.
Laboratory Work. Cell biology methods: planning and running experiments, analysing and presenting data, writing results in scientific form.




Knowledge and Understanding. The student should be able to:

Describe the structure and function of the cell and explain methods used to study cell biological processes.
Explain the structure and function of cell membranes and the principles of membrane transport.
Describe fundamental principles of cell communication and signal transduction.
Describe how proteins are handled and regulated in the cell.
Compare the structure and function of different organelles and explain their roles in cellular homeostasis.
Explain the basis of cell shape, motility, and intracellular transport, and give examples of methods used to study these processes.
Describe the regulation of the cell cycle and the mechanisms of cell division.
Describe different forms of programmed cell death and their regulation.
Explain basic concepts of cell biological disease mechanisms.

Skills and Abilities. The student should be able to:

Present scientific content orally in a clear and structured manner.
Collaborate in groups to solve cell biological problems and communicate the results effectively.
Participate in structured scientific discussions and critically reflect on theoretical and practical content.
Plan and conduct basic experiments in cell biology.
Apply good laboratory practice and follow established protocols.
Analyze and present experimental data in written form.
Interpret results and draw conclusions based on scientific principles.
Demonstrate skills and the ability to identify, formulate, and propose solutions to a problem relevant to the education, based on labor market needs
Demonstrate the ability to define and describe projects as a working method.

Judgement and Approach. The student should be able to:

Identify one’s own learning needs and take responsibility for further learning




20 ECTS in chemistry, of which at least 5 ECTS in biochemistry (or 20 ECTS in chemistry combined with physics and/or mathematics, of which at least 5 ECTS in biochemistry); 20 ECTS in biology, including microbiology, molecular biology and genetics.



Lectures plus student-centred teaching: interactive seminars, case-based learning and practical work. All teaching except lectures is mandatory. Lab work requires knowing the lab safety rules and basic GLP. Taught in English (Swedish if no participant needs English).

How the written exam is built (this shapes the course material):

The exam has one section per ELO (1–9). To pass an ELO, at least 60 % of its questions must be correct. All nine ELOs must be passed.
Each ELO has one VG question, marked G or VG. Exam VG = at least 5 of the 9 VG questions at VG.
A student who passes at least 6 ELOs but not the whole exam may take a group oral exam (assessed individually) on the failed ELOs, or retake the full exam.
Course VG = all mandatory parts done + written exam at VG.




Not published online. The department uses Molecular Biology of the Cell (Alberts et al.). Students should not have to read the book to follow this course; each lecture ends with optional chapter pointers.
